News.title: Benefit claimants warned they could face TOUGHER rules to keep cash as PM vows he’s ‘serious’ about cutting welfare bill
News.content:
BENEFIT OF DOUBT Benefit claimants warned they could face TOUGHER rules to keep cash as PM vows he’s ‘serious’ about cutting welfare bill

ANDY Burnham has warned benefits claimants they could face tougher rules as he vowed to get “serious” about cutting the welfare bill.

The new PM signalled a benefits crackdown by suggesting people may have to meet stricter conditions to keep receiving benefits.



In his first major interview since entering No10, Mr Burnham said some claimants could be required to take up work opportunities if they wanted to keep receiving support.

He insisted there were people who could get back into work “with the right support”.



Mr Burnham told the BBC: “It’s about changing the nature of the support and making some of the support conditional upon people taking opportunities that are presented in front of them.

“So you might increase the conditions required to receive benefits.



“I think it’s a good thing that the government has given guarantees of opportunities for young people.

“And I think we need to continue down that approach and where mental health support is needed, for instance, it’s provided in work to support people in an opportunity.”

He added: “Let me just say something more though, about you’re driving at, which is the welfare bill. I think we’ve got to get really serious as a country at getting the welfare down.”

But the Labour leader insisted he did not “go straight to blaming” people claiming benefits.



Instead, he argued many young people had been “quite seriously let down” because they had not received the support they needed while growing up.

The comments come after Labour’s welfare reforms descended into chaos after a backbench rebellion under Sir Keir Starmer last year.

Mr Burnham is now under pressure to tackle Britain’s ballooning benefits bill, with Sir Alan Milburn’s review warning more than one million young people are not in education, employment or training and a separate review under way into the disability benefits system.

Sir Alan’s final recommendations are due this autumn.

Elsewhere during the interview, the PM also issued a stark warning over the future of the NHS.



He said the health service would “collapse” unless Britain finally fixes the country’s social care system.

Mr Burnham vowed to spend “whatever political capital I have” on reforming social care but he stopped short of promising to deliver a new system before the next general election.

Pressed on whether he would do so, he said: “I can’t put a timeline on it right here, right now.”

He added: “If we don’t do it, the NHS will collapse under the weight of trying to care for people who’ve really not needed to end up in the NHS system.”

News.title: Police forces spent eye-watering £631m on diversity and equality since murder of George Floyd, says report
News.content:
COP COSTS Police forces spent eye-watering £631m on diversity and equality since murder of George Floyd, says report

Credit: Getty

POLICE forces have spent a whopping £631million on diversity, equality and inclusion programmes since the murder of George Floyd, according to a new report.

The cash could have funded around 2,000 extra frontline officers every year or 8.3 million hours of policing, according to Policy Exchange.



The think tank says the spending came after the introduction of a national Police Race Action Plan after Floyd’s death in Minneapolis in 2020, with nearly three-quarters of UK forces later adopting their own local versions.

It found 87 per cent of forces now have “anti-racist” commitments in their plans, while 58 per cent focus primarily on Black communities.



Policy Exchange says the changes have eroded the principle of policing “without fear or favour” and left officers at risk of treating people differently based on their race.

It comes after two Hampshire officers were placed under investigation over the death of Henry Nowak, who was handcuffed as he lay dying after his killer falsely accused him of carrying out a racist attack.

David Spencer, a former Metropolitan Police detective chief inspector and the report’s author, said: “Police forces have sought to entrench the radical ideology of ‘anti-racism’ into British policing.

“In doing so some police chiefs have set policing against its own foundational principle – to act ‘without fear or favour’.”

Chief Constable Rachel Kearton, chair of the NPCC’s Diversity, Equality and Inclusion Committee, insisted the spending represented “a very small proportion” of the policing budget.

She added: “Improving culture and inclusion is not separate from frontline delivery, it underpins it.



Investment in this area also supports forces in meeting their legal responsibilities.”

News.title: Dramatic moment huge cargo ship sinks in Black Sea as Putin’s armed forces launch strike that ‘killed 10’
News.content:
THIS is the moment a cargo ship sinks in the Black Sea after a deadly Russian missile attack left 10 dead.

Footage shows a suspected dry cargo ship capsizing in Odesa Bay after taking heavy damage from Russian strikes targeting Ukrainian supplies.



The strike comes apart of a wider escalation as Russia retaliates against Ukrainian drone attacks that targeted 200 of its “shadow fleet” of tankers and cargo vessels.

The sunken vessel was reportedly holed several days ago but eventually succumbed to the damage on Sunday.



As the vessel keels over, its massive red-painted hull is exposed before it plunges deeper into the water.

Some Ukrainian outlets identified the stricken vessel as the Turkish-flagged Golden Leo which was likely carrying grain supplies.



The vessel was struck by three Kh-59/Kh-69 cruise missiles while leaving the port in Odesa on July 19, according to reports.

It is understood one of the missiles hit the superstructure on the starboard side after which a fire broke out on the ship.



Ten people were killed as a result.

Eight sailors were evacuated and taken to hospitals.

Another vessel hit in the strike was the AGN Ragnar, a Palau-flagged ship with almost 2,800 tonnes of corn on board.

The Ukrainian pilot and seven crew members were rescued but two Indian sailors are missing after reportedly being thrown into the sea on impact.

Ukrainian officials have previously condemned Russian strikes on grain vessels as potential war crimes.



Russia has stepped up attacks in recent weeks on deepwater ports in southern Ukraine ⁠that ​handle much of the country’s ​grain and other critical cargo.

The retaliations haven’t been limited to the sea – Russia unleashed a 40-minute barrage of ballistic missiles on Kyiv overnight on July 18.

It was one of the most intense blitzes of the war so far.

The action sparked dozens of fires, killed one person and wounded 40.

Among the targets were civilian homes, office buildings, a metro station and a key logistics hub linked to Ukraine‘s armed forces.

News.title: Freeview switch-off could leave Britain dangerously exposed if the internet goes down, ministers warn
News.content:
BRITAIN risks being dangerously exposed if the internet goes down under Government plans to cut off Freeview, ministers have been warned.

The National Preparedness Commission (NPC) said terrestrial television should be protected until at least 2044 over fears using the web alone could cut off the most vulnerable.



A new report concludes that the “tall tower” network carrying digital TV is an asset the UK cannot afford to weaken.

It comes as ministers decide whether to turn off Freeview in 2034 or 2044, and rely on internet streaming services.



The Sun’s Save Our Sets campaign has warned that pensioners and families will be forced to pay for faster broadband on top of the licence fee if terrestrial signals are cut off.

The NPC report found that broadband routers go down immediately after losing power, while TV and DAB radio transmitter sites can stay online for days or even weeks.



It would ensure information could be transmitted to Brits in a national emergency even if the internet had gone down.

The paper adds that the costs of an early switch-off would fall hardest on rural areas with poor broadband connections and few fallback options.

Nigel Huddleston MP, Shadow Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport, said: “It is a fundamental security concern if we lose our emergency broadcasting capability in the event of a cyber attack or internet outage.

“We cannot risk being so vulnerable in these highly uncertain times.”



Lord Toby Harris, who is chairman of the National Preparedness Commission, said: “The UK’s tall tower network is a sovereign, resilient asset that reaches almost every household and supports radio, emergency services and critical infrastructure.

“Protecting terrestrial broadcasting until at least 2044 would preserve a vital, independent route for trusted public information when it is needed most.”

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy last week hinted that ministers would settle on the 2044 date, admitting many believed the earlier switch-off “isn’t possible”.

News.title: Man arrested after ‘stealing 44 bottles of fine wine’ from house evacuated during horror wildfires in France
News.content:
A MAN has been arrested for allegedly breaking into an evacuated house and making off with 44 bottles of fine wine during horror wildfires.

More than 220,000 people have been forced to flee their homes as wildfires ravage southwestern France.



Two huge infernos are ripping towards Bordeaux, with tourists warned to stay away or get out of the region if they’ve already arrived.

Yet as hundreds of thousands flee their homes, authorities are having to step in to stop mass opportunistic break-ins.





One man was arrested in Eysines, Gironde on suspicion of burglary.

Police said the man was stopped in front of an empty home at around 6.15pm on Saturday.

When cops searched his car they found 44 bottles of the finest plonk stowed away inside.

The suspect – already known to police – was arrested and taken into custody.



The arrest comes as French authorities are ready to evacuate the entire city of Bordeaux – “erratic” fire whirlwinds are sending flames ripping towards its nearly one million residents.

Two major wildfires have broken out west of the city and “overwhelmed” firefighters are “far from” bringing the blazes under control.

Local official Sophie Brocas told holidaymakers to stay away and to pack their bags if they have already arrived.



She said: “We urge tourists not to come to this region, at least until the situation is under control.

“I encourage tourists who are already here to consider another destination.”

More than 300,000 people in France and Spain have been forced to flee their homes as fires fuelled by tinder-box conditions and strong winds continue to rage.

Firefighters battling the encroaching blaze in the Gironde area are said to be “overwhelmed” as concerns grow about Bordeaux.

Head Gironde firefighter Sebastien Berge said: “When there’s a fire of this magnitude, it creates its own weather pattern…it’s difficult to monitor.



“Especially when there’s a fire front that stretches for more than 20km (12.5 miles).”

Thousands of evacuees in the area have already been forced to bed down in an exhibition hall as they face an anxious wait over the state of their homes.

Residents and tourists were forced to flee the holiday hotspot Cap Ferret in their droves on Friday as the inferno took hold.

The French military has even been deployed to help battle the blazes.

Meanwhile in Spain, where a national emergency has been declared, favourable weather conditions have helped firefighters in their fight against merging fires outside Madrid.

But Spanish PM Pedro Sánchez conceded there were “complex times ahead”.

A man, believed to be in his 70s, was found dead in his car by firefighters as they extinguished a blaze in Valencia.

News.title: Mystery as decision to charge arthritic 5ft 5in woman, 72, with murder of ‘love rival’ Brit expat stuns French village
News.content:
THE idyllic, honey-bricked Dordogne village of Tremolat has twice been the backdrop for murder.

Eerily, local mother-of-three Marie-Laure Autefort, 70 — a divorced former nurse — has a connection to both.



In 1969, she had a walk-on part in cult horror movie The Butcher, the fictional tale of a woman’s corpse being discovered with multiple blade wounds.

Today, she is centre stage after being charged with the real-life murder of British-South African expat Karen Carter who, in April last year, was discovered bleeding to death after being stabbed eight times.



It has left close-knit Tremolat in deep shock, with many locals perplexed that Marie-Laure is now a prime suspect.

Could a woman of her years, standing less than 5ft 5in tall, who friends say has high blood pressure and severe osteoarthritis in her hands, have the strength and guile to commit such a savage murder?



After all, one of the blade blows almost severed Karen’s arm, while another pierced her kidney and reached her spine.

And was this ferocious assault really a crime of jealousy and passion as investigators now seem to believe?

Many in remote Tremolat — population 600 — had thought Karen’s ­clinical slaying must have been the work of a hired assassin.

In a crime that appears to have been meticulously planned and executed, the murderer arrived and left the scene undetected.



No murder weapon has been found despite fingertip searches, and ­forensic investigators seem to have drawn a blank.

One local said last week: “I’ve always said it was a hit job and I can’t see how they have a case against her [Marie-Laure], but ­perhaps they might have some hard evidence we aren’t aware of.”

Born in South Africa to parents originally from Preston, Lancashire, Karen Carter had intended to see out her years in slow-paced Tremolat.

An attractive brunette of 65 who kept trim playing over-50s football, she and her husband of 30 years, Alan, had first visited the pretty French village from their South African home in 2008.

Karen instantly fell in love with its 12th century charms.



They bought and did up Les Chouettes, a 250-year-old cottage and barn, which Karen managed as holiday lets in summer.

Shortly after his wife’s murder, South African Alan, 66, said: “One of the reasons we bought this property was that Karen had previously been diagnosed with breast cancer and had fought so hard to survive that.

“When we came to the village for the first time, Karen immediately loved it so much that I wanted to make that dream possible.”



Alan, who runs an environmental consultancy and formerly worked at the London Stock Exchange, was keen to keep their base in the South African coastal city of East London, renamed KuGompo City this year.

Yet Karen, who was enamoured with the delights of French rural life, preferred to remain in Tremolat.

The couple — who have four grown- up children, the eldest from Karen’s previous marriage — were soon spending time apart on different continents.

Karen volunteered at Cafe Village, a vibrant community hub and bar, where well-heeled French retirees, British expats and locals mingled over wine and music.

A framed poster of horror flick The Butcher — a claim to fame for Tremolat — hangs on the wall inside the bar.



The movie had portrayed the village as outwardly peaceful and respectable — but with a secret, dark undercurrent.

Another volunteer at the cafe was Paris-born Jean-Francois Guerrier, 75, a retired executive at IT firm Fujitsu.

He and Karen began an affair.

Clutching glasses of wine, the pair were seen dancing and singing to Gloria Gaynor’s I Will Survive in a video posted on the cafe’s Facebook page in December 2024.

However, another woman was also said to hold a candle for urbane Jean-Francois — and that was Marie-Laure Autefort.



Born into a local farming family, she had become infatuated with the retired businessman.

A one-time nurse and carer, she landed her role as an extra in The Butcher aged 12, when filmmakers arrived in the village.

Marie-Laure appeared in a funeral scene where firefighters sprayed the crowd with hoses to make it look like it was raining.



A keen local historian and “intensely proud” of her roots in the village, she has co-authored a book on Tremolat’s history and curated an exhibition of old photos of the place.

It is unclear if she was resentful of wealthy outsiders like Karen who had moved into the village in the years since The Butcher was filmed.

What is certain is her obsessive infatuation with Jean-Francois.

Her brother, retired fireman Philippe Monribot, revealed last year: “She made no secret of the fact she was in love with Guerrier. She was telling everyone in Tremolat, ‘I love him, I love him’.

“He took her to see the chateaux of the Loire Valley, to Paris, to fancy restaurants and so on. She had very little money and fell in love with him — and as soon as he realised that, he bailed on her.”



Others in the village insist it was a one-sided infatuation and accuse Marie-Laure of being a “fantasist”.

Despite Tremolat’s intimate size, Karen is said to have knowingly clapped eyes on Marie-Laure only once, although she was well aware of her existence.

A close friend of the guest house owner said last week that they crossed paths at Cafe Village just six days before the murder.

Jean-Francois was also present.

It was a Wednesday, when the Dordogne Chippy fish-and-chip van visits the bar, and there is music and dancing.



Karen’s friend said: “We hadn’t seen Marie-Laure at Cafe Village for over a year. We were amazed when she turned up with a group of about six friends. She didn’t come over, but Karen picked up on the tense atmosphere. She said, ‘What is it?’.

“I told her Marie-Laure was there and she asked me to point her out. It was common knowledge Marie-Laure was in love with Jean-Francois. She was shouting it from the rooftops.”

Five days later, Karen had dinner with her best friend in the village, Beverly Needham.



Originally from Manchester, Beverly, 69, said last year: “She brought wine, she always did, and I can’t bring myself to move the bottle from where she left it in the kitchen.”

That night, Karen told her friend she had served divorce papers on Alan.

Beverly revealed: “She told me the relationship was over and said, ‘I’m done’ . . . That was her words.”

Alan has subsequently denied Karen filed for divorce and believed the marriage was salvageable.

He had suspected Karen and Jean-Francois were having an affair, but his wife had denied it.



He later revealed: “I told her the gossip was tarnishing her reputation, but she said there was nothing in it. She told our friends the same.”

On April 29, 2025 — the evening after Beverly and Karen’s dinner — Jean-Francois held a wine tasting at his hilltop property on the outskirts of Tremolat.

The 15 guests, including Karen, left around 10pm. Karen — who had turned 65 two days before — drove her Dacia Duster the five minutes to her Les Chouettes guest house. It was a mild, overcast evening.

A light wind rippled through the walnut trees around the property.

Karen exited the vehicle, opened the front door and turned on the light.



Returning to the Dacia, she leaned into the back seat to pick up her crossbreed puppy, Haku.

The killer then emerged from the shadows and launched into a “frenzied” assault with what the police believe was a long-bladed knife.

Karen’s body was found soon after by distraught Jean-Francois, who had come to spend the night with her.



He later told a friend it was a scene of “just gore”.

A day later, cops arrested Marie- Laure and questioned her for around 40 hours.

She was released without charge after giving a credible alibi.

For the next 14 months, the investigation seemed to be going nowhere.

Marie-Laure’s brother Philippe said cops had turned up at his house on the edge of the village with a search warrant on five separate occasions as they hunted for the murder weapon.



Tremolat-born, police hoped he could guide them in a search of nearby caves. Nothing was found.

Now, it has emerged Marie-Laure was charged with Karen’s murder on July 2 after “inconsistencies” were found in her alibi.

An investigating source said: “She made out she was looking after somebody that night, but the facts were very vague.”

Marie-Laure denies any wrongdoing. She was released on bail on the condition she doesn’t stay in Tremolat.

A friend says the osteoarthritis in her hands has left her “barely able to cut open an envelope”, let alone wield a blade.



Philippe said it was “impossible” to imagine his sister could be involved in murder, adding she was “scared of going out in the dark”.

Prosecutors have not ruled out further arrests.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

An investigating source told The Sun there was “the possibility the suspect may have been working with someone else — somebody who was a lot stronger and fitter”.

Meanwhile, idyllic Tremolat will be under a dark pall until whoever killed Karen Carter is behind bars.

News.title: Man dies & one taken to hospital after ‘getting into difficulty’ in sea at popular UK beach
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

SEASIDE TRAGEDY Man dies & one taken to hospital after ‘getting into difficulty’ in sea at popular UK beach

A MAN has died after getting into difficulty while in the sea at a popular UK beach.

Emergency services rushed to the coast near Pound Road near West Wittering beach at around 2.30pm on Sunday.



The force pulled two men out from the sea and sadly pronounced one dead at the scene, while the other was taken to hospital.

A West Wittering Beach spokesperson said: “Our thoughts and sincere condolences are with the man’s family, friends and all those affected by this tragic incident.



“We would like to thank our lifeguards, emergency service colleagues and members of the public who assisted during the response.”

Sussex Police were called to the area following reports of two men getting into difficulty in the sea near the Beach Café.



A police spokesperson said: “Both were pulled from the sea and received treatment from emergency services at the scene.

“Sadly, one of the men was pronounced dead at the scene.

“The other man has been taken to hospital as a precaution.

“Next of kin have been informed and the matter has been passed to the coroner’s officer.”



Pictures taken from the beach show coastguard and ambulance vehicles parked up next to the water.

It is believed the men did not know each other.

They were given medical treatment at the scene.

The family of the deceased person has been informed.

News.title: I’ll quit if Burnham fails to find billions to rebuild Britain’s Armed Forces, vows new Defence Sec Wes Streeting
News.content:
DEFENCE Secretary Wes Streeting yesterday vowed to quit if PM Andy Burnham fails to stump up the billions needed to rebuild Britain’s Armed Forces.

The Cabinet minister said fully funding Labour’s Defence Investment Plan was a “matter of principle” and said he would resign if the money failed to materialise.



The Government must plug a £4.7billion black hole in the plan over the next five years, on top of finding £10.3billion of savings from elsewhere across Whitehall.

Mr Streeting insisted that the DIP “will be fully funded” with Chancellor John Healey expected to set out the specifics at future fiscal events.



It comes as Mr Burnham refused to commit to lifting defence spending to three per cent of GDP.

He told the BBC his “first challenge” was making sure the DIP was fully-funded ahead of the Budget, but would not give an answer to when exactly Britain would reach the three per cent target.



Mr Healey long championed the demand himself before he entered the Treasury.

He quit as Sir Keir Starmer’s Defence Secretary over the failure to stick to a firm timetable for the key spending target.

The Office for Budget Responsibility has estimated reaching three per cent by the end of the decade would cost an extra £17.3billion a year.

Meanwhile, Mr Streeting backed Donald Trump’s calls for Europe to shoulder more of the burden for its own security — but insisted the Government would not “suck up” to the US President.



Mr Burnham also said he would put the UK’s interests first in dealings with Mr Trump, even if it means disagreeing with him.

News.title: UK issued urgent wildfire warning as fourth heatwave to bring scorching temperatures
News.content:
UK issued urgent wildfire warning as fourth heatwave to bring scorching temperatures

First responders fear parts of the UK have become a tinderbox this summer, with arid conditions set to continue as the mercury rises, creating a perfect storm for fires

View 4 Images (Image: RSPB Scotland/PA Wire)

First responders are bracing themselves for another week of wildfires as a fourth summer heatwave looms, days after some of the UK's most arid areas missed out on some much-needed rain.

‌



Northern and western regions of the United Kingdom saw some rainfall over the weekend, with further showers and unsettled conditions expected over the next few days in some places. But in the south, where the least amount of rain has fallen as once green grass turns dry and brittle, temperatures are set to climb once more.

‌



More dry and sunny weather is on its way in the south, with the mercury thought to peak at around 35C in parts of south-east England. The fourth heatwave also comes off the back of wildifires across the country, and even a drought declaration in Wales.

‌



Parts of southern, central and eastern England remain in a state of "prolonged dry weather", the final status mark before a drought is officially declared.

View 4 Images Another heatwave is coming (Image: © SWNS)

A far-reaching yellow heat health alert has been issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), which carries a warning of possible “significant impacts” on health and social care services, including a rise in deaths among the elderly, the vulnerable, and people with health conditions.

‌



In addition, fires, if they start, are likely to become exceptionally severe on Wednesday in pockets of the east, south, and south-east England, according to Met Office data used by Natural England and Natural Resources Wales.

The “exceptionally severe” warnings focus on eastern England on Thursday.

The Fire Severity Index looks at data including rainfall, temperature and humidity and agencies use it to assess the severity of fire if it starts. It does not cover the chances of wildfires occurring.

‌



View 4 Images Brits will be heading for the beaches as another heatwave arrives (file) (Image: Getty Images)

Emergency crews have already spent days fighting large wildfires in Wales and Scotland that forced people to evacuate from their homes.

A National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC) spokesperson said: “With the Met Office warning that a fourth heatwave could develop this week, bringing another period of very hot weather to parts of the UK, fire and rescue services remain on alert and are continuing to prepare for renewed wildfire risk.”

‌



Battling nearly 20 wildfires at once demonstrates “the scale of the challenge posed by the prolonged hot, dry conditions”, they added.

“Most wildfires are preventable and we are asking everyone to play their part in helping to protect our communities, wildlife and natural spaces, while easing the pressure on firefighters who have already faced an exceptionally challenging summer.”

Temperatures cooled, winds picked up and a smattering of rain fell for many during the weekend.

‌



But parts of southern England will yet again meet their heatwave criteria on Wednesday, which could reach highs of 32C or 33C, and more will on Thursday.

At the height of the third heatwave, in mid-July, firefighters were battling 19 significant wildfires simultaneously in England and Wales.

View 4 Images UK weather maps show 39C heatwave and hottest day of year as 10 counties hit 38C (Image: WXCHARTS)

‌



The latest update on the impending heatwave comes as a Met Office meteorologist said UK heatwave thresholds will need to be adjusted to take into account the warming climate, which has seen temperature records repeatedly broken this year.

Forecasters are expecting this week’s hot spell to be a “north-south split”, with clouds and outbreaks of rain continuing in Northern Ireland, Scotland and northern England.

As per senior Met Office meteorologist Dan Stroud, July was 3C above average across the UK, according to provisional Met Office data on the month so far. This could put it among the hottest three or four months of July on record, said Stroud.

‌



Fellow senior Met Office meteorologist Marco Petagna added that heatwave thresholds for some counties were nudged up by a degree four or five years ago. “Going forward they’ll need to be adjusted to take into account… current climate, otherwise we’re going to more frequently go into heatwaves. It’s a moveable thing, really, as we go through a warming world”, he said.

Southern England has had just one per cent of its average July rainfall. England has had five per cent and the UK as a whole 20 per cent, according to Met Office data.

Where will the Yellow Heat-health strike?
