News.title: Andy Burnham makes heartbreaking dog decision to protect Larry the cat
News.content:
Andy Burnham makes heartbreaking dog decision to protect Larry the cat

Andy Burnham has revealed his pet dog Axel will remain in the north because he has 'that angry little man thing going on' and might end up scrapping with Larry the cat

View 3 Images Andy Burnham with his pet dog Axel, who he adopted in 2017 (Image: X/@andyburnham)

Andy Burnham has revealed his pet dog will not be travelling back and forth between London and Manchester now he's PM.

‌



The Prime Minister has owned rescue dog Axel since 2017. But in an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg, he described the bichon poo – a cross between a bichon frisé and a poodle - as having "that angry little man thing going on". He said he was worried his pet would clash with Downing Street mouser Larry the cat - and the nation would not thank him if the two clashed.

‌



It means Axel, who was adopted through the Dog Trust, will remain up north - but with the PM working from No10 North at least once a week, he will still get quality time with his owner.

‌



Ms Kuenssberg asked: "I don't know what is with this country's obsession with politicians' pets, but you have a family dog, Axel Burnham."

Streeting backs Burnham to sort out Britain's social care crisis with dig at Starmer READ MORE :

200 refugee charities call for end of asylum 'gimmicks' in letter to Andy Burnham READ MORE :

View 3 Images Mr Burnham said the nation would not thank him if Axel started scrapping with Larry (Image: Getty Images)

Mr Burnham interruped to describe him as "Famous Axel". The BBC journalist asked whether he is going to Downing Street or staying up north.

‌



The Prime Minister replied: "I think he's going to have to stay up north I think because he's kind of got that angry little man thing going on.

"You know he's a he's got a bit of poodle in him. He's a bichon poo I think they call it, or a pooch on whatever that whatever the phrase is. He wouldn't get on with Larry let me put it that way.

"And I don't think the nation would thank me would they if I brought Axel down to disturb Larry's world. So I think staying up here I think.

‌



View 3 Images Boris Johnson with his unruly pet Dilyn (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

"These are the big decisions that have been made."

In recent years other Prime Ministers have brought their dogs with them when they moved into Downing Street. Boris Johnson's unruly Jack Russell cross Dilyn who used to cling on to guests' legs, unable to control what his owner described as "romantic urges".

Article continues below

Better behaved was Rishi Sunak's dog, Labrador Retriever Nova. She joined the Sunak family as a puppy in 2021 and was frequently pictured with her Prime Minister owner during his tenure.

News.title: Andy Burnham issues dire warning NHS will collapse if social care isn't finally fixed
News.content:
Andy Burnham issues dire warning NHS will collapse if social care isn't finally fixed

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he will use his 'political capital' to push for sweeping reform to the 'broken' social care system - and hinted that claiming benefits could become harder

View 2 Images Andy Burnham says he wants to be the leader who finally gets a grip of the social care system

Andy Burnham has warned the NHS faces collapse unless the social care system is finally sorted after years of promises.

‌



The Prime Minister vowed to use his "political capital" to find solutions - saying he does not want to leave office without bringing about substantial change. In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg, said to air on Monday, Mr Burnham also indicated he wants to make it harder to claim benefits, saying the country must "get serious" about bringing the welfare bill down.

‌



Mr Burnham is expected to give a speech this week indicating his desire to get a grip with the social care system. He told Ms Kuenssberg: "I will go as quickly as I can on the reform of social care... I think there are major changes you can make before the next election.

‌



"This costs the NHS billions of pounds and we will never get the NHS back to good waiting time standards until we fix social care."

Streeting backs Burnham to sort out Britain's social care crisis with dig at Starmer READ MORE :

200 refugee charities call for end of asylum 'gimmicks' in letter to Andy Burnham READ MORE :

View 2 Images Former Health Secretary Wes Streeting backed Mr Burnham to get a grip of the crisis (Image: SKY NEWS)

It is expected that Mr Burnham - whose dad Roy has Alzheimer's disease and lives in a care home - will start setting out his position on social care in a speech this week.

‌



Ms Kuenssberg told him that proposal after proposal has been put forward, and asked: "This is about political will, is it not?" The Prime Minister responded: "I'm not going to take different positions than the ones I've long put to you in interviews. Whatever political capital I have, I will put in to fixing broken social care, and I would not want to leave office without having brought in the substantial change, the new system of social care that you described.

"I can't put a timeline on it right here, right now. If we don't do it, the NHS will collapse under the weight of trying to care for people who've really not really needed to end up in the NHS system."

Last month there were 14,000 people stuck in hospital each day in England - mainly because they cannot get social care to be safely discharged somewhere else. This was up 70% since 2021. Mr Burnham first proposed a universal social care system in England back in 2009, when he was Health Secretary under Gordon Brown.

‌



On Sunday Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who was Health Secretary for nearly two years, backed his boss to get a grip on the system. He said: "It's why Andy Burnham's leadership matters, because I have no doubt that he will prioritise this issue. I think you'll see him this week spelling out why and how he intends to grip this issue, and why it means so much to him in a way that I think will resonate with so many people across the country."

Elsewhere Mr Burnham suggested it should be harder for people - particularly young people - to be able to claim benefits. He indicated he plans to "increase the conditions on people required to receive benefits".

The PM said: "Well, I wouldn't necessarily go straight to blaming those people. What I would say is that there are people in the benefits system, young people in their 20s, who have been, I would, say, quite seriously let down because the support wasn't there for them when it should have been there...So I don't blame them. I don't think the support has been there for them in the way that it should have been."

‌



Pressed to elaborate he said: "It's about changing the nature of the support and making some of the support conditional upon people taking opportunities that are presented in front of them. So you might increase the conditions required to receive benefits.

"I think it's a good thing that the government has given guarantees of opportunities for young people. And I think we need to continue down that approach and where mental health support is needed, for instance, it's provided in work to support people in an opportunity.

"Let me just say something more though about. What you're driving at, which is the welfare bill. I think we've got to get really serious as a country at getting the welfare down."

Article continues below

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden is drawing up proposals to reform the benefit system. Last year plans championed by Keir Starmer and former welfare chief Liz Kendall had to be abandonned following a rebellion by Labour backbenchers.

News.title: Two dead and multiple injured after mass shooting at food festival in Seattle
News.content:
Two dead and multiple injured after mass shooting at food festival in Seattle

Fire chiefs have confirmed two people have died at the scene of the Bite of Seattle Food Festival, which is held at the Seattle Center, the city's Space Needle building

View 2 Images Police at the scene of the shooting in Seattle (Image: Fox 13 Seattle)

Two people have been killed and five others injured after a gunman opened fire at a food festival in Seattle.

‌



Reports first emerged of the attack, near the city’s iconic Space Needle building, at nearly 3:30am in the UK. It’s thought the shots were fired at the Bite of Seattle food festival.

‌



The BBC reported two people were pronounced dead at the scene of the attack. It added five people injured in the attack including a 56-year-old woman, who is said to be in hospital ‘in a serious condition’, according to the fire department.

‌



Another three people were hospitalised in ‘a stable condition’, including a two-year-old boy, a 39-year-old woman, and a 23-year-old man.

A fifth person, a 40-year-old woman, was also hurt ‘with minor injuries’ but ‘declined transport to hospital’, fire chiefs added.

After first announcing two people had been arrested, Seattle city mayor Katie Wilson announced shortly before 6am on Monday in the UK that one suspect has been detained. Their identity has not been disclosed.

‌



She said in her initial statement: "I want to thank the Seattle police officers who responded to the scene and took two suspects into custody.

"Impacted families are living through the worst moment of their lives, and an entire community is trying to understand how a gathering built around culture, connection, and joy ended in gunfire."

"Tonight, our attention belongs to the people whose lives were taken, those fighting to recover, and the families beside them," she added. "Seattle grieves with you, and we will stand with you in the difficult days ahead."

‌



The developing situation is being ‘monitored closely’, a Democratic Congresswoman for Washington added.

View 2 Images A Seattle Police Department vehicle (Image: @X)

Pramila Jayapal said on X a short time ago: “We are monitoring closely information from the shooting that took place at the Seattle Center this evening.

‌



“We are in close touch with Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson and Governor Bob Ferguson, and coordinating across multiple levels of government to get updates on the situation.

“We are grateful to law enforcement at Seattle Police Department and first responders who are at the scene and working hard. Our hearts go out to all those impacted by this senseless violence.

“We ask that the public please stay away from the Seattle Center as there is still an active investigation happening at this time. We will provide updates as we have additional information.”

Article continues below

This is a breaking news story, please check for updates.

News.title: Baby 'stolen from womb' after mum murdered as police hunt for killer-kidnappers
News.content:
Baby 'stolen from womb' after mum murdered as police hunt for killer-kidnappers

More than four people may have been involved in the young mum's kidnapping and murder, police have said, with a $62,000 reward on offer for information that helps locate the baby and those responsible

View 4 Images María Camila Potosí suffered a horrific death (Image: Jam Press)

The gruesome slaying of a 21-year-old pregnant woman has sent shockwaves through an entire city, with the body of the young mum found dumped beside a river with her baby nowhere to be found.

‌



María Camila Potosí was eight months pregnant when she was last seen riding on the back of a motorcycle in Polvorines, a town in the southwestern city of Cali in Columbia last week. She was declared missing on July 16 and, after days of searching by her family and by authorities, she was found by a the banks of the River Meléndez.

‌



Her body had been discarded after she was stabbed to death, with her baby nowhere to be found; cut from her womb.

‌



As per local radio station La FM, the baby was reportedly to be named Alahia and had been expected to be born in August. A baby shower was planned just days before the horrific tragedy unfolded.

View 4 Images María Camila Potosí at her own baby shower days before her grim murder (Image: FaceBook / La Favorita Stereo)

Confirming the discovery of María's remains, Cali Police deputy head of criminal investigations Maj Alirio Acuna said: "The body of a pregnant woman was found at kilometre 3 on the La Buitrera road, specifically on the banks of the River Meléndez. Preliminary findings suggest that the physical characteristics and clothing match those of the 21-year-old woman who had been reported missing since last Thursday, July 16."

‌



María was last spotted climbing onto a motorbike with an unidentified woman who, at the time of writing, remains unknown. According to Noticias Caracol, María had just attended an appointment at the Los Polvorines health centre in southern Cali before boarding the motorbike that was recorded on CCTV.

Discussing María's appointment just hours before her tragic death, Ladera Health Network manager Diana Carolina said: "It was a routine consultation, in line with clinical practice guidelines.

View 4 Images A woman was found dead on the banks of a river in Colombia (Image: Jam Press)

‌



"She arrived at our healthcare centre at around 9am. She entered the consultation room alone and underwent the necessary check-up."

María's mum Ana Rubi Gomez has made a desperate plea for her granddaughter's safe return, urging the public to assist in locating the missing infant.

She revealed to La FM: "The first thing I asked was whether the baby was still in her womb, and they told me no, that the baby wasn't there.

‌



"That filled me with hope that the baby might still be alive. So I'm asking the public and the community to help me find my little girl."

Potosí was at her boyfriend's home when they say when she received a phone call from a woman later identified in a video as driving the motorcycle. The family said that Potosí told them that she was going with the woman to pick up gifts for her baby. She had recently met the woman at a Cali center for expectant mums.

On Friday (July 24), a man named Carlos Rincón posted a video on social media in which he identified himself as the female suspect’s former boyfriend and revealed that she did not return to sleep at his home the day that Potosí disappeared.

‌



View 4 Images Police are investigating the death of Maria (Image: Jam Press)

He added that his ex-girlfriend told him in January that she was pregnant. “I was excited about (her) pregnancy,” he said.

“And many people think I had something to do with it — the kidnapping and murder of the 21-year-old woman — because I had been the motorcyclist’s partner.

‌



“We had nothing to do with it. We knew nothing. My family was another victim. We trusted her, we believed in her.”

After María's body was discovered, the Cali Ombudsman's Office has demanded a swift and thorough probe into her death. Additionally, they've stressed the urgency of tracing the missing infant immediately in case she remains alive.

Officials reportedly stated that the post-mortem findings confirming the baby's removal "makes it even more urgent to clarify the facts and locate the newborn baby".

Article continues below

They continued: "As the Public Prosecutor's Office, we call on the Attorney General's Office and the relevant authorities to carry out all investigative measures as swiftly as possible and to put in place the necessary measures to locate the baby, ensuring the protection of her life and safety.

"We also urge members of the public to provide any information through official channels that may assist the investigation. Every minute counts."

Investigations into María's death are ongoing.

News.title: Met Office names next 'heatwave window' as UK facing sweltering temperatures yet again
News.content:
Met Office names next 'heatwave window' as UK facing sweltering temperatures yet again

Three heatwaves in three months has baked Britain dry, with a drought declared in parts of Wales, and other regions on track to follow suit if it doesn't rain soon

View 2 Images Beachgoers flock to Margate in June's heatwave (Image: Krisztian Elek/SOPA Images/Shutterstock)

The Met Office has named the UK’s next heatwave window — suggesting a fourth hot spell of the summer is on its way.

‌



This summer has been exceptionally warm, with three heatwaves baking Britain in May, June, and July. In late July, the mercury hit 37C in Norfolk, only a few degrees off the record high of 40.3C recorded in Coningsby, Lincolnshire, in July 2022.

‌



The heatwaves have dried the country out, with a drought being declared in Wales last week. Multiple regions are in ‘prolonged dry weather’, the stage before drought, officials say.

‌



And a fourth heatwave in four months could hit the country later in August, the Met Office believes. Its long-range forecast for August 10 to August 24 is when temperatures could climb again.

The forecast said: “Dry and settled conditions will probably dominate much of this period with high pressure patterns tending to affect the UK. This may be interrupted at times by Atlantic frontal systems, especially in the north, or thunderstorms in the south.

“However, overall rainfall amounts will likely be below normal. Temperatures will probably be above normal and some spells of hot weather and heatwaves are possible, especially in the south.”

‌



A heatwave will feel a million miles away for most of the UK, which had a wet weekend on Sunday (July 26). Showers are set to stay in the north of England, while the south will stay dry and see relatively normal temperatures for the time of year.

View 2 Images Wildfires have raged in National Parks, like the Peak District, for much of the summer (Image: Men Media)

The start of August will be ‘very warm’ in the south-east, the Met Office medium-range forecast for July 31 to August 9 said: “Temperatures ranging from around average in the north-west to warm in the southeast, perhaps becoming very warm in the southeast through the weekend.

Article continues below

“It will probably become more changeable thereafter, with potential for an area of low pressure to move close to or across the UK early in August.

“This could bring spells of heavy rain and perhaps some strong winds for a time. It may become more settled again toward the end of the first week of August.”

On Monday (July 27), the highs will be 25C in London, 19C in Edinburgh, 21C in Cardiff and Belfast, and 19C in Manchester, where it will rain.

News.title: Gatwick Airport issues update on Monday opening after ‘no water’ problem
News.content:
Gatwick Airport issues update on Monday opening after ‘no water’ problem

Bosses at Britain's second busiest airport issued the update late on Sunday, after most passengers had a disrupted start to their holidays when restaurants, cafes, and toilets closed

View 3 Images File photo of Gatwick Airport south terminal

Gatwick Airport has issued an update to passengers over its Monday opening plans following major water supply issues.

‌



Britain’s second-busiest airport lost its water supply for much of Sunday (July 26), prompting restaurants, cafes, and even toilets to close in both terminals. Passengers were given complimentary bottles of water by staff.

‌



The water outage came at the start of the busiest period of the year to fly, so most had a disrupted start to their holidays.

‌



Roger Wood, from Tunbridge Wells in Kent, was one. He arrived at Gatwick South Terminal at around 11am on Sunday to fly to New York.

View 3 Images An easyJet flight to Athens will be the first to leave Gatwick on Monday (Image: william87 via Getty Images)

He told PA: “There was no communication. We arrived at 11ish and it had only started recently.

‌



“We met friends at the bar but they couldn’t serve us as they were unable to wash their hands.

“I’ve never seen Wetherspoons empty. No idea when it’ll be resolved, the toilets also lacked water to wash hands.”

The issue plagued the airport for most of Sunday, but shortly before 10pm yesterday evening, management said water supply has been restored for ‘most’ of its buildings. They hope to reopen the terminals as normal on Monday.

‌



“Following an issue at the Bough Beech Water Treatment Works which impacted the local area today, we are pleased to report that the water supply has now returned to the vast majority of the London Gatwick campus,” the statement said.

“Most toilet facilities are now open and we expect all toilets - as well as food and beverage outlets - to be open for tomorrow’s first flights.

View 3 Images Aerial photograph of Britain's second busiest airfield, Gatwick Airport. (Image: Getty Images)

‌



“Since becoming aware of the issue, we have been working closely with SES Water and our airport partners to help minimise the impact, and ensure all today's flights departed as scheduled. Additional staff remain on hand across both terminals to support passengers and maintain operations as we return to normal operations.

“We recognise the inconvenience caused by today’s water shortage and thank passengers for their patience and understanding. We'd also like to thank airport staff and our partners, who have gone above and beyond to support passengers and keep disruption to a minimum.”

The first flights out of Gatwick leave at 5:20am on Monday. The North terminal’s first departure is easyJet’s service to Athens, while the south terminal’s first take-off will be Wizz Air’s jet to Podgorica, the capital of Montenegro.

News.title: Toddler escapes death after suffering cocaine overdose as man arrested
News.content:
Toddler escapes death after suffering cocaine overdose as man arrested

A 39-year old man was arrested after calling for help after the two-year-old began struggling to breathe, with paramedics administering a NARCAN nasal spray which the boy responded to

View 2 Images Alexander T. Moles was arrested on charges of child endangerment (Image: Cape May County Prosecutor Office)

A toddler has nearly died after overdosing on cocaine, with first responders forced into action after the two-year-old was found struggling to breathe.

‌



Police on the Jersey Shore in the United States confirmed they have arrested a man, 39-year-old Alexander T. Moles, on charges of child endangerment after a July 20 callout in relation to a sick toddler. When first responders arrived, it was discovered that had been on his way to hospital, driving the two-year-old to A&E as he was having difficulty breathing.

‌



Paramedics administered two doses of Naloxone nasal spray - also known as NARCAN - to the boy, to which he responded. NARCAN is an anti-opioid drug which has no effect on a patient if there are no opioids in their system.

‌



View 2 Images FILE IMAGE: A white powdery substance in a small, clear plastic bag similar to what police found at Moles' Airbnb (Image: eliosdnepr – stock.adobe.com)

The two-year-old boy was then transportedto Cooper University Hospital Cape Regional for further medical attention, with blood tests later confirming the tot had tested positive for cocaine.

‌



Police officers later found a pill, tinfoil packets labelled “tapentadol hydrochloride,” a clear plastic bag containing a white, powdery substance, and several short plastic straws following a judge-ordered search of Moles’s Airbnb, according to an affidavit.

As per a statement released by prosecutors in New Jersey, a joint investigation was then initiated by the Wildwood Police Department and the Cape May County Prosecutor’s Office Special Victims Unit. A spokesperson said: "Through the investigation it was determined that Alexander T. Moles was vacationing at a residence in Wildwood, New Jersey when the two-year-old male became ill.

"As a result of the initial investigation, on July 21, 2026, Alexander T. Moles was arrested and charged with one count of Endangering the Welfare of a Child, a crime of the second degree; one count of Possession of Cocaine, a crime of the third degree; one count of Possession of Drug Paraphernalia, a Disorderly Persons Offence; and one count of Possession of Prescription Legend Drugs, a crime of the fourth degree.

Article continues below

The Cape May County Prosecutor's Office added: "Prosecutor Sutherland advises persons convicted of a second degree crime are subject to a term of imprisonment of five to 10 years in New Jersey State Prison. A person convicted of a third degree crime are subject to a term of imprisonment of three to 5 years in New Jersey State Prison."

The 39-year-old was arrested and placed in the Cape May County Correctional Facility, but was released three days later on bail with conditions.

News.title: NHS 'will collapse' without social care reform, PM tells BBC
News.content:
Andy Burnham has told the BBC "the NHS will collapse" if social care is not reformed but said he could not put a timeline on changes.

In his first major interview since becoming prime minister, Burnham said he would not want to leave office without bringing in "substantial change" to the social care system.

The prime minister also suggested making it harder to claim benefits, saying the country had to get serious about getting the welfare bill down.

Kemi Badenoch has meanwhile written to the prime minister, saying he should rule out tax rises or increased borrowing to fund social care reform.

In his interview with the BBC, Burnham said if the government did not reform social care, the NHS would "collapse under the weight of trying to care for people who've really not needed to end up in the NHS system".

But pressed on whether he would create a new system before the next election, he said he "couldn't put a timeline on it right here, right now", though he would put "whatever political capital I have into fixing broken social care".

Burnham first proposed a universal system of social care in England in 2009 when he was health secretary under Gordon Brown.

Now as prime minister he is due to make a speech on adult social care on Wednesday.

The BBC understands the PM will stop short of unveiling plans for a new system in this speech, instead announcing he is speeding up the Casey Commission, an independent review which has been considering possible solutions for social care.

Currently Baroness Louise Casey is not expected to give her final recommendations until 2028, but Burnham wants to bring her schedule forward.

He told the BBC: "Social care was on longer path and I have brought it straight forward."

Adult social care provides support to help people live more independently, ranging from personal care such as washing to household tasks.

Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use. In England and Northern Ireland people with savings worth more than Â£23,250 are not entitled to help with care costs from their council.

In Wales and Scotland different rules apply in terms of eligibility.

Adult social care has proved a complex issue to tackle for successive governments.

Two years ago Sir Keir Starmer was criticised when Labour scrapped plans for an Â£86,000 cap on the amount people in England would spend on social care in their lifetime.

Conservative leader Badenoch wrote in her letter to Burnham that "any solution to the issues around social care must also be fair to those who have made provisions and saved up over the course of their lives".

News.title: Laura Kuenssberg: Our exclusive behind-the-scenes access at No 10 as Andy Burnham became PM
News.content:
Listening carefully during our interview, it seemed Burnham had distinct gears. He was fluent and passionate on his familiar ground: his desire to sort out social care, his track record in Manchester, his desire to run a government that feels relevant and effective where you live, local leaders eager to make many more decisions and able to spend taxpayers' money more freely without permission from Whitehall.

Those are his core beliefs, arguments he's made hundreds, if not thousands of times.

But when it comes to how he'll apply what he thinks in principle to what he does in practice, that was not always so clear. On social care for example, he's long believed there ought to be a National Care Service, like the NHS. But in a speech on Wednesday, that's not likely to be what he unveils.

Instead, he told me he'd "brought it straight forward", understood to mean speeding up the government review by Baroness Louise Casey of what ought to be done, not saying, "here's the plan".

When it came to questions that are on his desk for the first time, there was a contradiction. Burnham told us all many times that he will stick to the manifesto the country voted for in 2024.

But he's also vowed his arrival in office will usher in the biggest change in four decades. You don't have to be a student of political history to find a mismatch there - he's going to stick broadly to Sir Keir's plan, yet shift the government more fundamentally than leaving the EU, or the financial crash? Really?

And beyond the rhetorical tension in several areas, Burnham gave clear indications that he will apply "new eyes". Will he stick to the home secretary's plans to make migrants wait 10 years or more before they can permanently stay in the UK? He's looking at that again he told me, and hinted that care workers could possibly be exempt.

News.title: Girlguiding unveils first major uniform redesign since 1990
News.content:
The organisation said the uniform combines the charity's heritage with modern colours and prints.

The range is made up of 30 items of clothing, 15 accessories and neckerchiefs - with prices starting at Â£12, for a T-shirt.

Design features include hidden pockets in waist bands, thumb holes, and badge sashes which double as cross-body bags.

This is the first time in 30 years Girlguiding has updated its entire range at the same time.

Oswald said the range was "all about providing girls with the freedom to express themselves, whilst feeling part of our amazing organisation".

Members do not have to buy the new range straightaway, the website explains, and they can continue to wear the old uniform until they need a replacement.

A Girlguiding survey in June of 2,000 girls aged six to 16 in the UK found that 93% said they felt most comfortable when able to choose how they styled themselves.

Angellica Bell, a Girlguiding ambassador and presenter, said the new design gives "girls and volunteers the freedom to style it the way that suits them".

She added: "The new uniform empowers girls and volunteers to embrace their individuality."

News.title: UK's most parched regions miss chance for rain ahead of next heatwave
News.content:
Some of the driest regions of the UK have missed their chances for rain ahead of another heatwave beginning this week.

Parts of the northern and western UK saw some rainfall over the weekend, with further showers and unsettled conditions expected over the next few days.

But southern parts of the country - where the least amount of rain has fallen - are set to see temperatures climb once again, with more dry and sunny weather in the forecast.

It comes as parts of Wales have officially entered drought status, while parts of southern, central and eastern England remain in "prolonged dry weather", the final stage before drought is declared.

The coming days will only exacerbate dry conditions as another heatwave is expected to be declared, with temperatures peaking around 35C (95F) in south-east England.

In advance of the high temperatures, heat health alerts have been issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).

The south-west, south-east, London, East of England, West and East Midlands and Yorkshire and The Humber are all under the alerts from 9:00 BST on Tuesday 28 July until 9:00 BST on Friday 31 July.

The UKHSA warns that heat is expected to cause minor impacts for health and social care services, with an increased risk to life for vulnerable people.

News.title: Trump paused attacks on Iran to make space for talks, US ambassador says
News.content:
President Donald Trump has paused attacks on Iran for the second night in a row to give diplomacy more time, the US ambassador to the UN said.

Speaking to Fox News on Sunday, ambassador Mike Waltz said the president was "giving talks some space, he's giving it a little bit of room".

An Iranian army spokesperson said on Sunday that Tehran had halted "retaliatory" attacks in the region in response.

The pause follows nearly two weeks of daily US strikes and tit-for-tat attacks, effectively unravelling the ceasefire struck in June.

Asked whether Trump had decided against escalation for now, Waltz told NBC: "I wouldn't go that far at all. The president is keeping all options on the table."

Waltz also rejected reports in the New York Times, external that administration officials had warned expanding hostilities could dangerously drain a diminished stockpile of air defence munitions.

"The US military... has everything that it needs to conduct this campaign as effectively as it needs to be," he said.

As of Sunday evening, Trump had not spoken publicly on the latest developments, but earlier posted computer-generated images on his Truth Social account that depicted US military planes bombing Iranian ships and Kharg island.

Meanwhile, Iran and Oman held several rounds of technical talks in Tehran on Friday and Saturday to discuss management of the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei.

Disputes over control of the strait reignited US-Iran tensions earlier this month and it remains a major block to permanently ending the war.

Iran and the US signed a memorandum of understanding in June to halt military operations and reopen the strait, as well as to reach an agreement to end the war over the following 60 days.

But after Iranian forces attacked tankers in the Strait of Hormuz on 13 July, the US resumed airstrikes on the country and reinstated its naval blockade on Iranian ports.

Iran retaliated with attacks on US military facilities and bases across the Middle East, killing four American soldiers. The US strikes have since killed dozens of people, according to Iran's health ministry.

In the UK, new Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said he would meet his US counterpart Pete Hegseth in the coming week to discuss the strait, which is one of the world's key transport routes for oil, liquid natural gas and other essential commodities.

"When it comes to securing maritime freedom and free commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, that's where we are absolutely aligned," Streeting told the BBC.

Earlier this week, oil prices hit $100 a barrel for the first time since May, as the renewed fighting stoked fears over global energy supplies.

As the war nears its fifth month, it remains largely unpopular in the US, with a new poll from CBS/YouGov suggesting 57% of Americans are frustrated about the conflict and only 19% optimistic.

Thousands of people have been killed across the Middle East since the US-Israeli war with Iran began in February, official figures show, with the vast majority coming from Iran and Lebanon.

President Trump is set to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the White House on Tuesday.

News.title: Four people including baby die after car crash
News.content:
Four people, including a baby, have died after a car crashed into trees on a busy dual carriageway in Derby.

Emergency services were called after a red Hyundai car left the A38 and crashed into trees - between the A50 Toyota Island and the A516 - at about 23:00 BST on Saturday.

Derbyshire Police said the passengers, two women, 18 and 30, and a man, 36, died at the scene. The baby girl was taken to hospital where she died shortly after.

The force said the driver, a 33-year-old man, was arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving. He was subsequently taken to hospital for serious injuries.

Police said all those involved were from Leeds in West Yorkshire, adding their relatives have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers.

"Our thoughts are with them at this most distressing time," a spokesperson said.

The carriageway was closed for several hours while emergency services dealt with the crash, but it has since been reopened.

Anyone who witnessed the crash or has any dashcam footage has been urged to contact police.

News.title: Littler wins Matchplay and smashes records
News.content:
Luke Littler defended his World Matchplay title in sensational style - and smashed Phil Taylor's tournament and final average records in the process.

The 19-year-old beat seventh seed Gerwyn Price 18-9 in Blackpool to become just the fourth person to win back-to-back Matchplay titles.

World number one Littler finished the week with an average of 111.04, beating Taylor's record of 106.31 in 2010.

He averaged 111.53 in the final, setting a new record as he bettered Taylor's 111.23 against Adrian Lewis in 2013.

Littler claimed Â£225,000 in prize money for winning the event and now has Â£3,143,500 over the PDC's two-year order of merit. That is Â£2.13m more than Luke Humphries in second spot.

"It's been a crazy week, one of the best weeks of my life with the darts I've played," Littler told Sky Sports.

"It's been tough. The stats may look like it's easy, but when you're on this stage with how hot it is, it's not easy."

Price averaged 104.97 in the final and has enjoyed a successful week, climbing to fourth in the order of merit and reclaiming the Welsh number one spot from Jonny Clayton.

News.title: Would you choose £50,000 over the chance of £1m?
News.content:
You have the choice of instantly receiving Â£50,000 or flipping a coin for a 50/50 chance of Â£1m.

Which would you choose?

The vast majority decide on taking the Â£50k, according to a survey of thousands of people by YouGov. Women voted 82% in favour of the guaranteed cash.

The poll has sparked a debate about why Brits appear more risk-averse than people in the US.

So why are the results so clear-cut, and what are the financial and psychological factors at play?

Sadly, there is little chance of ever having such a choice, but there are some interesting lessons for how we manage our money nonetheless.

News.title: 'Antisemitism felt relentless' - Jewish students on life at UK universities
News.content:
Like many campuses across the UK, Cardiff University has seen pro-Palestine protests in recent years and Oliver said he believed some behaviour he witnessed crossed the line from criticism of Israel into antisemitism.

Holding Jewish people responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is a form of antisemitism, according to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance.

"That first year was absolutely terrifying," he said.

"You go home and think, 'do I carry on? Do I try to go to the next day?'"

Oliver said he stopped speaking Hebrew outside his home, and hid his Star of David pendant when on campus.

Over the following three years, Oliver said the antisemitic abuse he experienced at university became "relentless".

"I've been in clubs [or] just wandering around the uni and you hear these conversations and you see pamphlets being handed around where it's literally saying that your belief and your history is fake," he said.

"I've been at house parties where, when someone's found out I'm Jewish they started calling me Netanyahu behind my back.

"Like you found out my religion and you've decided I'm a bad person."

Oliver said when he had reported antisemitic incidents that had happened to him and others, he had felt they had been often "swept under the rug" by the university.

Although he said some positive action had been taken, he feels more needs to be done.

Cardiff University said it was sorry that "any student felt unsafe" on campus and that it adopts a "zero-tolerance approach to harassment and discrimination of all kinds".

It said there was no place for antisemitism or hatred at the university and they have "robust procedures" in place for investigating allegations of antisemitism. Where it is found, the university said appropriate action would be taken.

It said it had reached out to the university's Jewish Society and reminded students to report incidents to them.

News.title: Four men charged with murder after Leicester stabbing
News.content:
Four men have been charged with murder after a 24-year-old man was killed in Leicester.

Arad Niakan died after being stabbed on Wednesday in De Montfort Place, off London Road, Leicestershire Police said.

The four men charged with murder are Talha Satar, 21, of Stoughton Street South, Spinney Hills; Said Mahamed, 20, of Sparkenhoe Street, Spinney Hills; Husni Benramadan, 19, of no fixed address; and Yousouf Khan, 18, also of no fixed address, the force said.

All four have also been charged with one count of having an imitation firearm with intent to commit an indictable offence and another count of possession of a knife/bladed article in a public place.

A fifth man - Kassam Tarmahoomed, 21 - has been charged with assisting an offender, police said.

All five men are scheduled to appear at Leicester Magistrates' Court on Monday.

Leicestershire Police said two men aged 52 and two women aged 43 who were arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender as part of the investigation were released on bail.

Separately, a 33-year-old man who was arrested on suspicion of murder has since been released with no further action, the force added.

News.title: Teen charged over record crossing on 'mega dinghy'
News.content:
A teenager charged over a small boat Channel crossing was allegedly piloting a "mega dinghy" carrying a record 165 migrants from France to England, the National Crime Agency has said.

Sudanese national Chan Mathok Atak, 19, is accused of endangering another during a journey by sea to the UK on Thursday and is due to appear at Margate Magistrates' Court on Monday.

The number on the dinghy broke the previous record from July, when 128 crossed the Channel from France on one vessel.

According to Home Office figures, more than 13,000 arrivals have been recorded in 2026, which is 45% lower than this time in 2025 and down 18% on the same period in 2024.

Border Security Command was pictured towing a dinghy - estimated to be about the same size as a standard bus at 13m (42ft) long - when it arrived in Dover in Kent on Thursday afternoon.

Home Office figures showed 366 people arrived after crossing in three boats on Thursday during warm, sunny weather and calm conditions at sea.

On Wednesday, 172 people made the journey in three boats, bringing an end to an 11-day hiatus because of windy conditions in the Channel.

Refugee charity Care4Calais said the crossing route was becoming "more and more dangerous" because of the increasing number of people in each boat.

News.title: Badenoch says PM must rule out tax rises to fund social care reform
News.content:
Kemi Badenoch has written to the prime minister asking him to "rule out any tax rises or increased borrowing" to fund social care reform.

In a letter to Andy Burnham, the Conservative Party leader said she would be happy to work with him to find a solution, but only if he sticks to her party's "two core principles".

She said any reform must be funded by reducing current spending and not raising taxes, and also be fair to those who have "made provisions and saved up over the course of their lives".

Burnham is expected to make a speech on adult social care this week. A No 10 source said this was part of his plan to "run towards problems that have been neglected".

News.title: Water returns to Gatwick Airport after major outage
News.content:
Gatwick Airport says its water supply has returned after passengers faced long queues for toilets and closed restaurants and bars after a major supply outage.

Both terminals at the UK's second busiest airport lost running water on Sunday morning after a power failure at a treatment works that serves the area.

People told the BBC of confusion and frustration as all bars and restaurants were shut, some were left with nowhere to sit and waits built up outside toilets.

SES Water, the company that supplies the airport, said earlier the power outage was fixed, with Gatwick reporting on Sunday night that water had returned to "the vast majority of the London Gatwick campus".

The water company, which also supplies parts of Kent, Surrey and south London, said complications caused by a power outage at Bough Beech treatment works meant some customers had experienced low water pressure or a temporary loss of supply.

A spokesperson had earlier confirmed that Gatwick Airport was affected.

On Sunday afternoon, SES Water said its treatment works were back up and running, but later added it would take time for the network to fully return to normal as it had been "a highly unusual and complex issue".

"We want to reiterate that our teams are working as quickly as they possibly can and we are grateful for everyone's patience," the spokesperson added.

Gatwick apologised and said staff had been handing out bottled water.

A spokesperson added: "Our staff are on hand to support passengers and provide assistance where needed, some restaurant partners have opened to provide additional seating."

Gatwick said additional teams had been deployed across both terminals to support passengers.

The airport added there had been no flight cancellations as a result of the supply issues and that it was working closely with SES Water to minimise the impact.

"Our teams are working hard to reopen toilets and other facilities as quickly and safely as possible," a spokesperson said.

News.title: Iran's 'sabre-rattling' should not intimidate UK, Wes Streeting says
News.content:
When asked if Iran had the capability to attack the UK, Streeting said: "I think we shouldn't put too much stock in the sabre-rattling of Iran, and we certainly shouldn't be intimidated by what the regime has said this week".

He also repeated the UK's position from the outset of the US war against Iran saying "we have not joined and will not join offensive US military action in Iran.

"That's an area where we have not agreed with the United States, but when it comes to securing maritime freedom and free commercial shipping in the straight Hormuz, that's where we are absolutely aligned".

Streeting said he is to meet with US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth in the coming week after "kicking around" ideas for ways "to bring the countries together" and had been "delighted" to speak to Hegseth by phone already.

He also said that the UK is ready to lead a naval mission to help remove mines from the Strait of Hormuz "when the conditions are right".

Securing safe shipping routes through the area was important because of the impact the crisis is having on energy prices and the cost of living, he added.

Streeting also dismissed a Russian warship's recent live-firing exercise in the English Channel as "performative" but added it was a "reminder of the frankly unsafe and unprofessional way in which they have been conducting themselves".

Branding the Channel incident "irresponsible", Streeting said Russia posed a threat to UK security, adding that the public does not see "the enormous efforts that take place every day to counter Russian aggression".

News.title: Boy, 16, charged with murder after Luton stabbing
News.content:
A 16-year-old boy has been charged with murder after the fatal stabbing of a 17-year-old boy in Luton on Friday, police have said.

Four other teenagers have been arrested on suspicion of murder relating to the same incident.

Officers were called to reports of violent disorder in Kingsway Recreation Ground at about 18:30 on Friday, where police said a number of teenagers were seen carrying large knives.

The 17-year-old was taken to hospital with multiple stab wounds but was pronounced dead shortly after. He has not been identified.

Following the stabbing, two teenage boys, a 16-year-old and a 17-year-old, were initially arrested on suspicion of violent disorder, before later being arrested on suspicion of murder.

Police said on Sunday the 16-year-old has since been charged with murder and has been remanded in custody.

Bedfordshire Police said the 17-year-old also arrested on Friday on suspicion of murder was being treated in hospital for serious injuries.

A further three boys, all 17, have been arrested on suspicion of murder, violent disorder and carrying a weapon, police said.

Det Ch Insp Nick Gardener appealed for anyone who was in the area and may have witnessed events leading up to the disorder to get in touch.

"Our officers are continuing to carry out additional high-visibility patrols, and we are continuing to engage with local members of the public.

"We would also like to remind the public not to share any distressing videos or images as this can be concerning for families involved, but also form a vital part of the police investigation," he added.

Zanib Raja, a councillor for the Biscot Ward in Luton, has also asked people not to share alleged videos of the incident online.

In a statement on Facebook, she said: "A tragic incident took place today in Kingsway Park, a place many of us grew up in, played in, and built memories in.

"A place that should be safe for families, children, and every resident of our town. Instead, a man lost his life in broad daylight. A family has been shattered. Luton is hurting."

Raja urged the community to come together.

News.title: It's me, Cathy – thousands pay tribute to Kate Bush classic
News.content:
The sun may be hiding behind grey clouds, but for hundreds of people in flowing red dresses dancing on Yorkshire moorland it'll take more than a threat of rain to dampen their spirits.

This is BrontÃ« country, after all, so it's fitting that it's also perfect BrontÃ« weather.

The group, swaying in unison, have come together to re-create the music video for Kate Bush's 1978 song Wuthering Heights, inspired by Emily BrontÃ«'s novel.

Every year, thousands of people around the world don red robes â and in some cases long black wigs â for The Most Wuthering Heights Day Ever.

Events have previously taken place in places such as Sydney, Copenhagen, Berlin, Folkestone and Preston.

This particular "Mass Wuther" perhaps has an even stronger claim than most â it's held on Penistone Hill, not far from the famous BrontÃ« parsonage in Haworth, in the Pennines.

From the field on a clear day can be seen the ruined farmhouse of Top Withens, believed to be the inspiration for the titular farmhouse of BrontÃ«'s novel.

News.title: Two dead and boy, 2, among those injured in shooting at popular Seattle food festival
News.content:
A shooting at the Bite of Seattle food festival near the Space Needle on Sunday evening resulted in two dead and five injuries.

Among the injured, a 56-year-old woman is in serious condition, while a two-year-old boy, a 23-year-old man, and a 39-year-old woman are stable; 40-year-old woman sustained minor injuries.

Police are investigating the incident, which occurred around 6pm, and urged the public to avoid the area, though no arrests have been made yet.

Washington Governor Bob Ferguson expressed condolences and deployed State Patrol SWAT officers to assist local police.

Witnesses described widespread panic, people fleeing, and hearing multiple gunshots, with some taking shelter in nearby buildings.

News.content:

One suspect has been taken into custody after at least two people were killed and five were wounded — including a 2-year-old boy — during a mass shooting at a popular Seattle food festival Sunday evening.

The Seattle Fire Department said the child and three other wounded victims were rushed to the hospital in stable condition, with the fifth person treated at the scene for minor injuries, The Seattle Times said.

There was no word on the identity of whoever’s behind the carnage at the Seattle Center, home to the city’s iconic Space Needle, which was hosting the annual Bite of Seattle event over the weekend.

The barrage of gunfire erupted around 6 p.m. local time.

Estan Wakonabo, 25, told The Seattle Times he was at Bite of Seattle with his girlfriend when he heard gunshots.

“It was just pure chaos,” he said.

Those injured in the shooting include a 56-year-old woman in serious condition, a two-year-old boy, a 40-year-old woman, a 39-year-old woman and a 23-year-old man.

News.title: Two-year-old boy overdoses on cocaine on the Jersey Shore
News.content:

A New Jersey man was arrested after a 2-year-old boy overdosed on cocaine while allegedly in his care at the Jersey Shore.

Alexander Moles was charged after the youngster fell ill in North Wildwood on July 20, suffering from difficulty breathing.

Prosecutors say that firefighters were called to Moles’ vehicle, stopped at an intersection, after they received a report of a sick boy.

“EMS administered two doses of Naloxone nasal spray (NARCAN), to which the child responded to, and transported the two-year-old to Cooper University Hospital Cape Regional for further medical attention,” the Cape May County Prosecutor’s Office said.

“Preliminary blood tests of the two-year-old male were also positive for cocaine.”

Alexander Moles arrested after 2-year-old boy in his care overdoses on cocaine ( Cape May County Jail )

Moles, of Ringwood, New Jersey, faces charges of child endangerment and possession of cocaine, among others.

Investigators say that Moles, 39, was on vacation at a property in Wildwood at the time of the incident.

Court documents obtained by New Jersey 101.5 state that Moles was staying at a rental property with a woman and other children.

The documents state that he was responsible for the children while the woman took a shower. When she returned, she found that the boy was “sleepy”. Moles allegedly called her on his way to the hospital, saying that the child was falling asleep and the woman called 911.

Investigators say that during a search of the property, they found pieces of a pill, several tinfoil packets labeled “tapentadol hydrochloride”, and a clear plastic bag containing a white powdery substance, the outlet reported.

Moles was booked at Cape May Correctional Facility and released following a detention hearing on July 24, officials said.

The parents of a British student killed on a school trip to the Maldives are still seeking justice for their daughter nearly two years on from her death.

Jenna Chan died on 8 November 2024 after being struck by the propeller of a boat during an excursion, organised by the Singapore-based St Joseph’s Institution International Ltd and a UK-registered charity.

The 15 year-old was knocked unconscious and sustained critical injuries before she was pulled up to the boat with help from her traumatised classmates, a lawsuit from the family says. She regained consciousness briefly, whispering “help me”, before being pronounced dead less than an hour later.

Her parents, Dr Jennifer Liauw and Alan Chan, told The Independent that they have spent more than 20 months pleading with the school to work with them to establish exactly what happened to their daughter and ensure it can never happen again.

Speaking from Singapore, Jenna’s parents remembered their daughter as “pure sunshine - warm, smiley, and always thinking of other people.”

“She was the person who held our family together and was especially close to her sister, Alisha, who was her soulmate,” they said. “She hoped to become a geriatrician because she loved older people and wanted to care for them. That was Jenna: kind, helpful, and full of love.”

open image in gallery Jenna's mother, Dr Jennifer Liauw, said they have spent more than a year and a half pleading with the school to work with them to establish what happened ( Family handout )

They said the most important objective for them was to “hold the school accountable by ensuring transparency” in risk management, emergency planning and post-incident decision making.

“We hope the process will lead to meaningful improvements in how overseas school expeditions are planned, supervised, and managed, with clear accountability when those standards are not met,” they said of their lawsuit.

“If this case results in stronger governance and better protection for future students, it will have achieved something far beyond our own family.”

In the lawsuit filed on Monday, Jenna’s parents allege that the school has “refused to be held accountable” for their daughter’s death and “instead remained belligerent”.

St Joseph’s, a fee-paying international school for more than 2,000 students aged 4-18 in Singapore, denies any wrongdoing.

“For us, accountability means transparency, recognition of the school’s responsibilities, and clear evidence that meaningful changes have been made,” the family said in a joint statement. “In our view, the school has failed to live up to these expectations.

“We did not want to be here,” said Dr Liauw. “For over a year and a half we asked the school to work with us to find out what happened so this can never happen to another child. Every door was closed. This claim is about accountability, and about making sure Jenna is the last.”

open image in gallery Tragedy struck during the school trip to the Maldives (file photo) ( AFP/Getty )

They point to a letter from the school’s lawyers asserting bluntly that the school “does not owe Ms Jenna Chan a positive non-delegable duty of care to protect and safeguard her from the risk of harm”.

The family believe that the school, which charges fees of up to £26,900 per year, failed to do due diligence around the Maldives Expedition in 2024, which was compulsory for Grade 9 students and a requirement to progress to the next academic year.

Jenna died after entering the water during a whale shark excursion aboard the MV Sapphire Black in the South Ari Marine Protected Area in the Maldives, while on an expedition run by the UK-registered Maldives Whale Shark Research Programme (MWSRP) charity.

After the teenager entered the water, the captain or a member of the crew started the engine of the boat, causing the propeller to strike her on the underside of the boat.

A “loud thud and a crackling sound could be heard”, the lawsuit states, but the boat continued “towards those in the water”.

A teacher from the school then dove under the boat to free Jenna, who was then brought back on board unconscious with her leg sliced open and an open wound on her back. Another student also sustained cuts to her ankle from the rotating propeller.

Jenna’s teachers attempted to resuscitate her in front of her school friends, who were said to be traumatised by the incident. A nearby diving boat provided them with emergency oxygen as the MV Sapphire Black did not have any on board.

Without a helicopter in the area available to help them, Jenna was finally taken to the Dhigurah Health Centre on Dhigurah Island at around 10:15am, some 45 minutes after they entered the water.

Her parents say the school failed to take reasonable steps to ensure that MWSRP was suitable and qualified to run excursions for school children, and failed to properly vet the Maldives, which they say has seen a pattern of fatal marine incidents on diving and boat tours.

As many as 112 tourists died in marine-related incidents in the Maldives between January 2020 and October 2023, according to police figures circulated last summer.

They also say that other parents found out about Jenna’s tragic passing before they did.

And while her parents were working out how to repatriate their daughter’s body, the school sent out an email to parents of children on the trip writing, “Another day when we got what we hoped for!” and listing the various activities that had taken place that day.

The email included photographs of the students, including Jenna, despite the school’s management having already learned of her death hours earlier.

A spokesperson for the school said: “The loss of Jenna was a tragedy, and our hearts remain with her family. As a school, we continue to offer them our unwavering support and hold them in our thoughts and prayers every day.

“We can confirm that Jenna’s parents had on Tuesday filed a claim against the school in the Singapore High Court.

“The school denies the allegations stated in the claim, which have misattributed fault to the school. As such, the school has retained legal counsel to defend the claim.”

A letter to the parents from the school’s solicitors dated 21 November 2025 said that “it was the boat captain’s act of putting the vessel into reverse after Jenna had entered the water that caused the incident,” according to the lawsuit.

They said as a result that the school “cannot be and is not liable for the boat captain’s act”, the statement of claim said.

The spokesperson for the school added: “The school also informed Jenna’s parents that it did not agree with any suggestion that the school was withholding information from them and that while the school had taken steps to obtain information from the Maldivian authorities who were investigating the incident, the school did not receive any such information.

“The school has reached out to Jenna’s parents on numerous occasions and remains open to meeting with them when they are ready. We are deeply mindful of their immense loss and strive to be respectful and sensitive in every way possible.

“As the matter is now before the Singapore Courts, the school will refrain from commenting further on the matter publicly at this juncture.”

Maldives Whale Shark Research, formerly the Maldives Whale Shark Research Programme, did not respond to a request for comment.

Immo Feldmer carefully tipped smoldering charcoal into a tall mound of earth to kick off the ancient tradition of coal burning.

The inside of the mound was tightly stacked with beech wood which smolders for weeks until it's been turned into charcoal — a craft that's been practiced in the Harz mountain region in eastern Germany for hundreds of years.

“We are making charcoal in traditional earthen kilns, just as it was done here in the Harz Mountains over 1,000 years ago,” Feldmer told The Associated Press in a recent interview as he stood between the mounds in the middle of the Harz forest near the small town of Hasselfelde.

Feldmer and his brother Sascha took over the Harzköhlerei Stemberghaus business of producing charcoal from their father. They also have a handful of workers as the smoldering wood inside the mounds needs to be attended to and carefully watched day and night so it won't start catching fire and burn down to useless ashes.

Once covered in earth, the beech wood — which is known for its high density and the high temperatures it creates once it's been turned into charcoal — burns from top to bottom with the help of air holes. The charcoal is then swept clean of soil, and when it has cooled down, it's packed into 10-kilogram (22-pound) bags for sale.

Charcoal production was essential for mining ore in the Harz Mountains. To extract valuable metals such as silver, lead, copper, and zinc from the hard rock, the ore was crushed and then smelted in a furnace using intense heat. The extremely high temperatures required could only be achieved using charcoal.

Over the centuries, hundreds of families in the Harz region earned their living as charcoal burners. These days ore is no longer mined there and only a few coal burners are left in Germany. The Feldmers mostly sell their charcoal to people using it for barbecues at home.

“Our charcoal is, first and foremost, made from pure beech wood,” Feldmer said, adding that most of the charcoal sold at hardware stores in the country is imported and made of “mixed woods, scrap wood, and waste wood so it can be produced cheaply.”

As Feldmer and his brother would not be able to live from the coal burning business alone — they produce around 40 tons annually — they've also opened a museum about the history of coal burning, a small store and a restaurant where guests can get local specialties including steaks grilled over homemade birch charcoal.

Though the craft of char burning has essentially died out in Germany, Feldmer hopes that his family will keep the tradition alive.

“Of course, we hope ... that our business here will be taken over by our children, that it will continue to operate, and that the traditional craft of charcoal burning will be preserved here," he said.

There is nothing like prime ministers attempting to repeat the mistakes of their predecessors to stir up the political firmament.

But it appears that just a week into his premiership, Andy Burnham is willing to take that risk.

In the great debate over what was the nail in the coffin for Keir Starmer’s two-year premiership, there are a number of candidates.

Included in the roll of dishonour are the gifts from Lord Alli, poor polling, taking away winter fuel payments for pensioners, and appointing Peter Mandelson , a known-friend of convicted paedophile Jeffrey Epstein.

But in truth what really did for Sir Keir Starmer happened a year ago, when a massive backbench rebellion forced him to back down on taking £5bn a year off the burgeoning welfare bill and cut benefits.

open image in gallery Burnham wants to bring down the welfare bill ( Reuters )

When Sir Keir finally had to admit defeat just before the summer recess of 2025, he in that moment lost his authority as a party leader and prime minister. Worse, he lost control of the political agenda and the finances of the country.

At a time when international events like the war in Ukraine and turbulence in the Middle East made matters even worse, the UK’s already high debt and a failure to generate economic growth left his government with no room for manoeuvre.

Added to that, he became a prisoner of his own backbenchers, forced to spend even more on welfare by lifting the two child benefit cap.

It was no coincidence that the left-wing MPs at the heart of that welfare rebellion were also the leading cheerleaders for Andy Burnham to sweep in via the Makerfield by-election to replace Sir Keir this month.

And yet, despite the humiliation to his predecessor, Mr Burnham has used his first major interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg to signal that he wants another go at bringing down welfare.

So why does he think he can succeed where Sir Keir so spectacularly failed?

You have to hope for the sake of the sanity of the Labour MPs that Mr Burnham is not going to just rely on the cheery chappy from the north routine to get this through.

open image in gallery Pat McFadden is still work and pensions secretary ( Getty )

Videos about blind tasting with pub snacks or showing off his personal art collection in the Number 10 of the North may generate a number of likes and make Labour MPs feel a bit happier about themselves, but it will not replace substantial arguments on policy or deal with the letters, emails and social media posts from constituents who will lose out on benefits.

We should have seen Mr Burnham’s intent when he kept on Pat McFadden as welfare secretary rather than sack him with the 11 other Starmerites removed from the cabinet with brutal efficiency.

In a now infamous text to Peter Mandelson, Mr McFadden dismissed the welfare Labour MP rebels: “Every meeting I have is ‘who can we tax in order to pay benefits to others?’ They’re asking the wrong questions.”

If we look carefully at what Mr Burnham is now saying to Ms Kuenssberg, it is clear he plans to be tough.

He said: “What you're driving at, which is the welfare bill. I think we've got to get really serious as a country at getting the welfare down.”

And we know how he will do it, making welfare conditional on work.

“It's about changing the nature of the support and making some of the support conditional upon people taking opportunities that are presented in front of them. So you might increase the conditions required to receive benefits. I think it's a good thing that the government has given guarantees of opportunities for young people.”

There are important differences though. Mr Burnham is not putting a figure on the savings, a mistake made by Sir Keir, his chancellor Rachel Reeves and his then-welfare secretary Liz Kendall when they identified £5bn.

By doing that, the previous government made the argument about money, not what is best for claimants.

open image in gallery Sir Keir Starmer suffered a career ending rebellion on welfare ( AFP/Getty )

And in that vain, Mr Burnham is going out of his way to insist that it is society who is failing claimants not claimants themselves being to blame.

In the end though the political and economic realities are the same. The welfare bill has to come down dramatically if the country is to fund the issues like fixing social care, ending rough sleeping, boosting defence spending, business rates cuts for pubs, £2 bus fare caps, VAT cuts for energy bills and whatever next policy Mr Burnham announces.

The one big thing Mr Burnham now has on his side is that it will be very difficult for Labour to replace another leader before the next election. Their systems are much more difficult than the Tories and we all know what happened to the Tories after multiple changes.

So maybe with the right language and some good early vibes, Mr Burnham will be able to make the unpopular tough decisions on welfare that are necessary.

But you still would not bet against a rebellion on the issue possibly with Sir Keir ruthfully chuckling in the background.

News.title: I pitted Dyson £450 airstrait against Shark £199 silkipro – here’s which one to buy
News.content:
The Dyson airstrait was one of the most intriguing launches in haircare when it debuted, largely because it ditched traditional hot plates in favour of a precisely directed airflow that dries and straightens hair simultaneously. The promise was a streamlined approach: your hair dryer and straighteners into one slick tool, cutting both costs and time. (At £450, though, you can buy a high-quality dryer and straightener for the same price, if not less.)

The tool has separate wet and dry styling modes, three heat settings, two airflow speeds and a small LCD to let you know which mode you’re operating. It also features an automatic pause mode that cuts the airflow after a few seconds of putting the tool down, and restarts as soon as you pick it up again. This helps you to save energy and, if you’re guilty of a “Did I turn the straighteners off” panic, this function will give you peace of mind.

The display makes it easy to monitor what mode, temperature and speed you're using (Lucy Smith/The Independent)

The plates can be locked together to allow you to rough-dry your roots and I’d recommend taking your hair from wet to damp by rough blow-drying if you have thick hair. The styling process is the same as if you were to straighten your hair. Try as I might, though, to give some flick to the ends, I’ve never found the bounce to last.

My hair was looked and felt soft and frizz-free after use (Lucy Smith/The Independent)

When in use, the biggest strength against Shark’s iteration is its speed. The airstrait spreads hair evenly across the arms, creating more tension and drying larger sections thoroughly in a single pass. On my naturally straight-to-wavy hair, I consistently needed fewer passes than with the Shark, cutting my styling time by around two to three minutes overall. The finish was sleek, soft and impressively shiny, and my hair had none of the telltale signs (for example, a burning smell or frazzled ends) of heat damage.

While it performs exceptionally well, it’s a seriously expensive tool. The oversized plug, which is about the size of a mango, also isn't at all travel-friendly.

The Shark silkipro plug (left) vs the Dyson airstrait plug (right) (Lucy Smith/The Independent)

If minimising heat damage is your priority, Dyson still has the edge. Without ceramic plates making direct contact with the hair, it delivers excellent results using air alone, making the £450 sum easier to justify for frequent users who style their hair straight several times a week.

News.title: Lando Norris comes in from the cold with dominant Hungarian GP victory
News.content:
Welcome to our live coverage for the 2026 Hungarian Grand Prix from the Hungaroring. This is the 40th anniversary of the race at this track and the 41st edition. I think over the years this track has had a bit of an unfair reputation but we have certainly had some interesting and exciting races over the years. Even over the last few years.

The nature of the track means it is a bit of an outlier. And that means you often get results that go away from the norm of the season. Mercedes took a couple of poles here in the ground-effect era whilst Charles Leclerc did so last year. We have had a handful of first-time winners at this track, too: Damon Hill, Fernando Alonso, Esteban Ocon, Jenson Button and… errr Heikki Kovalainen.

So far that has been true this weekend. Although McLaren and Ferrari have been closing in on Mercedes, the SIlver Arrows have usually had the edge or found it when it comes to qualifying. That was not the case yesterday: Lando Norris took the first non-Mercedes grand prix pole of the season, pipping the Ferrari of Lewis Hamilton by just 0.012sec.

Hamilton, though, takes a three-place grid penalty for impeding Oscar Piastri in Q3. Kimi Antonelli, who had qualified fourth, takes the same penalty for not slowing sufficiently under yellow flags. It was Ferrari who had been expected to be the team to beat but they were the team that dropped the ball. In fairness Norris, in the upgraded McLaren had looked competitive throughout qualifying and was simply able to deliver when Ferrari could not.

The grid is slightly mixed up because of the penalties. George Russell’s season did not get any easier after qualifying seventh but he at least moves up because of those grid drops. The Mercedes’ race pace is expected to be strong but will it be enough to put them into contention with the McLarens and the Ferraris? And let’s not forget Max Verstappen in fourth, either…

We find out at 2pm BST, when the race gets under way.

News.title: Anthony Joshua knocks out Kristian Prenga after worst round of his career
News.content:
Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Anthony Joshua’s heavyweight clash with Kristian Prenga, taking place in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia.

The kingdom plays host to yet another major boxing event, and this is the second part of a weekend that serves as a build-up to a potentially huge match-up later this year.

Prenga’s 20 wins have come against pedestrian opposition, and if he wins tonight then it would be such an upset as to probably finish Joshua’s career as a real name in the sport.

Joshua, the former unified champion, has plenty of defeats to his name. Oleksandr Usyk, twice, as well as Daniel Dubois and Andy Ruiz Jnr.

Tonight should show us where he is. After his loss to Dubois in 2024 he did not fight again until December 2025, when he rearranged Jake Paul’s ability first to stand up, and second, to chew.

A win for Joshua tonight means that all eyes turn to the end of the year, when he is expected to finally meet Tyson Fury in the ring to settle their rivalry.

Now both are deposed champions, the interest has waned a tad, but it remains the biggest all-British clash that anybody could conceive.

Fury, for his part, had little trouble against Mariusz Wach last night, the 46-year-old journeyman who he fought in Thailand. While that was not broadcast live, the clips online hardly suggested it was a classic, but it was enough to keep Fury active as he maintained his focus and avoided his own banana skin.

Joshua now needs to show that he is capable of finishing a fight. If he struggles, he invites pressure for the next four or five months in the build-up to meeting Fury.
