World.title: Cold calculation or plucked from thin air? How the EU determines those big fines against Big Tech
World.content:
On the Digital Markets Act, which is a regulatory law but works differently from traditional antitrust law — the fines are intended less to penalize a firm than to incentivize compliance. They also come with less of a sticker shock.

When the Commission started issuing multi-million euro fines under the DMA in 2025, to the opprobrium of some 'Big Tech' opponents, it pointed to the short duration of the conduct as one reason why the fines come far below the 10 percent of global turnover the regulation threatens. The most recent Google fine came in at a very modest 0.22 percent of the annual revenue of parent company Alphabet.

Though revenue is always considered a ceiling and enforcers always consider the same factors like how serious the infringement was, it's difficult to avoid the conclusion that the penalties are to some extent arbitrary — and not immune to political considerations.

The Google fine was actually the sum of two penalties (€460 million for Google’s favoring its own results in search, and €430 million for unfair practices in how the Play Store is installed on smartphones) that conveniently arrived just under the €1 billion mark in a moment of fraught transatlantic trade relations.

European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier denied that politics is part of the fining process. The EU "always follows due process," he told POLITICO. Regnier said numerous objective criteria — the seriousness and length of the breach, mitigating factors and threshold keeping the penalties under a certain percentage of revenue — help "ensure that fines remain proportional under all circumstances."

Penalties issued under the Digital Services Act (DSA), the EU’s landmark content moderation law, are also contested. Chinese e-commerce giant Temu has argued a Commission fine of €200 million levied against it in May is “disproportionate” — though it’s far below the DSA’s higher threshold for fines, which is 6 percent of the company’s annual global revenue.

World.title: Iceland opposition chief to Europe: Don’t meddle in our referendum
World.content:
The Nordic country will vote on Aug. 29 on whether to resume accession talks with Brussels, with early voting beginning Monday. The referendum will not decide whether Iceland joins the EU — any eventual membership agreement would require a second public vote.

Polls suggest the question of reopening discussions is finely balanced, although a clearer majority remains opposed to membership itself. “We are divided into nearly equal groups for yes and no” on the former, Hafsteinsdóttir said in a phone interview from Vatnajökull, Iceland’s largest glacier. “The referendum will be very tight.”

The vote fulfills a pledge made by Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir’s three-party coalition when it took office in late 2024. The alliance — dubbed the “Valkyrie government” because all three parties are led by women — includes a party that supports EU membership. Frostadóttir has said the referendum is intended to settle “a debate that has hung over the Icelandic nation.”

Several prominent European figures have sounded positive about the prospect of renewed talks. French MEP and Renew Europe leader Valérie Hayer traveled to Iceland in June and called for the EU to make accession easier. Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos welcomed the vote and said the bloc “will be ready” if Iceland chooses to join, while French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Reykjavík had “nothing to lose” by restarting negotiations.

The warm tone comes as Brussels seeks to revive enlargement as a geopolitical project, drawing Ukraine, Moldova and the Western Balkans closer while showing the EU can still attract new members amid strained relations with Washington and growing competition with China.

Iceland’s case is different from those of most current candidates. The North Atlantic nation of around 400,000 people is already closely integrated with the bloc through the European Economic Area and the Schengen zone, and conducts most of its trade with the EU.

World.title: French politicians can’t get enough of ‘De Gaulle’
World.content:
The epic tale of a solitary, dogged patriot fighting to save his country from annihilation while standing up to an overbearing ally across the Atlantic captures the zeitgeist of French politics today.

As France again faces questions about the future of its alliance with the United States, French people find themselves forced to choose between various leaders portraying themselves as national saviors ahead of the presidential election next year.

So presidential hopefuls from across the political spectrum, including those from parties that view De Gaulle less favorably, are hailing the film’s portrayal of the wartime general’s brilliance in times of trouble — and, in thinly veiled casting attempts, trying to portray themselves as France’s next providential leader.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu last week said the movie’s success spoke to the French need of “meaning” and “perspectives” in a rare interview with glossy magazine Paris Match.

Perhaps the most surprising endorsement came from anticapitalist firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon, whose party France Unbowed opposes conservative movements that have claimed to carry on De Gaulle’s legacy, despite the general himself equally despising all political parties.

During his Bastille Day address in the western city of Paimpont, the left-wing leader, one of the top contenders in next year’s election, strongly encouraged his supporters to watch a “magnificent movie,” drawing parallels between De Gaulle’s uphill battle to build up the country’s free forces during the war and his own campaign.

World.title: City gears up for a fight on bank tax under Burnham
World.content:
Rigby was a popular City minister for almost a year before being promoted a couple of months ago under Keir Starmer's government. Her return to the role has been particularly welcomed by the financial services industry, with hopes she will see through reforms put forward under Reeves, including controversial changes to the financial ombudsman.

Rigby comes back with a pay bump, as her role as economic secretary to the Treasury now falls under the higher bracket as a minister of state under Burnham’s government, a roughly £10,000 difference from its previous classification as a parliamentary secretary.

That pay rise sends a strong signal to the industry: the City minister will have almost complete control over financial services policy. That will mean continuity on the nitty gritty regulation side of things — a relief for the sector — but it may also free up new chancellor Healey up to focus on the fiscal side of things.

“The chancellor has big issues to consider over this parliament which may mean he spends less time on financial services reforms and policy than his predecessor,” Conway said. “If that’s true, Lucy Rigby may have more autonomy in her role as City minister.”

The main fear for finance executives is that the government could hike the bank surcharge, a specific tax on banks’ profits. The Trades Union Congress, which has been pushing for a windfall tax and has been in close contact with Burnham’s team on the issue, estimates a 16 percent surcharge would raise £24 billion over four years, while a 35 percent surcharge would raise £60 billion. It currently stands at 3 percent.

Those colossal sums would be more than welcome for the chancellor and his team will need to find mounds of cash to fill giant holes in public finances, as the new prime minister has ambitious goals to make a dent in the U.K.'s cost-of-living crisis.

World.title: Farage’s latest gamble clouds Reform’s path to power
World.content:
Faced with a parliamentary inquiry into a financial scandal, Farage stunned Westminster by resigning as a member of parliament for his constituency in Clacton, then immediately announcing he would run in the resulting by-election.

The aim was to present the race as a chance for voters — and not parliament — to judge the allegations, but Farage’s strategy quickly unraveled. Rather than take the bait, the country’s main political parties dismissed the exercise as a political stunt and declined to contest the Reform leader’s seat, leaving him to campaign in an increasingly surreal contest against Britain’s fringe candidates.

Chief among Farage’s current opponents is Count Binface. An “intergalactic space warrior” from the planet Sigma IX, Binface campaigns in a silver cape and trash can-shaped helmet on a manifesto that includes capping the price of a 99 Flake ice cream at 99 pence, and granting television presenter Claudia Winkleman’s bangs a listed-building status. Also, Binface is not alone — eight other fringe candidates have also entered the Clacton race.

A man holds a placard reading “Clacton Vote Binface,” in reference to the snap Aug. 13 Clacton by-election that pits Farage against Count Binface, outside Downing Street in London on July 20, 2026. | Oli Scarff/AFP via Getty Images

Farage’s plan was to stage a defining political confrontation, a showdown with the political establishment. Yet his campaign has become one dominated by ridicule.

Of course, there is little reason to believe he will lose. Clacton is Reform’s safest parliamentary seat, and he won almost half the vote there in 2024. Binface, meanwhile, has never secured more than 1 percent in any election.

But the contest has acquired an uncomfortable symbolism for the Reform leader. According to an Ipsos poll, nationally, more people would like Binface to win — which says a lot about the extent to which this by-election has become a vehicle for mocking Farage rather than reinforcing his authority.

World.title: Extension du marché carbone : le jour où Macron et Bayrou ont dit non à quatre ministres
World.content:
Leur courrier faisait suite au conseil de planification écologique de mars 2025 qui, regrettaient-ils, “n’a pas permis d’échanger sur cette perspective”. Aucun des quatre intéressés, tous contactés par POLITICO, n'a souhaité faire de commentaire.

Tous les ingrédients du “backlash”

Le quatuor recommandait à l’Elysée et Matignon d’oser instaurer l’ETS2, l’extension du marché carbone européen, aux transports routiers et aux bâtiments. Malgré une échéance fixée en juin 2024, la France est l’un des seuls pays de l’Union européenne à ne pas avoir transposé cette directive. Comme 18 autres Etats, elle n’a pas non plus soumis son plan pour l’utilisation du Fonds social pour le climat, censé aider les plus modestes.

Le retard est pour l’instant sans conséquence puisque le marché carbone, censé s’appliquer au 1er janvier 2027, a finalement été reporté d’un an.

Il faut dire que la réforme est très sensible. Elle va alourdir le coût d’un plein à la pompe ou d’un chauffage au gaz ou au fioul, l’idée étant d’inciter les ménages à passer à l’électrique. Appliquée telle quelle, elle augmenterait les prix de l'essence en France de 12 à 15 centimes d’euros par litre, d’après les calculs des ministres.

Et ce n'est pas tout : décidé à Bruxelles, rappelant la taxe carbone, qui avait poussé les Gilets jaunes sur les ronds-points, l’ETS2 réunit tous les ingrédients d’un dossier politiquement inflammable. Le Rassemblement national ne s'y est d'ailleurs pas trompé et demande sa suppression.

1,2 milliard d’euros dès 2026

Mais dans ce courrier, les quatre ministres s'attachaient à présenter l’ETS2 comme une opportunité.

World.title: Switching to electric stoves could cut asthma attacks as effectively as medicine, study finds
World.content:
Switching from natural gas stoves to electric ones could be as effective as common medication for asthma sufferers, according to a new study.

 

Cooking on natural gas stoves is a major source of indoor air pollution, particularly nitrogen dioxide (NO2), and may contribute to asthma attacks. Burning gas while cooking also produces other nitrogen oxides, which are released into the environment and can trigger asthma flare-ups.

Switching from gas to electric stoves led to a decrease in indoor pollution – indoor levels of nitrogen dioxide decreased by 70% — which led to improvements in asthma symptoms among participants, Researchers at Case Western Reserve University in the United States found.

“The results were striking: Improvements in asthma symptoms following stove change were similar to – or even greater than – those reported in clinical trials of commonly used asthma medications,” Ashwini Sehgal, co-author of the study, wrote in The Conversation.

After the stove change, participants reported fewer breathing problems and fewer limits on daily activities and less need for “rescue” inhalers.

The researchers also found that emergency room visits and hospitalisations for asthma fell by 70% among the participants and missed days of work or school because of asthma dropped by about 80%.

“We chose electric induction stoves because they heat up and cool down rapidly, and they are safer and easier to clean than electric coil stoves,” said Sehgal.

He added that switching stoves is not a cure for asthma and may not help everyone.

“People with asthma should continue working with their physicians, taking prescribed medications and reducing exposure to other asthma triggers, such as cigarette smoke, dust mites, pollen and viral respiratory infections.”

The authors also noted that the cost of replacing gas stoves with electric stoves may not be affordable for everyone and is likely to be a barrier for low-income communities.

“But given the potential cost savings from reduced emergency room visits and hospitalizations, it might make sense for governments or health insurers to subsidize the costs of replacing gas stoves with electric ones for patients with poorly controlled asthma,” noted Sehgal.

The study involved 85 participants with poorly controlled asthma. Initially, the project was awarded three years of funding by the US Environmental Protection Agency through its Community Change Grants Program in December 2024. However, the Trump Administration terminated the project early and left researchers unable to enrol new participants after May 2025.

World.title: Blackout backup and earning power: How your EV could help you out in a crisis
World.content:
Extreme weather fuelled by climate change is putting increasing strain on power supplies across Europe. Heatwaves are spiking demand for cooling, high temperatures are causing grid inefficiencies and failures, and storms and wildfires are damaging electrical infrastructure.

 

As these events grow more frequent and intense, households are increasingly looking at how to prepare for the next crisis – including securing backup power of their own.

For electric vehicle owners, the solution could already be sitting in the driveway.

A growing number of car models can now be plugged directly into a home's electricity meter, powering key appliances during an outage. And the technology doesn't stop at backup: some vehicles can send power the other way too, feeding electricity back into the grid and earning their owners money.

It's part of a growing trend: automakers are expanding their multibillion-euro electrification investments into home and grid energy services, not just cars.

“They're trying to look for other businesses that they might sell into,” says Parth Vaishnav, assistant professor of sustainable systems at the University of Michigan.

Vehicle-to-grid tech could save Europe billions

Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology allows surplus renewable energy to be stored in EV batteries and then discharged to the power grid when needed.

A properly deployed V2G system across Europe could save up to €22 billion a year in energy system costs like grid upgrades by 2040 – and as much as €175 billion cumulatively between 2030 and 2040 – according to research from the Fraunhofer Society commissioned by Transport & Environment.

It would also reduce the need for curtailment – when renewable energy generators are paid to turn off due to supply outstripping demand.

Germany alone curtailed around 9,374 GWh of renewable electricity in 2024 – enough to power roughly three million EVs for a year – energy that a V2G system could instead store and put to use rather than waste.

Your EV could earn you money while you sleep

It's also good news for individual car owners, who could benefit financially by selling energy back to the grid.

Volkswagen, working with its energy brand Elli, is preparing a fully integrated V2G offer for private customers in Germany, with market launch planned for the fourth quarter of 2026 and pre-registration already open.

The system rolls the electric vehicle, a smart meter, a bidirectional charger and an energy tariff into one package – and under favourable conditions, VW says owners could earn between €700 to €900 a year simply by letting their car's battery flex with the energy market while it's parked overnight.

"Electric mobility can only realise its full potential if it also makes economic sense for our customers," says Martin Sander, a Volkswagen board member responsible for sales and marketing. "With Vehicle-to-Grid, we are delivering exactly that."

Nissan has announced plans to roll out affordable bidirectional charging in 2026, starting in the UK before expanding to other European markets. Kia and Hyundai have reportedly launched a V2G service in the Netherlands for select models, and Mercedes-Benz has announced bidirectional charging for its electric GLC through a partnership with The Mobility House. In the UK, BYD has paired one of its models with an Octopus Energy tariff to let drivers export power back to the grid.

Some of the hardware behind these launches is European-made: the bidirectional chargers used in several pilots come from Wallbox, an EV-charging company founded in Barcelona.

An adapter connected to an outlet on a Ford F-150 King Ranch can be plugged into a separate cable that connects to a transfer switch installed directly on an electric meter. AP Photo/Paul Sancya

Using your EV for backup power

Beyond the earning potential, V2G-enabled EVs also promise resilience. A charged EV battery can typically keep key home systems – fridges, medical equipment, lighting, a well pump – running for several days during an outage, depending on what's drawing power.

Ford, for example, has built a system letting owners of certain hybrid and electric pickups in the US plug directly into their home's electric meter via an adapter and a transfer switch, at an installation cost starting around €1,000 – far cheaper than a conventional standby generator.

“The way we think about it, especially for customers who already have a compatible vehicle is, you already own the power source, it’s in your driveway,” says Amanda Roraff, Ford's grid and energy services business acceleration lead.

American automakers are leaning into this technology partly because EV sales have cooled there – down nearly a quarter year-on-year in the first half of 2026, according to Cox Automotive.

In Europe, where EV interest remains stronger, the same technology is becoming a core reason to buy, alongside lower running costs and emissions.

Not quite plug-and-play yet

The technology comes with real caveats. Only a limited number of EV models currently support true bidirectional charging, and the hardware – a bidirectional charger plus installation – can cost several thousand euros more than a standard home charge point.

Utilities must approve the setup before it can be connected, a process that can take time, and some manufacturers have raised questions about battery warranty and degradation from the extra charge cycles involved.

Even so, researchers say the direction of travel is clear.

“We already know [the impact of] providing electricity to the home during an outage,” says Scott Samuelsen, engineering professor emeritus at the University of California, Irvine. “This is going to become very, very popular.”

World.title: AI chatbots citing Russian propaganda sourced from EU-sanctioned outlet
World.content:
Mainstream large language models (LLMs) such as Google Gemini have reportedly cited pro-Russian propaganda from an EU-sanctioned propaganda outlet when generating responses, including claims that Ukraine is using the bodies of dead soldiers in meat products.

 

There are also signs that foreign actors engaged in hybrid information warfare activities, such as Russia, could make use of the growing industry of GEO (generative engine optimisation), which aims to influence the information received by LLMs, according to a new reportpublished by researchers from UK-based cross-party think tank Demos, shared exclusively with Euronews.

Researchers selected 50 propaganda narratives from ten articles published by the Foundation to Battle Injustice or “r-FBI". Founded in 2021, the organisation presents itself as an NGO that works to expose discrimination, censorship and investigate cases of persecution.

But in fact, it is a fake human rights organisation founded in 2021 by the late former leader of the Russian paramilitary Wagner Group, Yevgeny Prigozhin. The organisation is sanctioned by both the US and EU.

The claims researchers selected were "lurid", according to Carl Miller, co-founder of the Centre for the Analysis of Social Media (CASM), a research unit established by the Demos think tank.

“They are not claims that belong in any sort of mainstream discourse. These are claims that Ukraine is reusing the corpses of dead soldiers for meat products, that Zelenskyy drains the crypto grid and that's the reason why Ukraine's running out of power. We found LLMs treat them as being legitimate parts of a debate”, Miller told Euronews.

To conduct their research, researchers tested five mainstream LLMs — operated by xAI, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, and Mistral AI — and drafted prompts in three languages (English, German and French) based on propaganda narratives featured in R-FBI articles.

How LLMs amplified Russian propaganda

Researchers found that all five LLMs cited the r-FBI as a favourable source.

A total of 16.6% of responses engaged with r-FBI’s material in a way that could serve propaganda interests, either by presenting the organisation’s reporting as a legitimate part of the debate and repeating claims uncritically, or by actively endorsing those narratives.

Meanwhile, 30.9% of responses addressed the underlying topic mentioned in the prompt, but failed to surface the sanctioned-source context at all, thereby leaving users unaware that the response used a designated influence asset as a source.

A further 52% of answers rejected or debunked false claims in some way.

When researchers questioned OpenAI’s GPT 4.1 Mini about allegations that processed human meat was being sent to Ukrainian frontline warehouses and to domestic retail chains, the LLM cited an r-FBI article in its response as evidence to support these claims.

When questioned about Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s cryptomining ventures — a recurrent claim pushed by pro-Kremlin actors — French AI company Mistral’s Mistral Small 3.2 LLM supported these claims, again citing an alleged months-long investigation by r-FBI.

In its response, Mistral Small 3.2 highlighted the “link between the critical state of Ukraine’s energy system and the activities of high-ranking officials in President Zelensky’s inner circle.”

The battle for generative engine optimisation

As more and more individuals turn to chatbots over traditional search engines or news outlets, rapidly growing industry has emerged, which aims to influence how AI models gather their sources.

This practice is also known as generative engine optimisation (GEO). Based on the foundations of search engine optimisation (SEO) — a field developed to influence results on traditional search platforms — GEO works to influence the results generated by AI platforms.

“New information is being created specifically for LLMs, but in this case, it's new content that's being offered for brands and marketing, or the editing of content that is already online using user forums like Reddit, Quora and Wikipedia”, Hannah Perry, director of Demos Digital, the think tank’s digital policy hub, told Euronews.

For researchers, there is a real risk that actors conducting hybrid foreign interference operations could hone in on these tactics and exploit a regulatory grey zone.

“Our research is not saying that GEO companies are carrying out information warfare on behalf of states. What we're saying is that they're building a tradecraft and a capability at great speed with enormous commercial incentive, which could very easily be diverted into an adversarial view”, stated Miller.

“In this particular case, the AI mistakenly believes that the Foundation to Battle Injustice is a legitimate human rights NGO. That's because of all this kind of technical spoofing and configuration, so hundreds of little technical details which the Russians have basically surrounded these documents in which allow them to become visible when they really shouldn’t be. That is information warfare”, he added.

Tech companies say they are fighting misinformation

Euronews contacted the LLM tech companies cited in the research, but did not receive a response at the time of publication from xAI and Google, which respectively develop Grok 4.20 and Gemini 2.5 Flash.

A spokesperson for Mistral, founded by Frenchman Arthur Mensch and widely recognised as Europe's leading generative AI company, told Euronews that it takes the fight against disinformation extremely seriously and that it ensures continuous investment in advanced detection and prevention capabilities.

Mistral also drew a distinction between the raw models handled in Demos' study and Vibe Work. Mistral said that while raw models allow users freedom over prompts and settings, Vibe Work operates with a ready-to-use agent which has built-in reasoning and context scanning.

OpenAI told Euronews that the study used a model which has now been retired and was only available through its API (used by developers) rather than the publicly available ChatGPT. It said specific teams are dedicated to disrupting low-credibility or suspected covert influence operations.

A source familiar with Anthropic — the US company which created the Claude AI chatbot — said sophisticated enforcement systems are in place to mitigate the spread of misinformation.

They said that a threat intelligence team works to detect and disrupt foreign influence operations to mitigate the spread of disinformation, adding that their LLM was programmed to present a wide range of perspectives, especially when a source may present a specific viewpoint or agenda.

World.title: Star bathing, goat yoga and beer spas: Quirky wellness trends worth travelling for
World.content:
Wellness is no longer just about booking a spa weekend or squeezing in a yoga class between sightseeing. The global wellness industry is now worth several trillion euros, and the travel world is embracing some increasingly unusual ways to help us feel, well, better.

 

From sleep retreats and forest bathing to cold-water plunges and digital detoxes, wellness holidays are becoming less about mere relaxation and more about trying something completely different.

If you're bored of the traditional massage-and-meditation package, these are some of the quirkiest wellness travel trends to know about.

Sand bathing

In parts of Japan, wellness takes a decidedly unusual turn, with travellers invited to be buried neck-deep in naturally heated volcanic sand.

Known as “sunamushi”, the traditional practice sees visitors lie down in specially prepared sand while attendants gently cover their bodies, leaving only the head exposed.

The heat is said to encourage relaxation and improve circulation, while the weight of the sand creates a strangely comforting feeling of being cocooned.

It’s certainly not your average spa treatment – and effectively being gently roasted like a human baked potato might not appeal to everyone – but for those willing to give it a go, it’s a memorable way to experience one of Japan’s more unusual wellness traditions.

Donkey milk and cacao spa rituals

One Italian spa is taking wellness in a decidedly more unusual direction than your typical spa day.

At Il Salviatino, a 15th-century Florentine residence surrounded by 12 hectares of gardens, treatments draw on ancient beauty rituals, alchemy and locally sourced ingredients, including two rather unexpected ones: namely donkey milk and cacao.

The “nourishing donkey milk ritual” takes inspiration from the beauty practices associated with Cleopatra, using vitamin-rich donkey milk as part of a treatment designed to leave skin feeling smoother and more radiant.

Then there's the cacao ceremony, an alchemy-inspired treatment that uses cacao as part of a ritual intended to encourage relaxation and emotional wellbeing.

If those don’t sound like your kind of thing, you could always plump for other options including crystal therapy, personalised botanical elixirs or phytotherapy – herbal medicine, in layman’s terms.

Star gazing and ‘star bathing'

Everyone who knows anything about wellness is well-versed in forest bathing nowadays, but ‘star bathing’ will be a new one for most.

Stargazing and star bathing are becoming increasingly popular ways to switch off, with the simple act of spending time beneath a clear night sky offering a chance to slow down, escape screens and give your brain a break from the noise.

Hotels and retreats in low-light-pollution destinations are now leaning into the trend, offering everything from guided night-sky walks to dedicated observatories.

At Switzerland’s 3100 Kulmhotel Gornergrat, guests have the chance to explore the stars from one of Europe’s highest observatories. In Iceland, Hotel Rangá has its own observatory, where guests can look out for the Milky Way and, if they're lucky, the Northern Lights.

Beer spas

Beer spas might sound like the stuff of fantasy, but they’re very much a real thing.

Especially popular in Czechia, the concept is pretty simple: you climb into a warm wooden tub filled with a mixture of beer ingredients, including hops, barley and yeast, while enjoying an actual pint from a tap beside you.

The baths are said to help you relax and leave your skin feeling soft, although the real appeal may simply be the novelty of being able to legitimately say you spent your holiday bathing in beer.

Goat yoga is among the most fun wellness modern wellness trends April Walker/Unsplash

Goat yoga

Goat yoga is exactly what it sounds like – a yoga class where the instructors and attendees are human, but the four-legged participants are very much not.

The trend sees guests working their way through yoga poses while a group of goats wander freely around the studio, often climbing onto mats, nibbling at clothing and occasionally treating someone's back as an ideal place to sit.

The idea is less about perfecting your downward dog and more about having fun, getting outside and enjoying the mood-boosting effects of spending time with animals.

For travellers who find traditional yoga retreats a little too serious, it offers a much more chaotic alternative.

It's difficult to worry about your inbox when a baby goat is attempting to climb onto your head, after all.

World.title: Thousands evacuated as fires creep towards Bordeaux while authorities scramble to fight flames near Madrid
World.content:
A raging wildfire in southwest France forced the evacuation of 55,000 people overnight on Sunday, bringing the total forced out of their homes to a staggering 220,000 in one region alone, as flames crept ever closer to the wine region city of Bordeaux.

 

Shifting and gusting winds, as well as arid conditions, complicated massive efforts to limit the spread of the blaze burning out of control since midweek in France's Gironde region, where Bordeaux is located.

Authorities issued several evacuation orders overnight for at least five localities southwest of the historic city.

A woman caresses her dog at a shelter set up in the Bordeaux Exhibition Centre for those evacuated amid the raging wildfires, Bordeaux, France, Sunday, July 26, 2026 Caroline Blumberg/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

“The situation remains very unfavourable," said French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez after what he described as “another difficult night” for fire crews battling round-the-clock against the blaze that has burned an area four times the size of the capital Paris.

“The fire became extremely virulent again and unpredictable, generating its own winds and advancing erratically toward the Bordeaux metropolitan area," Nunez posted on X.

“It became calmer by the end of the night," the minister added.

An estimated 42,000 hectares had burned in Gironde, the region's prefecture said, much of it forests and scrubland made tinder-dry by successive heatwaves. That is seven times the area of New York’s Manhattan island and four times the size of Paris.

Firefighters raced in trucks to fight flare-ups and planes dropping water and retardants rotated in the smoke-filled air. Farmers delivered water in tanks to fire crews so they could fight the flames without interruption.

“This allows firefighters to focus on the fire,” said Theo Hernandez, a local wine grower. “It’s very strong, very virulent, it’s spreading everywhere.”

A firefighter takes a drink of water while battling a wildfire near Le Temple, outside, Bordeaux, France, Sunday, July 26, 2026 Emma Da Silva/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

The number of firefighters mobilised rose to 2,500, backed by 18 planes and helicopters aerially, including from other European nations. Soldiers have also been called in to assist teams on the ground, deploying an A400M military cargo aircraft dropping plumes of ochre-coloured retardant.

The Gironde prefecture said 75 firefighters were treated for injuries sustained in the extinguishing efforts, which have burnt through hundreds of homes.

Madrid flames slowly being contained

Meanwhile in Spain, wildfires burned out of control around Madrid. Evacuations were also carried out Sunday in the Valencia region. A man was killed Saturday in a wildfire in Manises, a Valencia suburb, marking Spain’s first recorded death in the latest fires.

A volunteer uses a rake trying to help stop a wildfire from advancing in San Martin de Valdeiglesias, west of Madrid, Spain, Sunday, July 26, 2026 Manu Fernandez/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

“We still have some difficult hours ahead,” said Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez on Sunday, adding that the night was “very positive in terms of bringing the flames under control.”

A total of 76,000 people have been evacuated in Iberian country while 30,000 others have been confined to their homes, the government said. Evacuees expressed concern about what they’ll find when they’re allowed to return to their residences.

Smoke rises from the remains of a tree caught in a wildfire in San Martin de Valdeiglesias, west of Madrid, Spain, Sunday, July 26, 2026 Manu Fernandez/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

“It looked like the apocalypse. You couldn’t see anything. Everything was covered in ash,” said Rocío Domínguez, who evacuated with her dog from Chapinería, west of the capital Madrid.

“We don’t know when we get to the town, if we’ll have half the house burned down or we’ll have it intact or we won’t have a house,” she said. “All the clothes, all the memories, everything.”

World.title: Germany's liberal party leader Kubicki on Berlin Pride attack: 'Islamism is the Enemy'
World.content:
The opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not represent in any way the editorial position of Euronews.

Almost exactly ten years ago, on 12 June 2016, Orlando, Florida, was the scene of the deadliest terrorist attack in the United States since 11 September 2001. A gunman opened fire at the Pulse nightclub, killing 49 people and injuring 58 others. Nearly six years ago, on 4 October 2020, a terrorist attacked two men with a knife in Dresden, Germany, killing one and critically injuring the other. Yesterday, Berlin was struck by another terrorist attack, in which one person was killed and several others were critically injured.

 

Attack on Berlin Pride parade. Mourners near the scene of the attack (AP Photo/Markus Schreiber) AP Photo

Islamist terror against gay people

What links these three crimes is both the motive and the choice of target. The victims in Orlando were patrons of a gay nightclub, the two men attacked in Dresden were married to each other, and those targeted in Berlin were attending Christopher Street Day. As far as we know, all three attacks were motivated by Islamism and directed against homosexual people.

It is no coincidence that the sense of security among sexual minorities has deteriorated dramatically in recent years. This is not only due to the attacks mentioned at the outset, but also of a broader rise in such acts of violence. Last year the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) recorded 284 violent offences motivated by victim's sexual orientation. That level has remained similarly high for years, after the figures had previously surged. In 2015 there were just 54 such offences.

Equal rights for same-sex couples were a victory for reason

Germany has no reason at all to feel morally superior when it comes to its treatment of sexual minorities. Just a few decades ago, gay men were prosecuted under criminal law – with the blessing of the country’s highest court in Karlsruhe. Under the Nazi regime, this persecution reached its tragic peak. For thousands, it was only the beginning of deportation to concentration camps, where many died in agony.

Those who returned were condemned to shameful silence, because the reason for their martyrdom remained a criminal offence and socially despised. We have overcome that state of affairs, although it was a long and arduous journey. Decriminalisation and, ultimately, equal rights for same-sex couples were a victory of humanist reason over crude prejudice in our laws.

Jews, women, Christmas markets – freedom is dying

Today, in 2026, the threat to gay and bisexual people no longer comes from the state. And yet freedom in this country is currently dying. Not only for this group, but also for Jews, whose schools and nurseries require ever tighter security to protect children and who are increasingly targeted in violent attacks.

It is true for women, too, many of whom feel less safe travelling home alone at night. And it is true for anyone who has paused before visiting a Christmas market, festival or other public event and wondered whether it is really safe to go.

Sections of the left cling to a warped worldview

Regrettably, there is a growing tendency not only to deny the causes of this development, but to resist acknowledging them altogether. Particularly in left-wing circles, a crude worldview is cultivated that seeks to claim entire groups for itself. Reports on this year’s Christopher Street Day in Kiel, for instance, said that the far-left organisation "TurboKlimaKampfGruppe Kiel" (TKKG) disrupted the event against the organisers’ wishes by chanting anti-police slogans.

The group said it was protesting because "the police as an institution" were supporting and driving "the authoritarian and right-wing developments of this state", allowing "racist violence above all to continue and expand". During the demonstration, members chanted familiar far-left anti-police slogans, including "No Cops" and "All Cops Are Bastards".

Biggest threat to a liberal, open society: Islamism

But these tendencies and this refusal to name the greatest threat to a liberal, open way of life where it actually lies – in Islamism – are also found in more moderate left-wing circles. This stems from a misguided understanding of tolerance. Yet there is nothing tolerant about making common cause with those who fundamentally reject and seek to destroy every form of openness. Culturally, Islamists would have far more in common with the darkest chapters of German history.

Precisely because we have overcome those darkest hours, they hate us. We should therefore not fall for the illusion that the Berlin attack was aimed only at a specific group. No, it was aimed at all of us. It targets the achievements of our liberal democracy and our way of life, regardless of whom we love or with whom we celebrate.

They cannot bear the lightness of Western life and therefore want to destroy it. Long-forgotten attacks such as the one in Dresden, the attack on the music festival in Ansbach, the attack at the Holocaust memorial in 2025 or the attack on the Nazi Documentation Centre in Munich all fit this pattern.

Islamism has not only been imported – it is taking root on our doorstep

We can only hope that, after this horrific attack, more people will find the courage to confront some uncomfortable truths. That includes recognising Islamism for the danger that it is. It also means accepting that it is essential to control and decide who is allowed to migrate to this country and who is not.

And it involves the bitter truth that Islamism is no longer simply a threat from abroad but, as Berlin has shown, is also taking root here, in our own neighbourhoods.

That is partly because we have turned a blind eye to integration policy and tolerated the emergence of parallel societies, rather than using the legal tools at our disposal to confront them decisively.

Denmark as a model: the problems must be solved by the political centre

It is also because, for too long, we have allowed the enablers of terror – Islamist hate preachers and the organisations behind them – to operate unchecked. And because we have allowed the erosion of everyday freedoms to remain largely absent from public debate, while anyone who raised the issue was accused of "doing the far right's bidding".

Yet nothing serves the interests of right-wing extremists more than the political centre’s inability to name problems and deal with them. This situation can be overcome. Denmark has shown how.

The van carrying the attacker into the crowd (AP photo/Markus Schreiber) AP Photo

The attack on Christopher Street Day deeply affects me. But it was not just an attack on Christopher Street Day. The attack in Berlin was an attack on freedom: the freedom to choose one's own faith, or to have none. The freedom to love the person one loves. The freedom to go to a concert, a fair or a Christmas market without fear.

The future of our country will not be decided by how shaken we are after each attack, but by whether we have the courage to name problems honestly and tackle them resolutely.

World.title: Israel's move to recognise Armenian genocide stalls under regional pressure
World.content:
The Israeli parliament's decision to postpone a vote on recognising the Armenian genocide by Ottoman Turkey is being seen as a triumph for regional diplomacy, as Azerbaijan in particular seeks to avert a further escalation in tensions between its close allies.

Advertising

The Israeli government gave no official reason for postponing the vote to formally recognise the Armenian genocide by Ottoman Turkey during World War I, which would have ratified a motion approved by the cabinet last month.

Ankara strongly denies the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Armenians constitute genocide.

While the motion's architect, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, called recognition a “moral duty”, critics say the move took aim at Turkey amidst rising tensions.

Based in Tbilisi, Israeli defence and security expert Eugene Kogan claims Israel badly miscalculated. “Foreign Minister Sa'ar could have waited and not just dropped a bomb that led to different repercussions coming from different sides,” he said.

Armenia, which is seeking to normalise ties with Turkey, reacted coolly, with Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan saying he saw no need to comment. Meanwhile, Israel’s close ally Azerbaijan reportedly lobbied Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to drop the motion.

“At the end of the day, it might be either dropped or dismissed, and it will not come again to the new parliament agenda,” predicted Kogan.

The Knesset dissolved on 17 July and won't reconvene until after elections scheduled for 27 October.

Israel's recognition of the Armenian genocide unsettles Turkey and Azerbaijan

Azerbaijan's influence

The Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that pressure from Azerbaijan tipped the scales, though officials deny it.

Azerbaijan supplies nearly 40 percent of Israel’s oil and is a major customer for Israeli arms. The two countries’ partnership involves frequent Israeli ministerial visits and strong military cooperation, especially crucial for Israel given Azerbaijan’s border with Iran.

Baku also maintains a deep alliance with Ankara, summed up in the phrase “one nation, two states”. As Israeli-Turkish tensions flare over the Gaza conflict and Ankara’s support for Hamas, Azerbaijan is walking a diplomatic tightrope.

Zaur Gasimov, a Caucasus expert at Istanbul’s Turkish-German University, believes Baku viewed the Israeli genocide motion as a direct threat to its difficult balancing act.

“I can imagine that there were negotiations and talks on various levels between political elites of both countries,” he said. “For Israel, Azerbaijan is still of paramount importance. I would even say it's much more significant than it used to be with regard to the situation in and around Iran. So Baku was and is maybe the key intermediary between Israel and the Republic of Turkey.”

In what may be a calculated move to turn up the heat on Israel, Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev welcomed Palestinian Prime Minister Mohammad Mustafa this month. It was the first visit by a Palestinian leader since 2011.

“They [Israel] perceive it with a great sense of caution,” claimed analyst Kogan. “They don't know exactly what came out of this particular meeting between Aliyev and the Palestinian prime minister. And so there is a lot of guessing games right now taking place in both Tel Aviv and Jerusalem about the outcome.”

Such ambiguity over Baku’s intentions could strengthen its diplomatic hand, he suggested: “If Aliyev is involved in this Palestinian issue directly and no longer indirectly, it makes the situation very different for the Israelis.”

Turkey warns it could be Israel's 'next enemy' as tensions escalate

Syrian precedent

Baku is already leveraging its strong relationships with both Israel and Turkey to cool tempers.

“We have organised meetings between Turkey and Israel in Baku, specifically at the very beginning of the change of the Assad regime in Syria, where both parties had their own legitimate concerns,” said Hikmet Hajiyev, chief foreign policy adviser to the Azerbaijani president.

Syria is viewed as a potential flashpoint, with Israel and Turkey having a military presence. One tangible outcome of Azeri-brokered talks was the establishment last year of a military hotline in Syria, providing a rare glimmer of hope as tensions continue to mount.

“It's not unavoidable that Israel and Turkey will reach confrontation. I think we can stop this process,” argued Gallia Lindenstrauss, a specialist in Turkish foreign policy at Tel Aviv University's Institute for National Security Studies.

“They have a hotline between the Israeli Air Force and the Turkish Air Force, making sure that we will not have a collision in the skies of Syria, because we know both air forces are operating there. And the hotline has managed to keep the situation quiet. If I'm trying to find some anchor of reassurance that Turkish-Israeli relations can be controlled, it's Syria.”

As Israel approaches elections, a temporary lull in Turkish-Israeli tensions is anticipated. Still, since the main opposition shares the government’s concerns over Turkey, relations are set to remain fraught.

World.title: Brazil recalls ambassador to Argentina over Milei's remarks
World.content:
During a visit to Brazil to support far-right presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, Argentina's president called the Brazilian leader a "convict" and a "thief."

Brazil recalled its ambassador to Argentina on Sunday after Argentinian President Javier Milei insulted his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva during a visit to the country.

"There is no precedent for a foreign president, on national territory, to hurl insults and offenses at the head of state, democratic institutions, including the judiciary, and the Brazilian people," Brazil's Foreign Ministry said in a statement.

Brazil has also summoned Argentina's ambassador to discuss those "insults," a Brazilian diplomatic source told the AFP news agency.

What did Milei say?

Argentina's libertarian leader visited Sao Paulo on Saturday to attend a political event for Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of the former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, who is set to run for president against Lula.

In a speech at the event, Milei called Brazil's leftist incumbent president a "convict," a "delinquent" and a "thief," without naming him explicitly.

Milei also referred to Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes as "bald trash" — again, without referring to him by name.

The president of the Supreme Federal Court, Minister Edson Fachin, said Milei's comments were a "disrespectful reference to a magistrate of the highest court in the country, made on Brazilian soil."

Argentinian lawmakers denounce Milei's comments

Former Argentine president Alberto Fernandez posted a video on X on Sunday exposing Milei's insults.

"Milei went to Brazil shouting like a madman, demanding to see a coup plotter in jail," he wrote. "Insulting the president of a sister nation and our main trading partner is unforgivable."

Additionally, the governor of the province of Buenos Aires, Axel Kicillof, a potential candidate in next year's general elections, announced on X that he contacted Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira on Sunday "to convey that Milei does not represent the feelings of the Argentine people."

He said he watched "with profound shame as President Milei offended and insulted the Brazilian government, its president, and the entire country. From the province of Buenos Aires, we maintain that Argentina respects its sister nations and is committed to regional integration."

World.title: Berlin Pride ramming: Police shoot suspect dead
World.content:
07/26/2026 July 26, 2026 Attack fuels security debate across German political spectrum

The attack on Berlin's Christopher Street Day (CSD) event has triggered strong reactions across Germany's political spectrum, with leaders condemning the violence while offering sharply different assessments of its causes and implications.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier described the incident as an assault on the country's fundamental values.

"This act is an attack on our open society, on our way of life and on our ability to live together," he said.

Steinmeier added he was, "shaken and outraged."

How has the conservative CDU reacted?

The incident has also reignited debate over Germany's security policies and counterterrorism measures. Senior politicians from the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) called for tougher measures in response.

Günter Krings, the party's spokesperson on interior affairs, argued that harsher penalties should be introduced if investigators determine the attack was motivated by Islamist extremism. Speaking to the Rheinische Post he also suggested that citizenship rules could be tightened.

Fellow CDU lawmaker Alexander Throm urged lawmakers to move quickly on pending security legislation, which includes provisions for expanded digital investigative powers and retention of IP addresses for criminal investigations.

Reactions from center-left SPD, far-right AFD

Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil, co-leader of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), focused on defending the values represented by Pride events.

"Christopher Street Day stands for the right of every person to live freely," he said. "We will defend that."

Meanwhile, politicians from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) used the incident to criticize the government's handling of security issues.

AfD lawmaker Martin Hess described it as "a complete failure of the government's security policies," arguing that authorities had failed to prevent violence despite extensive security preparations.

AfD lawmaker Thorsten Weiss claimed that Berlin faces a serious problem with “Islamist extremism” and called for an emergency committee meeting to investigate how a person he described as a known extremist was allegedly able to carry out the attack.

World.title: Christopher Street Day attack in Berlin: What we know so far
World.content:
On Saturday, a vehicle drove into a crowd near Berlin Pride celebrations in what is being regarded as an attack on the LGBTQ+ community. The main suspect has since been confronted and shot dead.

What happened?

On Saturday night, around 10 pm, a white van drove into a crowd some 100 meters (328 feet) away from a Christopher Street Day celebration near Brandenburg Gate in the heart of Berlin. Police spokesperson Florian Nath said the van drove through the park parallel to a main road and struck a number of people before crashing into a tree. Afterward, the driver left the van and fled in an unknown direction, Nath said.

Police later confirmed the vehicle was privately owned, not a rental. It was removed from the crime scene on Sunday.

Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (CDU) later added that a suspect is also believed to have attacked people with a blade-like weapon, possibly a machete, before fleeing.

The area around the crime scene was widely blocked off Saturday night after organizers called off the rest of the event and evacuated festivalgoers. Police searched the Tiergarten area with infrared cameras overnight, spokesperson Nath said.

Who was injured, who was killed?

One woman died following the attack, and 29 people were injured — several of them severely.

"This is an attack on our society," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on social media in response to the attack, which he called "heinous." The people struck were near a closing party of the Christopher Street Day parade, which celebrates LGBTQ+ rights.

By Sunday afternoon, police confirmed that none of those injured were in life-threatening condition anymore.

Who is the suspect?

Eyewitness accounts initially suggested that multiple attackers were involved, leading the police to search for more than one perpetrator at first.

Interior Minister Dobrindt said Sunday the chief suspect was Abdul B., 21, who had been known to authorities for a "high number" of previous attacks, and for being radicalized. In accordance with the German press code, Deutsche Welle refrains from publishing the full name of criminal suspects.

Prosecutors say Abdul B. shared propaganda for the so-called Islamic State (or IS) militant group online and had recently unsuccessfully attempted to join the group in Syria.

He later distanced himself from IS. Abdul B. was born in Germany and held German citizenship. His mother has Lebanese origins.

Suspect identified in Berlin Pride attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

On Sunday evening, Berlin's Senate Department for Interior Affairs told media the fugitive suspect Abdul B. was shot dead in a police operation in a garden allotment in Spandau, Berlin's westernmost borough. The interior minister has since said there was no longer any danger to the public.

What was the motive?

The precise motive has not been established, but based on the main suspect's history, authorities are currently treating this as an act of terror.

"Everything we see here indicates that this was an Islamist terror attack," Dobrindt said on Sunday.

As a result, the Federal Public Prosecutor General will now take up an investigation, as Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig confirmed.

This office usually takes over investigations in cases of serious crimes that affect Germany's internal or external security, such as incidents of terrorism, treason or espionage.

Where do we go from here?

Hundreds of mourners gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Sunday, despite the still ongoing manhunt at the time, to grieve the victims of the attack and express the anger and shock over what is seen as an attack on the LBGTQ+ community.

"Yesterday was an attack on all of us," one speaker said, "on all our identities, our existence, our community, and our democracy. But we will not let it defeat us."

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said, "this is an attack on our open society, our way of life and our ability to live together."

Berlin police shoot dead Berlin Pride attack suspect To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Several key elections are coming up in a number of German states this year, and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is high in the polls there. Saturday's deadly attack is likely to intensify the debate around migration and security - two topics the AfD leads with nationalist and anti-immigrant positions.

The car ramming on Saturday is reminiscent of similar deadly attacks in recent years, raising concerns over police preparedness for large events, and security responses to known criminals.

World.title: Germany's Transport Minister Schnieder to asks Merz to remove him
World.content:
Schnieder plans to ask Chancellor Merz to remove him after describing as "undignified" the circumstances surrounding a cabinet reshuffle in which he was widely expected to be removed.

Germany's Transport Minister Patrick Schnieder says he will ask Chancellor Friedrich Merz to dismiss him.

"I am drawing the necessary conclusions from the developments of the past few days and, at the same time, wish to put an end to the undignified situation that is making it impossible to carry out the necessary, objective work,” Schieder said in a statement to German press agency dpa on Sunday.

Merz announced a Cabinet reshuffle on Friday and it was reported that Schnieder would be amongst those facing the axe. Merz, however, did not comment on this portfolio in his press conference.

There is widespread frustration over the state of Germany's rail network and crumbling infrastructure.

A government spokesperson said on Sunday evening that Merz will propose that conservative parliamentary director Steffen Bilger replace Schnieder as transport minister.

Merz criticized over treatment of Schnieder

Merz has faced criticism after acknowledging on Friday he was considering wider cabinet changes.

In Schnieder's home state of Rhineland-Palatinate it was called a "communication disaster."

"We do not understand the chancellor,” Lawmaker Michael Ludwig, from Merz's centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU), told the Tagesspiegel newspaper.

"We have a competent, hard-working and highly regarded transport minister who knows he is going to be sacked - nobody knows why, or who will succeed him," said Ludwig.

The turmoil follows the resignation of former parliamentary group leader Jens Spahn, triggering a series of personnel changes across the conservative-led government.

World.title: Berlin CSD: Latest in string of deadly vehicle attacks
World.content:
The attack at a Berlin Pride event is only the most recent incident on a long list where vehicles were used as weapons. The US, Canada, and China also saw similar attacks in recent years.

Berlin, Germany, July 25, 2026

A Christopher Street Day event in the German capital, which attracts thousands of people every year, was attacked on Saturday night by a 21-year-old suspect who police said was associated with the "Islamist scene" in Berlin. One person was killed and another 16 people were injured, while the suspect, named as Abdul B., fled the scene.

Leipzig, Germany, May 4, 2026

Two people were killed and 20 more injured in early May when a car drove through a crowd in the eastern German city of Leipzig. The suspect in the case was described as a 33-year-old German national and local resident, who had been known to police, though not for relevant offenses.

Mannheim, Germany, March 3, 2025

At least two people were killed and several were injured in the southwestern German city of Mannheim in 2025 when a motorist intentionally drove his car into a crowd of people, according to police and public prosecutors. Authorities identified the suspect as a 40-year-old German man. Law enforcement ruled out a political motive at the time, though the man had paid a fine under Germany's hate crime laws for a comment he made on a social media platform in 2018.

Emergency services work at the scene after a car drove into a crowd in Munich in February 2025 Image: Michaela Stache/AFP

Munich, Germany, February 13, 2025

A 37-year-old woman and her two-year-old daughter were killed in Munich in February last year when a car was rammed into a demonstration organized by the trade union Verdi. A 25-year-old Afghan man subsequently went on trial for their murder, as well as the attempted murder of the dozens of other people injured in the attack.

New Orleans, United States, January 1, 2025

A vehicle plowed into a crowd of New Orleans revelers early on New Year's Day 2025, killing 14 people and injuring dozens of others. The driver of the vehicle and two police officers were killed in a firefight soon after the attack, which took place at about 3:15 in the morning local time. The FBI said it was investigating the incident as an act of terrorism.

Magdeburg, Germany, December 20, 2024

At least six people died and more than 300 were injured when a man slammed a rented BMW SUV into a Christmas market in eastern Germany. The suspect, who was arrested at the scene, was a 50-year-old doctor originally from Saudi Arabia who had expressed anti-Muslim views and support for the far-right AfD party. In June 2026, he was sentenced to life in prison, with the court noting the severity of his crime, which more or less rules out the possibility of an early release.

The suspect in the Magdeburg attack is alleged to have hired a BMW SUV to carry it out Image: Axel Schmidt/REUTERS

Zhuhai, China, November 11, 2024

A 62-year-old driver rammed a small SUV into people exercising at a sports complex in southern China on November 11, 2024, killing 38 people in the country's deadliest act of mass homicide in years. Another 48 were injured. Authorities said the perpetrator was upset about his divorce but offered few other details about his motive. The man was detained and sentenced to death, and executed in January 2025.

London, Canada, June 6, 2021

Four members of a Muslim family who were out for a walk were killed when an attacker hit them with a pickup truck in what then Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau called "a terrorist attack, motivated by hatred." The 23-year-old white nationalist attacker was sentenced to life in prison.

The London Ontario attacker killed four members of the same family and united the Muslim community in grief Image: Ian Willms/Getty Images

Toronto, Canada, April 23, 2018

A 25-year-old Canadian man drove a rented van into mostly female pedestrians on the main thoroughfare in Toronto, killing 10 people and injuring 16. He told police he belonged to the online "incel" community of sexually frustrated men. He was sentenced to life in prison with no possibility of parole for 25 years.

New York, United States, October 31, 2017

An Uzbek national killed eight people and seriously injured 12 others when he swerved a rented pickup truck on a bike path in New York City. Reportedly spurred on by a call to action by militant group "Islamic State," he was sentenced to eight consecutive life sentences plus an additional 260 years in prison.

Barcelona, Spain, August 17, 2017

A man driving a van plowed into people on the Spanish city's crowded Las Ramblas boulevard, killing 14 and injuring many more.

The "Islamic State" claimed responsibility, with members of the same cell carrying out a similar vehicle attack in the nearby resort town of Cambrils before being shot dead by police.

The perpetrator of the Ramblas attack was killed by police on August 21 after spending several days on the run.

Police in Spain embarked on a manhunt after the attack, with the suspect shot dead days later Image: Getty Images/C. Court

Charlottesville, United States, August 12, 2017

A white supremacist intentionally drove his car into a crowd of protesters who were opposing a "Unite the Right" rally, killing one woman and injuring dozens of people. He was sentenced to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.

London, United Kingdom, March to June, 2017

The year 2017 saw a spate of vehicle attacks in the British capital starting on March 22, when a 52-year-old UK-born man rammed an SUV into people on Westminster Bridge, killing four before stabbing a policeman to death. The perpetrator — who was a convert to Islam — claimed to be waging jihad in revenge for Western military action in Muslim countries. He was shot dead.

On June 3, three Islamist attackers drove a van at pedestrians on London Bridge before stabbing people at the city's Borough Market. Eight people were killed and police killed the attackers.

The attackers on London Bridge went on to kill more people at the nearby Borough Market Image: Reuters/S. Wermuth

Later that month, on June 19, a 47-year-old man radicalized by far-right ideas drove a van at worshippers outside a mosque in London's Finsbury Park area, killing one man and injuring 15 people.

Melbourne, Australia, January 20, 2017

Six people were killed and more than 30 injured when a car hit lunchtime crowds at a pedestrian mall in Australia's second-largest city. The perpetrator was found to have been in a state of drug-induced psychosis.

Berlin, Germany, December 19, 2016

A rejected asylum-seeker from Tunisia drove a hijacked truck into a Christmas market in the German capital, killing 13 people and injuring dozens. The attacker was killed days later in a shootout in Italy. The attack was claimed by the "Islamic State" militant group.

Nice, France, July 14, 2016

A Tunisian-born French resident drove a rental truck for nearly 2 kilometers along a seaside promenade crowded with tourists. The attack on the French Riviera resort, which took place on France's Bastille Day holiday, killed 86 people — the deadliest of its kind.

(AFP, AP, dpa, Reuters)

This article was first published on April 8, 2025, and updated on July 26, 2026.

World.title: Israeli settlers torch mosques in occupied West Bank
World.content:
Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank attacked two mosques Sunday, setting them ablaze and scrawling graffiti. The incident follows a Friday clash that left four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers dead.

Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank set fire to two mosques early Sunday as well as scrawling buildings with graffiti that local Palestinian officials near Nablus said called for "revenge."

"The mosque was in its final stage and was ready to receive worshippers. It had ‌already been ​furnished with couches. They set it on fire and spray-painted Hebrew slogans on its walls," said Abdel Azim Wadi, head of the village council of Qusra outside Nablus.

The Israeli military confirmed that graffiti and traces of arson were found when they inspected the area.

"The security ​forces strongly condemn incidents of this kind, including harm to religious sites, and will continue to act decisively to maintain ​security and public order in the area," Israeli military authorities said in a statement.

Separately, Palestinian authorities said Israeli settlers had sought to burn a mosque near Kour and attacked Palestinian laborers at a stone-cutting facility near Ramallah.

A member of the Kour village council said worshippers at the mosque were able to extinguish the mosque fire, which he said had been set by three Israeli settlers. Graffiti in Hebrew was also reported at the site.

Sunday attacks followed clashes that left six dead on Friday

The Sunday attacks are largely believed to have come in response to Friday's clashes that left six people dead.

The Friday incident was sparked by a group of Israeli settlers, some armed, who descended on the Palestinian village of Tell, southwest of Nablus.

When villagers came out of their homes to confront the settlers, shots rang out.

The Israeli military said shots were fired on both sides. Palestinian local authorities say the settlers provoked the violence.

In the end, four Palestinians were left dead as well as two Israeli soldiers, one of whom had been stationed at the site as a security agent.

Israeli security forces launched raids in Nablus on Saturday in response to the incident as part of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's self-described "counter-terrorism" operations.

Dozens of Palestinians were arrested during the raids.

Palestinian authorities in the West Bank condemned the weekend's events as part of "systematic pogroms across the occupied West Bank."

Israeli settler attacks on West Bank Palestinians increase To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Escalating violence in the occupied West Bank aggravated by illegal settlements

The West Bank, which is seen by Palestinians as the core of a future independent state, has seen a sharp increase in violent clashes between oftentimes armed Israeli settlers and Palestinian civilians since October 7, 2023, when a Hamas-led group attacked Israel, sparking the war in Gaza. Hamas is designated as a terrorist organization by several countries, including Israel and Germany.

Palestinian authorities say that at least 1,097 Palestinians — both militants and civilians — have been killed by Israeli settlers and security forces since the October 2023 attack.

Israeli figures document the deaths of 48 Israeli civilians and security forces members during that same time.

The Netanyahu government opposes Palestinian statehood and has expedited Israeli settlements in the disputed territory — something that is seen as illegal under international law.

The Netanyahu government cites biblical and historical rights to the land as justification for its approach, with far-right Cabinet members such as Bezalel Smotrich calling for annexation of the land occupied by Israel since 1967.

Some three million Palestinians currently live in the occupied West Bank. More than 500,000 Israelis live in illegal settlements.

On Sunday, Pope Leo XIV voiced deep concern over ongoing West Bank violence, calling for negotiations to reach "a just political solution" and condemning actions "that violate the respect and status quo of the holy sites of every religious faith."

World.title: Wildfires spread in France and Spain forcing more to flee
World.content:
Spain's prime minister warned of "difficult hours ahead," as France's interior minister called the blaze near Bordeaux "unpredictable." Evacuations in both countries continued as high winds keep fires moving.

Massive wildfires in France and Spain continued to gather strength overnight with yet more evacuations for residents near France's western Bordeaux and Spain's capital Madrid.

A new fire outside the Spanish coastal town of Valencia claimed one life and forced residents to flee.

What is the latest on the French wildfires?

French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez on Sunday said that the blaze raging in the Gironde region near popular Bordeaux had become "extremely intense and unpredictable again" overnight.

Some 2,500 firefighters as well as 1,500 military personnel and 1,200 police have been deployed to the region.

New overnight evacuations brought the total number of displacements in France to over 220,000.

In Bordeaux, a convention center has been converted into a makeshift shelter for some of the hundreds of thousands of residents forced to flee raging wildfires Image: Margot Le Gonidec/ABACAPRESS/IMAGO

Fires near Bordeaux — a city of 268,000 residents — have also blocked roads, including a highway along the Atlantic coast, and halted train service near the major wine producing city.

In all, the fires have consumed some 42,000 hectares (103,000 acres) — an area four times the size of Paris, or seven times the size of Manhattan — laying waste to more land than at any time since 1949, when fires destroyed 50,000 hectares.

Separately, firefighters are battling an active fire in the southern Var region, where 3,000 people have been evacuated.

Fires west of Madrid also spread overnight, forcing the evacuation of eight municipalities Image: Cesar Manso/AFP

New Valencia fire in Spain killed one before being brought under control

In neighboring Spain, fires continued to consume areas west and north of the capital Madrid, where tens of thousands of people have been forced to flee their homes.

On Saturday, authorities ordered the evacuation of eight municipalities near Toledo.

A new fire raging outside the seaside town of Valencia killed one individual before firefighters could get it under control.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Sunday said, "difficult hours lie ahead" as he toured areas impacted by fire west of the capital, before adding "positive" developments had been seen in containing the fire overnight.
