Those representing the management side see the need to raise the minimum wage but at the same time are calling for careful discussions as business conditions for smaller companies have deteriorated due partly to the soaring cost of procuring materials due to the Middle East turmoil.

Because higher costs have not yet been fully passed on to consumers, whether smaller firms can cover potential hikes in the minimum wage should be carefully assessed, they argued.

Japan’s minimum wage is revised every fiscal year based on living costs, wage levels and companies’ abilities to pay. Relevant prefectural councils determine their respective minimum wage levels after the central government council comes up with its recommendation.

World.title: This Shiba is a great dog for the right person
World.content:
Shibas, they’re catlike and they’re not for everyone.

But people who love Shibas, accept them on their own terms, because there is special attraction between this Japanese breed and the people who would have no other.

Mushroom is a classic Shiba. Found wandering the streets, he came to ARK in January of last year and has become ensconced in the Tokyo office, where he spends a lot of time sleeping. At times, he’ll bring a toy to play with. He’ll set the toy near you and wait for you to notice.

Affectionate on his own terms, he expects people to respond on his terms too. He’ll feign a cool indifference to being noticed, but really he’s dying to be seen.

That said, Mushroom’s first love is not people. It’s food. His second love is napping.

Though he’ll come across as the strong, silent type, “Mush” cannot hide his joy when people return to the office after being away.

He’s not a fan of cats or small children and would most likely prefer to be the only canine in a household. But he will be a loyal and terrific friend for his owner. Mushroom is a great dog for the right person.

World.title: China’s memory chip makers ride AI boom to new power — and U.S. scrutiny
World.content:
For months, Chinese chip manufacturer ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) had been hiking prices on Huawei, one of the country’s biggest ⁠technology companies. The chipmaker held firm when Huawei demanded relief from the escalating costs, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The standoff came to a head on CXMT’s factory floor in June. A group of engineers from a chipmaking-equipment vendor with deep strategic ties to Huawei had been working in the cleanrooms at CXMT’s core research and development zone in Hefei, Anhui province. Without warning, CXMT ordered the engineers, who had been helping with equipment maintenance, to pack their tools and leave the factory floor immediately, the two sources said.

Executives at the Huawei-connected equipment vendor, SiCarrier, concluded the confrontation was the result of the power struggle between CXMT and Huawei, the people told Reuters. The companies still do business but the engineers haven’t been allowed back into the R&D zone, the two people said.

World.title: The tiny Okayama village providing Japan with a blueprint for forest management
World.content:
Threading through the woodlands encircling Nishiawakura, a village in a mountainous area of Okayama Prefecture wedged against the borders of both Hyogo and Tottori prefectures, an international group of curious outdoor enthusiasts follows closely behind tour guide Futoshi Nishioka.

Approaching the intersection of two adjacent forests, Nishioka gestures toward one side where evenly spaced rows of sugi (cedar) and hinoki (Japanese cypress) trees tower overhead in a seemingly endless stretch. This type of artificial forest accounts for around 85% of the village’s total forestland, he explains — a figure reflective of Japan’s post-WWII history, when coniferous trees were planted nationwide in order to quickly reforest areas devastated by war, while also meeting the surging demand for timber as the country rebuilt.

Noting the tendency of such trees to crowd out other types, Nishioka jokes, “You might describe them as homogenous Showa Era company workers.”

Next, motioning toward the abutting zone — the Wakasugi Primeval Forest, whose wild tangle of tree species includes mizunara (Quercus crispula), maple and horse chestnut — Nishioka continues his analogy by noting that the natural forestland comprising the remaining 15% features both diversity and competition, and thereby more closely resembles society today. Local efforts are underway to cultivate such biodiversity, he explains, to help restore the healthy wild forestland that existed some 400 to 500 years ago — before which time charcoal was burned to produce iron for the local tatara iron-smelting industry.

Futoshi Nishioka conducts a tour of a forest in Nishiawakura, Okayama Prefecture. | KIMBERLY HUGHES

This type of committed approach toward biodiversity is a significant part of what has helped Nishiawakura — with a population of 1,300 and covered in 95% forestland — earn increasing nationwide recognition for its innovative forest health management initiatives, which have served as a model for other communities.

A forest-forward ethos

Despite having the weakest economy in the prefecture, Nishiawakura declined in 2004 to join a merger with surrounding areas, opting instead to launch a multipronged effort toward sustainable forest management, robust economic health and strengthened local relations.

In 2008, the village announced a 100-year plan to promote forest health through measures including structured thinning of its artificially planted sugi and hinoki trees. The project, which recognized an inter-generational nexus aiming to ensure long-term forest health, received certification by the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) Japan.

Nishiawakura’s initiative has also collected additional accolades, including recognition by the central government in 2013 as an environmental model municipality. The village was also selected in 2019 as an SDGs Future City alongside major urban areas including Kobe, Kyoto and Yokohama. Notable efforts to date have included small hydro power generation, and switching from kerosene to a firewood boiler to power onsen (hot springs). The village also contributed toward disaster-resistant forests and decarbonization by adopting a carbon dioxide absorption project covering fiscal 2019 to 2027, through which it issued J-Credits totaling 7,500 tons of CO2 as of November 2022.

By holding regular conversations around creating value from local resources through sustainable products, and facilitating forest health amidst a robust circular economy, various community stakeholders came together to form a concrete action plan based upon shared goals.

Such entities have included Team Nishiawakura, a group of consultants and project leaders uniting numerous community actors through its “upriver to downriver” tours along the forestry chain. Its past initiatives have included crafting such structures as the Awakura Kaikan complex, which houses the village office, library and community space.

Another member organization, the A0 Group — pronounced “A-zero” and under whose auspices Nishioka’s tour was conducted — works to spearhead numerous creative initiatives to protect forest resources while stimulating business-related opportunities. Aptly, the organization is named for the fertile surface layer of organic matter that protects and cultivates the rich life on the forest floor.

Kenta Kawaguchi, a sales representative with A0 Group, at Mori no Gakko in Nishiawakura. The AO Group spearheads creative initiatives to protect forest resources while stimulating business-related opportunities. | KIMBERLY HUGHES

“Our projects include those aiming to reevaluate the human-nature relationship, such as one to restore biodiversity while increasing the value of our rice fields; and another to pass down local unagi (eel) food traditions to the next generation,” explains A0 spokesperson Haruno Hayashi.

“We have also launched a sustainable forest resource use project to construct a supply chain of FSC-certified wood to build entire structures, for which we are presently able to support around 300 homes,” she adds.

Forest wisdom

Another player at the forefront of local initiatives is Mori no Gakko (forest school), established in 2009. Besides conducting tours to promote deeper insight into the finer details of Nishiawakura’s forest environment, it also spearheads forest-thinning efforts. A critical measure to ensure forest health, the process involves removing around 30% of the local sugi and hinoki trees — mostly those that are dying or damaged — to allow sunlight to penetrate down to the forest floor, while also helping to prevent landslides.

The forestry school then cuts the felled trees to specification, often 4-meter-long logs, and sells them to customers including local furniture-maker Youbi. Half of all logging profits are returned to the owner of each tree’s specific mountain lot, with individual owners comprising three-quarters of the total, and local companies the remainder. While school officials note that this unique approach involves considerably complex calculations, they say it helps the village realize its combined goals of forest management and stimulation of secondary and tertiary industries.

The forest school additionally mills, dries, processes, finishes, and sells the thinned wood as an array of creative products. Aiming to facilitate firsthand encounters between consumers and artisans, it conducts its operations on the premises of Base 101% — a spacious building fronting the forest, which flaunts tall glass windows and inset latticed wood patterning. Also serving as a forestry education complex, the structure houses an adjacent wood-processing factory alongside an expansive woodcrafts marketplace known as the Hazai Market and DIY Space.

A showroom inside Base 101%, which houses a forestry education facility as well as restaurants and shops featuring local dishes and handicrafts, in Nishiawakura, Okayama Prefecture. | KIMBERLY HUGHES

Unique products at the market include aromatherapy vials borne from the forest’s lush plant life, along with items crafted from local wood-thinning efforts such as cutting boards and plates, and boxes of multisize, multiuse wooden boards and planks. Creatively titled hitotema (“that one extra effort”) kits also come with instructions on how to use the enclosed knife, carving tool and sandpaper to “sculpt, polish and craft” oversized hinoki-wood spoons and forks into usable utensils. Meanwhile, additional items such as lamps and yukahari natural wooden floor tiles are attractively styled in the attached showroom to provide inspiration for do-it-yourself (DIY) woodcraft enthusiasts.

Also onsite is a restaurant serving local dishes using deer meat and organic rice, along with rows of shelves featuring products from Nishiawakura growers and makers.

Another company, Feuerwork, features wood furniture, wrought iron products and unique forged items, thereby weaving together art, craftsmanship and design. Open since 2015, it is run by Israel-born Ohad Sheinwald Feuer — one of the numerous creatives, both Japanese and international, who have relocated to Nishiawakura after being attracted by the area’s vast nature.

Feuer explains that he and his wife Aki explored the village while traveling through the country via camping car with their 2-year-old son. Looking for a place to settle in Japan, they felt drawn to Nishiawakura after seeing a TV program featuring its 100-year forest concept. Stopping by the town hall, they were accepted warmly and both were offered part-time jobs at a wood factory. Renting a small house in the village, they later moved into a kominka (traditional house), which they renovated as their family expanded to welcome three more children.

After relocating to Nishiawakura, Israel-born Ohad Sheinwald Feuer founded Feuerwork, which features wood furniture, wrought iron products and unique forged items, thereby weaving together art, craftsmanship and design. | Courtesy of Ohad Sheinwald Feuer

Feuer was also granted a government subsidy to help open his business.

“My father is a craftsman and metal fabricator, and I worked with him since childhood,” he says, “so working in a factory was familiar to me.”

Feuer also runs workshops in skills such as iron blacksmithing, woodworking, and bushcraft. “We get visitors from all over Japan and the world; some who join a workshop experience, and others who maybe get inspired by our story,” Feuer notes, underscoring his goal of encouraging others to consider a similar lifestyle in tune with nature’s rhythms.

Deeper connections

The village is also engaged in collaborations with entities beyond Okayama who share a similar ethos.

These include the Dento furniture company in Joge, located in Fuchu, Hiroshima Prefecture, which has begun crafting items including trays and picture frames using wood thinned from Nishiawakura’s forests.

“Our project involves circular craftsmanship that connects the mountainous areas of the Chugoku region,” notes Dento President Toshihiko Fukumaki. “This is important not only environmentally; but also for passing on local industry and culture to the next generation. Our project with Nishiawakura is a wonderful example of putting the concept of circularity into concrete action.”

And as other locales across the country continue facing similar challenges in ensuring long-term forest health, the village’s initiatives have also served as inspiration for similar developments.

“Municipalities and companies nationwide have expressed interest in the forest resource-focused community development, human resources, and business creation which underpin our hundred-year forest project,” A0’s Hayashi recounts. “Similar initiatives have also been implemented in places including the town of Atsumi in Hokkaido, and Kinko, Kagoshima Prefecture, based upon their own local resources and challenges.”

Tour guide Nishioka, meanwhile, who oversees A0’s social relations, echoes this sentiment while also adding a dose of sobering reality to the historical moment of environmental precariousness we are facing today.

“Amidst today’s affluence, resources are exploited for economic reasons,” he observes. “Before the term ‘SDGs’ existed, we spoke in equal terms regarding the ‘triple bottom lines’ of resources, societies and economies. By contrast, our organization’s approach involves an inverted pyramid wherein resources come first, then societies, and economies last.”

“In other words, there is no way you can put these three entities on the same level,” he adds, laughing dryly. “Because you will obviously have no business enterprises if you have no earth.”

World.title: Cyberattacks becoming faster with AI, security firm president says
World.content:
Cyberattacks are becoming faster and more sophisticated with the use of artificial intelligence, Nobuo Miwa, president of Tokyo-based information security service provider S&J, said in a recent interview.

His remarks came after a series of cyberattacks on major Japanese companies, including frozen food maker Nichirei, household goods supplier Askul and beverage maker Asahi Group Holdings, which suffered serious disruptions to their corporate activities due to system failures.

Asked about trends in cyberattacks, Miwa said AI-driven attacks have increased in recent months, shortening the time between the discovery of a vulnerability and the launch of an attack. “Attack programs can be created in the blink of an eye with AI,” he said.

Because Japanese companies have historically faced fewer cyberattacks, many lack adequate defenses, making them attractive targets for cybercriminals, Miwa added.

While noting that it is difficult to eliminate points of entry, Miwa stressed the importance of identifying potential attack routes in advance and taking measures to mitigate risks.

“Countermeasures vary greatly depending on a company’s size and system configuration,” Miwa said.

Attacks with ransomware, a ransom-demanding computer virus, are often launched between late Sunday night and in the early hours of Monday, with data encryption typically completed by early Monday morning, according to Miwa.

“If there is a risk of a major system failure, it is also important to disconnect ordering systems,” he said.

He also emphasized the need for companies to work closely with external cybersecurity firms, while acknowledging challenges related to costs and the allocation of responsibility.

World.title: DeepSeek said to have told backers of funding pause after viral posts
World.content:
DeepSeek has told prospective investors in its second fundraising round that it’s suspending the deal for now, people familiar with the matter said, days after comments widely attributed to founder Liang Wenfeng about U.S.-Chinese AI competition went viral.

The Chinese AI pioneer verbally informed some of its would-be backers that they wouldn’t be signing investment agreements in the coming days, as they had expected, people familiar with the matter said. DeepSeek might choose to resume the deal process at a later date, the people said, asking to remain anonymous to talk about private discussions. The suspension stemmed in part from Liang’s frustration over online reports about his comments to investors during his first financing deal, which closed in June and raised $7 billion for the AI lab, the people said.

The authenticity of those posts, which concerned a transcript of a meeting Liang held with unidentified parties, haven’t been verified. Chinese media including Yicai reported this week that the billionaire founder talked about a reliance on Nvidia chips for AI development and China’s persistent lag in AI sophistication relative to the U.S.. DeepSeek didn’t immediately respond to an emailed request for comment about the transcript or the fundraising.

World.title: Worker, 62, dies after falling from platform while repairing plane at Hong Kong airport
World.content:
A 62-year-old worker has died after falling from a six-metre-high (20-foot) platform while repairing an aeroplane at the Hong Kong International Airport.

Police received a report at 8.35am on Monday that a worker had been injured after falling from a height at a worksite operated by the Hong Kong Aircraft Engineering Company (HAECO).

“Preliminary investigations have shown that when the worker was repairing a plane on site, he accidentally fell from a six-metre work platform,” a police spokesman said.

He added that the worker had been repairing the aircraft’s fuselage indoors. The fall was thought to have happened when the worker mistakenly stepped into a gap between two work platforms.

The male worker was unconscious when officers arrived at the scene and was taken to North Lantau Hospital, where he was pronounced dead at 10.07am.

Hong Kong has reported at least 62 industrial accidents, 24 of them fatal, in the first half of this year, according to data from the Association for the Rights of Industrial Accident Victims and media reports compiled by the South China Morning Post.

World.title: HKU president Xiang Zhang to step down in 2028 at end of second 5-year term
World.content:
In the email, sent to the university community in the early hours of Monday, Zhang described the past eight years spent working to elevate HKU’s academic standing as “a defining honour” of his life.

Two members of the university’s council told the SCMP that Zhang’s departure would be discussed at a meeting held on Tuesday.

In his email, Zhang also reflected on the university’s future in “a complicated, rapidly changing world marked by polarised views and conflicts”, saying the institution would have to meet the challenges brought about by artificial intelligence.

“I have realised that it is time for HKU to embrace fresh ideas and for a new leader to guide this great transformation,” Zhang said.

“I remain a scientist and a professor at heart. I yearn to return to my laboratory, to answer profound scientific questions, and to make a societal impact.

World.title: Black Lake CEO’s strategy to sell AI solutions to factories: turn to food couriers
World.content:
When Zhou Yuxiang, founder and CEO of Shanghai-headquartered Black Lake Technologies, wanted to sell his artificial intelligence (AI) automation solutions to millions of family-run factories across China, he came up with an unconventional strategy: hiring food delivery workers to make sales.

His entire sales team, hired from various industrial cities, survived a gruelling five-day boot camp on articulating how AI can solve specific manufacturing pain points.

“They are very street-smart,” the 36-year-old said in an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post. “Good college graduates are often thin-skinned. They linger in front of a factory and can’t get in.

“But for food delivery guys, they just give a cigarette to the security guard and get in … They can also bypass guard dogs, or find a back door to get into a factory to meet the owner because they deliver food.”

With a sales force of more than 420 delivery workers, Black Lake, established in 2016, has grown to serve 35,000 factory clients, 95 per cent of which are small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

The International Data Corporation also ranks it as mainland China’s top provider of cloud-based production management software.

Hong Kong ‘very attractive’ for next step

World.title: Hong Kong’s lawmakers don’t need to be coddled
World.content:
Eighty per cent of success is showing up, as they say. So, all but one of Hong Kong’s 89 legislators joining a week-long “ national affairs study visit ” to Beijing made a good impression.

Lawmaker Stanley Ng Chau-pei called it a “groundbreaking opportunity” for legislators to study and deepen their understanding of national conditions. Showing up eager to learn and to better grasp how Hong Kong can play a more proactive role in national development is indeed commendable.

The legislature had worked overtime to review the bill for the Huanggang Port and legislators committed their first week of summer recess to the study tour. It’s interesting that the delegation was referred to in one news report as “a class”. The group photos, complete with a banner in the front, resemble those of schoolchildren on summer study tours.

Lifelong learning is crucial. We don’t expect our lawmakers to be know-it-alls, but we do expect them to keep themselves abreast of the latest developments and constant shifts in this fast-paced world.

It is also excellent to see that the current slate of legislators has made genuine efforts to show up in the chamber. Only three lawmakers had an overall attendance rate below 90 per cent. It’s hard to imagine, but it hasn’t always been this way.

World.title: Amber rainstorm warning cancelled, while morning and full-day schools suspended
World.content:
The Hong Kong Observatory has cancelled the amber rainstorm warning, while the Education Bureau has announced the suspension of classes at all morning and full-day schools on Monday.

The weather forecaster cancelled the signal at 9.15am after earlier downgrading the warning from red to amber at 7.47am. It urged residents to stay alert to dangers that might be brought about by river flooding.

The forecaster said that, under the influence of an active southwesterly airstream, heavy showers and squally thunderstorms were initially expected to persist over the vicinity of the Pearl River Delta on Monday.

Classes at afternoon schools would proceed as usual, the bureau said.

The rainy weather comes in the wake of Typhoon Noul, which triggered a No 9 signal for six hours on Sunday morning.

World.title: Hong Kong international, private school enrolment grows amid drop in student numbers
World.content:
Enrolment at Hong Kong’s international and private schools grew for a third consecutive year following the introduction of a government talent scheme in 2022, despite an overall decline in the city’s student population, according to official statistics.

Latest Education Bureau data showed that kindergartens and local public primary schools bore the brunt of the decline, with a record 30 preschools, or 3 per cent of all kindergartens, having shut down or set to close this academic year.

A veteran admissions consultant said the talent schemes introduced in 2022 had brought a significant inflow of mainland Chinese families, many of whom enrolled their children in private and international schools.

The bureau’s annual headcount statistics, collected every September at the start of the academic year and released the following July, showed that 87,220 students were currently enrolled in international and private schools, marking a 12 per cent increase from September 2022, just before the launch of the Top Talent Pass Scheme.

Compared with a decade ago, enrolment in these institutions has jumped by 21 per cent, even though the total number of kindergarten, primary and secondary students in Hong Kong dropped from 797,157 in 2022 to 776,888 in 2025 – a 2.5 per cent decline over the three years.

“The steady growth in international and other private school students reflects mainland professionals and their dependants settling in Hong Kong. It also reflects a persistent demand from affluent local families opting out of the local curriculum,” said Ruth Benny, a veteran consultant for international school admissions in Hong Kong and Asia.

World.title: The one voice Hong Kong can’t ignore on ride-hailing? The public
World.content:
The long-awaited earthquake in Hong Kong’s taxi and ride-hailing scene is almost upon us and the questions are how big the initial shock will be, and how many aftershocks we can expect. The important thing in the coming months will be to keep the focus on protecting the interests of the travelling public.

More than a decade after Uber first set up in Hong Kong, operating in a regulatory grey area, the administration is finally moving to overhaul our ride-hailing system. Tech platforms will be invited to apply for registration this quarter, with the first batch of licences expected to be awarded by late November. In the fourth quarter, individual vehicle owners will be invited to apply for one of the initial 10,000 driver permits . The government expects regulated services to begin in December.

The reason Hong Kong is late to the ride-hailing party will be familiar to long-time residents: the determination of vested interests in the taxi trade to protect their turf and the government’s unwillingness until recently to confront them. However, interests within the taxi trade are not monolithic; most of the 40,000 or so drivers do not own their vehicles, instead renting on a shift basis from one of the 9,000 or so individual and company licence holders that control the fleet of around 18,000 taxis.

Up to now the interests of the two groups have largely coincided. Will the new regime cause these interests to diverge more sharply? Will more drivers wish to own their vehicles to enjoy the full fruits of the ride-hailing system?

Four tech platforms currently offer ride-hailing services here: Uber, Didi Chuxing, Tada and Amap. Amap is operated by Alibaba Group Holding, which owns the South China Morning Post. Assuming all apply and are successful – and assuming no last-minute gate-crashers – then an obvious question for 2027 is whether there will be amalgamation, which has tended to be the practice elsewhere in Asia.

Ride-hailing apps seen in a mobile phone as a local taxi drives past in Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong on August 29, 2025. Photo: Jelly Tse

The nature of the industry favours scale operators as they are better able to offer a comprehensive service, which in turn attracts more drivers to register with them, thus enabling them to provide a better service. We could start with four and quickly concentrate to one or two dominant players.

World.title: Infant formula maker insists product safe after recalls in Hong Kong and Macau
World.content:
The Dutch maker of Friso, a popular powdered infant formula brand, has stressed that tests show its product is safe, despite a recall of a product batch in Hong Kong and Macau after excessive levels of lead were found in samples.

In a statement on Sunday, Royal FrieslandCampina said: “We have conducted additional third-party quality testing on the affected batch. The test results showed that the product complies with Hong Kong and Macau standards.”

The company, meanwhile, stressed that “ensuring consumer safety and maintaining product quality remain our top priorities”.

It said it had been contacting distributors and retailers to arrange exchanges, while also promising swaps or refunds for customers.

Concerns about the product emerged over the weekend after Macau authorities said their tests showed some samples of a specific batch of the infant formula containing levels of lead that exceeded the city’s safety threshold of 0.02mg/kg for such goods.

Authorities in Macau promptly ordered a recall of the batch of Frisolac Prestige Stage 1 (800g).

World.title: Education, health fees among key concerns
World.content:
China to legislate on preschool education

China will push for legislation on preschool education to provide a legal guarantee for the operation and management of such institutions, Vice-minister of Education Tian Xuejun said on Nov 30.

Tian made the remarks at a news conference organized by the State Council Information Office regarding a child abuse case at RYB Education New World Kindergarten in Beijing that received widespread attention in November. He said the Ministry of Education was already doing research on the legislation.

"The ministry will also complete the requirements on qualifications of teachers engaged in preschool education and is considering formulating a code of ethics for them," Tian said.

He also said a plan is on the way to step up supervision of kindergartens and solve the problem of insufficient resources for preschool education. Tian said the case exposed the conflict between public demand for preschool enrollment and insufficient development of preschool education.

"It also showed that some local authorities and kindergartens still have problems of unsound management and failure to implement or fully implement regulations," he said.

Rural health fee increase explained in detail

The National Health and Family Planning Commission recently responded to public concern of newly increased fees for a new rural cooperative medical system.

Fees charged in the new rural cooperative medical system have recently been raised from 30 yuan ($5.5) to 180 yuan.

The NHFPC explained that while fees for individuals have been raised, government financial subsidies to individuals have also been raised accordingly in recent years from the previous 20 yuan per person to 450 per person. At the same time, the government has a comprehensive medical assistance system for those unable to afford such fees. Also, the reimbursement proportion for hospitalization costs for those in the new rural cooperative medical system has also been raised from 35 percent to 75 percent.

Anti-espionage law will help national security

The State Council issued a circular on China's anti-espionage law on Wednesday with detailed rules for implementing the law.

The circular explains several terms in the law, including overseas institutions and organizations, individuals, spy organizations, spy organization agents and hostile organizations. It was made clear that national security departments under the State Council will identify unacceptable behavior.

According to the circular, providing funds, venues and materials to spy organizations and individuals will be identified as helping them.

Conducting espionage activities in the territory, accepting overseas funds to endanger national security or connect them for spying activities will also be deemed as collusion.

Staff members at national safety departments are authorized to arrest and hunt criminal suspects, and their anti-espionage activities will not be interrupted by any other illegal actions.

It said that Chinese people and organizations retain the right and privilege to secure national safety, and their contributions such as providing clues about spying activities, collaborating with national security departments and fighting espionage activities will also be rewarded.

World.title: International group praises green revival
World.content:
High-level advisory panel pitches 15-year pollution fight, but holds China up as model

A high-level international advisory body applauded China's efforts to improve the environment and suggested a 15-year strategy against pollution in a draft recommendation report on Monday.

China has made building an ecological civilization an important goal and has taken comprehensive measures to improve the environment. This has resulted in positive results, including improved air quality, Vice-Premier Zhang Gaoli said when chairing the annual meeting of the China Council for International Cooperation on Environment and Development, a high-level international advisory body.

Like Zhang, Erik Solheim, executive director of the United Nations Environment Programme, said he was impressed by China's tremendous achievements regarding its environment in recent years, in particular curbing much of the smog problem.

"China is capable of solving the environment problems themselves," said Solheim, the council's vice-chairman, adding the best practices taken by China could provide guidance to other areas facing similar issues.

His praise of China's approaches to move toward being an ecological civilization won wide support from other members of the environmental council, which includes senior officials and experts from home and abroad.

The council's draft recommendation presents highlights of the war against pollution in air, water and soil, and suggests the creation of a 15-year strategy that will be "focused on cost-effectiveness, synergies and ways to build public confidence about eventual results".

Ideally, the integrated rollout should be ready before 2020, to be in line with the 2035 pivot point, when China expects to be a "basic modern country", the draft said.

Solheim said he is confident that China can reach the 2035 goal to build a "beautiful China", considering the determined and effective efforts adopted in recent years.

Along with the longer-term strategy to curb pollution, council members suggested creating conditions for fair competition and incentives for green industries.

Based on the input from Monday's meeting, the advisers and their support teams will modify their proposal and provide a final version to the State Council through the Ministry of Environmental Protection.

zhengjinran@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Beijing, Moscow drill for potential missile warfare
World.content:
China and Russia kicked off their second joint computer-assisted anti-missile drill on Monday, a move experts said could deter potential missile threats amid rising tensions on the Korean Peninsula.

The drill began on Monday in Beijing and is expected to conclude on Saturday, China's Defense Ministry said on its website on Monday. "This is a practical measure in fulfilling the important consensus reached by both countries' leaders on deepening Sino-Russian antimissile cooperation," it said.

"It will strengthen Sino-Russian mutual strategic trust, improve anti-missile cooperation between the two militaries and has great significance in jointly dealing with regional ballistic and cruise missile threats," the ministry said.

The exercise does not target any third party, it said. "China and Russia oppose the development of global anti-missile systems. The two militaries will increase practical cooperation in anti-missile defense, and jointly safeguard Chinese and Russian security interests and regional strategic balance."

The goal of the exercise is to "jointly train for anti-missile combat planning and preparation, launch command and firing coordination," Senior Colonel Wu Qian, the Defense Ministry spokesman, said in a news briefing in November.

Tension on the Korean Peninsula has been mounting since the Democratic People's Republic of Korea launched its Hwasong-15 intercontinental ballistic missile in November. DPRK media reported the missile could carry nuclear warheads and reach the continental United States.

Su Hao, a professor at the China Foreign Affairs Academy, said that it is crucial for China and Russia to bolster strategic trust and cooperate in anti-missile defense to protect their nations from potential threats.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Memorial Day a time to 'remember', 'inspire'
World.content:
A memorial service to mark the 80th anniversary of the Nanjing Massacre committed during the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-45) brought together hundreds of activists and members of the Chinese and other Asian communities on Sunday in San Francisco.

The memorial, organized by the Rape of Nanking Redress Coalition, the Committee to Promote Reunification of China, the Alliance for Preserving the Truth of Sino-Japanese War and Comfort Women Justice Coalition, has been held annually for the past 20 years with the aim of exposing the Japanese Imperial Army's war crimes and encouraging people to understand and never forget the dark chapter of history.

"The Japanese army blatantly violated international conventions and committed the extremely cruel atrocity in Nanjing, where 300,000 Chinese were murdered and one-third of the buildings were destroyed," Zha Liyou, acting Chinese consul general in San Francisco, said at the service.

Japanese troops captured Nanjing, which was China's capital at the time, on Dec 13, 1937. It then began a slaughter that lasted more than 40 days. Tens of thousands of women were raped.

"Our stories are linked. The fate of over 400,000 women sexually enslaved by the Japanese Imperial Army during World War II is part and parcel of what happened during the Nanjing Massacre," said Judith Mirkinson, president of the Comfort Women Justice Coalition.

She said the 20th century has been called the most violent century in the history of the world, and that one way to ensure peace in the 21st century is through truth and reconciliation.

"Reconciliation does not come without truth. So the Japanese government must acknowledge their crimes," she said.

"They must give justice to those few people who still survive from the Nanjing Massacre and to the memory of what happened there," she said.

From the time that Japan invaded Northeast China in September 1931, followed by a full-scale invasion that started on July 7, 1937, around 35 million Chinese soldiers and civilians were killed or injured during the occupation, which continued until 1945.

To honor the victims and the survivors and to pursue justice and an enduring peace, the Chinese community worldwide joined hands this year to commemorate this historic event, which was designated by the Chinese government as National Memorial Day for Nanjing Massacre Victims.

"To remember the atrocities committed by the Japanese army during World War II does not mean to pass on the enmity but rather to remind people not to forget the history and inspire them to love peace," said Zha Liyou.

In 2015, the Nanjing Massacre was entered onto the UNESCO Memory of the World Register, a compendium aimed at preserving documented heritage of universal value.

liazhu@chinadailyusa.com

World.title: More military technologies targeted for civilian sector to boost economy
World.content:
Greater integration will spur innovation and cultivate new engines of growth

China will strengthen innovation by developing high-tech industries with military technologies to boost military-civil integration, a move that aims to cultivate new growth drivers and boost the economy, said a recent State Council guideline.

This was one of the seven key tasks set by the guideline on deepening the military-civil integration in the defense technology industry, which was released by the State Council, China's Cabinet, on Monday last week.

The guideline targets sharing technological innovation bases and facilities between military and civilian sectors while more efforts will be made to apply military technologies to non-military areas.

The military integration will also focus on key areas such as space, cyberspace and maritime sciences, while private capital is encouraged to enter military industries, the document said.

The guideline was the latest move by the central government to promote the military-civil integration to widen military contract orders to civilian sectors and apply high-end military technologies for civilian purposes as part of the supply-side structural reform.

In June, the General Office of the State Council released a guideline on civil aviation development to open airspace less than 3,000 meters in altitude and other industries such as cybersecurity and satellite navigation.

Shi Haiming, an associate professor at the National University of Defense Technology, said the guideline brings benefits for both private and military enterprises while pre-entry approvals will be changed into post-entry reviews to streamline administration, except those linking strategic weapons.

Meanwhile, Shi said the guideline lowers the access threshold for enterprises to enter the field of weaponry equipment and will make the process more transparent.

The document also will further reduce institutional costs for private enterprise by building better platforms to promote military-civil integration, he said.

In fact, many developed economies are highly reliant on military-civil integration.

For example, the United States' airplane maker Boeing sells China civil aviation aircraft worth billions of dollars each year and is known for its high-end military aircraft. Many Japanese multinational companies such as Toshiba and Mitsubishi have a department to take military orders.

The integration is a worldwide trend to fully improve the national defense capability, said Jiang Luming, a professor at the National Defense University of the People's Liberation Army.

In countries such as the US, the United Kingdom and Germany, less than 15 percent of military technologies are solely for military purposes and more than 80 percent are used for civilian purposes, Jiang said.

Jiang said in October last year that China has about 290,000 national defense intellectual property rights not being used due to the previously separated military and civil industries.

For example, breakthrough technologies such as engines and aluminum alloy materials can help ease production overcapacity and transform China's economy, he said. These new technologies can essentially boost economic growth and national defense, Jiang said.

The military industry has the priority to apply cutting-edge technologies and also make breakthrough innovations, Lu Guangshan, chairman of the Avionics System Co under the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, was quoted by Shanghai Securities News as saying.

"For example, virtual reality headsets were first used in helmets for fighter jets and my company has developed six civilian industries such as virtual reality, drones, robotics and smart wearing," Lu said.

Military companies are encouraged to work with local governments to promote their advantageous expertise and develop a large number of new high-tech industries, Long Hongshan, chief engineer at the State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense, told a news conference last week.

These new industries will play a vital role in promoting local economic growth and creating new employment opportunities, Long said.

Currently, 30 percent of products made by China's military companies are for military purposes and the other 70 percent for civilian purposes, he said.

In the future, high-tech industries will cover half of the military-related economy, Long added.

World.title: Dangerous stunts get thumbs-down from video platforms
World.content:
Multiple social media and video streaming platforms will limit who can view videos that depict dangerous stunts - and may even prohibit such material - in an effort to discourage imitators.

In November, daredevil stunt climber Wu Yongning fell to his death while scaling a skyscraper in Changsha, Hunan province. Wu, 26, had more than 1.3 million followers on social media who regularly devoured his breathtaking videos and photos. He climbed with no protective gear.

Last month, Wu's account on Sina Weibo stopped updating, leading followers to worry about his well-being.

On Friday, Wu's girlfriend confirmed on social media that the "rooftop daredevil" had fallen and died.

"Today is Dec 8. It makes me think of Nov 8, the day that you left us, left this world," she wrote.

Wu's family also confirmed his death to Jiefang Daily, a newspaper in Shanghai.

Meipai, Kuaishou, Xiaohuoshan and other video platforms on which Wu posted content, expressed their condolences, according to ThePaper.cn. Platform representatives told the news outlet that China currently has no law regulating extreme stunt videos, but each platform will update its content policy to discourage imitators.

Kuaishou said Wu's account had been restricted - meaning that only the uploader can see it - in September because of its depictions of dangerous acts.

Xiaohuoshan said it will ban video livestreams of dangerous stunts because live interactions between the performer and the audience could be a distraction and lead to catastrophic results.

The platform also said it will respect the desires of Wu's family in dealing with the videos.

All of Wu's stunt videos on the three platforms had been restricted or taken down as of Monday. A cellphone video of Wu performing his last stunt and falling to his death on Nov 8, has also been taken down.

Wu was part of an informal community of young thrill-seekers around the world who engage in "roof-topping" - climbing to the top or to high ledges of buildings, often without a permit or protective gear, to take stomach-churning pictures and videos. The activity is generally illegal.

In January, an 18-year-old identified as Alexander Sh, fell to his death from Europe's second-tallest building - the 350-meter OKO Tower in Moscow. He was trying to take a selfie when he slipped and fell, Russian media reported.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Taiwan's New Party vows to help improve relations
World.content:
Delegation to Beijing reaffirms support for one-China, rejection of agitators

Top political adviser Yu Zhengsheng met with a Taiwan delegation representing the island's New Party in Beijing on Monday to discuss the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations and how to achieve the "great rejuvenation" of the Chinese nation.

Yu praised the New Party's unbroken stance upholding the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, since the party's establishment, as well as its peaceful approach to relations.

The 19th National Congress of the Communist Party of China, which was held in October, further clarified the guidelines and policies addressing Taiwan, Yu said.

In his opening address to delegates during the congress, Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Central Committee of the CPC, called the one-China principle the political foundation of cross-Straits relations, and said that attempts to move toward "Taiwan independence" in any form will be defeated.

Taiwan will share development opportunities on the Chinese mainland, and its residents will enjoy the same treatment as mainland people as they pursue studies, start businesses, seek jobs or come to live on the mainland, Xi said in the address.

Yok Mu-ming, chairman of the New Party and head of the Taiwan delegation, said the party has firmly upheld the one-China principle and promoted peace.

The delegation also met on Monday with Zhang Zhijun, head of the State Council's Taiwan Affairs Office.

Zhang and Yok agreed that the one-China principle must be upheld going forward, expressed firm opposition to separatist activities and vowed to make efforts toward peaceful relations.

Both sides agreed to establish and improve mechanisms of communication, share opinions on major issues in the relationship and promote exchanges and communication in all fields - especially between youth. They further agreed to create a constructive and convenient environment for the development of Taiwan youth on the mainland.

Zhang said cross-Straits relations have faced challenges because the island's Democratic Progressive Party has refused to clearly express support for the one-China principle, which led to the mainland suspending official communications with the island.

He said that a "Taiwan independence" force had recently stirred up the island, proposing the removal of Chinese mainland elements in a variety of fields.

"Its aim is to cut the historical ties between Taiwan and the mainland, reduce public awareness that Taiwan people are part of the Chinese nation and limit many cultural influences on the island," he said.

Some people advocating "Taiwan independence" have pushed for amending the law, and have proposed changing the island's constitution. "This shows that separatist activities and the group supporting 'independence' pose the most serious threat to the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations," Zhang said.

He warned that people from both sides should be vigilant and firmly oppose such activities.

luowangshu@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Former Chongqing political official facing corruption investigation
World.content:
Sun Zhengcai, the former secretary of Chongqing Municipal Committee of the Communist Party of China, has been placed under investigation on suspicion of accepting bribes, according to the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Monday.

According to the procuratorate, Sun has been placed under "coercive measures", which may include summons by force, bail, residential surveillance, detention and arrest.

The investigation is underway, the procuratorate said in a statement released on Monday.

In July, the CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection launched an investigation into Sun for "serious violations of Party discipline".

The CCDI said in a news release that Sun betrayed Party principles and ignored the Party code of conduct and rules.

He was found to have seriously violated the CPC's eight-point code on frugality and maintaining close ties with the masses, seeking pomp, ostentation and privileges, according to the CCDI.

The CCDI said he was guilty of nepotism and seeking benefits in selection of officials. He was found by the CCDI to have leaked confidential Party information and seriously breached Party rules on integrity.

Moreover, he abused power and used his job to gain benefits for others, then accepted their huge bribes in return, either paid in cash or properties, the CCDI said. He was found to seek substantial benefits for his relatives' businesses and accepted valuable gifts, the CCDI said.

The anti-graft inspectors also accused Sun of bureaucracy and sloth in work and degradation and power-for-sex trades, according to the CCDI.

Sun totally deviated from the Party spirit and political requirements of senior officials, the CCDI said in the statement, adding that his misconduct betrayed the trust of the CPC Central Committee and the public, inflicting huge harm to the Party and the country with "extremely bad" social influences.

The CCDI transferred the criminal evidence involving his case to judicial authorities for further investigation.

In September, the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee expelled Sun from the Party and dismissed him from public office.

China Daily - Xinhua

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018818/China’s Study Abroad Boom Finds a New Generation: Retirees
World.title: China’s Study Abroad Boom Finds a New Generation: Retirees
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018818/China’s Study Abroad Boom Finds a New Generation: Retirees
World.content:
After decades spent working, raising families, and putting personal ambitions on hold, two Chinese women in their 50s returned to school thousands of kilometers from home.

In Athens, 58-year-old Ella Wang found a new sense of purpose at university, studying Greek archaeology, history, and literature. While in New Zealand, 54-year-old Zhao found herself overwhelmed by an English program that was far beyond her level.

Both studied alongside classmates young enough to be their children, but their experiences could hardly have been more different. Yet both are part of a growing number of Chinese retirees looking overseas for education.

Having spent their working lives during China’s reform era, many now have greater financial security, more control over their time, and familiarity with overseas education after sending their own children abroad.

China already has about 105,000 universities for older adults, but overseas programs that combine learning with international travel have a particular appeal for retirees seeking cultural experiences beyond the classroom. EF Education First, one of the world’s largest international education providers, estimates that China’s broader overseas education market for older adults will reach 1.2 trillion yuan ($167 billion) by 2030.

Yet for those entering education systems designed around younger students, the challenge is finding a classroom that fits.

Lesson learned

Zhao discovered that within days of arriving in New Zealand.

She had enrolled in what she believed was a beginner English program. EF had assessed her at A1, the lowest level, and shown her an A1 textbook before she left China. But when lessons began, every available course was beyond her level, and teachers spoke only English.

“It was completely incomprehensible,” Zhao told Sixth Tone.

After one lesson, she returned to the same room for the next class, only to find it empty. The class had moved, but she had not understood the instructions. On another occasion, a teacher called on her, and she did not understand the question.

Zhao had paid about 160,000 yuan for tuition and an eight-month homestay. After retiring from Shanghai’s flower industry, she hoped the program would teach her enough English to travel while she was still healthy. EF’s promotional videos had shown students studying, immersing themselves in local culture, and traveling around New Zealand.

She soon considered quitting. The experience, she felt, had been “overly romanticized” by overseas education providers. “I completely broke down and burst into tears,” Zhao said. “I couldn’t tell my family how miserable it was. I only said I missed them.”

Zhang, 56, had enrolled in a six-week program at the same school and found the pace equally punishing. “It was like I hadn’t even learned to stand, and they were already asking me to run,” she said.

Both had hoped to learn practical English: how to read a menu, take a bus, ask for directions, and order food. Instead, their classes focused on subjects such as history, biology, and mathematics. Another Chinese retiree in the same course quit after three days.

Zhang began to question what she was struggling for. “Do I really need to learn history, biology, and math at this age?”

That mismatch has led some Chinese education providers to design programs specifically for retirees. Yao Xiaoqiong, head of private education provider New Oriental’s Global Campus Center, told Sixth Tone that one- to three-year courses remain difficult for many older students. Instead, the company offers two- to four-week overseas programs, including art courses in the UK and culinary courses in France.

The programs require no prior language skills and include 10 hours of preparation before departure, as well as interpreters and coordinators during the trip. Yao said older clients generally seek cultural immersion and hands-on learning rather than degrees.

Zhang encountered some of that outside the classroom. When she got lost or struggled to understand bus announcements, strangers stepped in to help.

But keeping up with the course consumed her. Zhang studied until 11 p.m. and woke at 4 a.m. to prepare. In class, she relied on a translation app but still “couldn’t keep pace with everyone else.” Younger students often avoided partnering with her for group work.

By the end of the program, she was physically and mentally exhausted. She still hoped to return to New Zealand one day as a tourist. “But this time, I just don’t have the mood to travel,” she said.

Zhang said the program did not match how it was promoted, and planned to file a complaint with EF. The company did not respond to Sixth Tone’s requests for comment.

Zhao’s longer course gave her more time to adjust. Gradually, she learned to manage the classes, grew more confident, found time to hike, and made local friends through a church.

“Now I’ve made it through,” Zhao said. “I’m mentally much stronger.”

Second chance

At the University of Athens, 58-year-old Wang found her way back to an undergraduate thesis she had never considered complete.

Titled “God, Humanity, and Their Destiny,” the thesis at the time fell short of the university’s highest assessment. At her defense, a professor told her she would need “at least another 30 years of life experience” before she could fully develop its argument.

In 2023, while staying at her family’s holiday home in Athens, Wang came across an English-taught undergraduate program in Greek archaeology, history, and literature. More than 30 years had passed since her professor’s remark. “If I finish the archaeology and literature courses here,” she recalled thinking, “maybe I can write the essay better.”

Born in northwestern China’s Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, Wang had worked as a Chinese teacher, an advertising executive, and later in publishing before retiring. With one child in college and the other already working, she was free to spend part of the year in Athens.

Most of her classmates were born around 2006. “The last students I taught were born in 1983 and 1984,” she said. “Now, their children are my classmates.”

Keeping up with them meant learning more than history. Wang typed with two index fingers and struggled to navigate the university’s online systems.

During her first semester, Wang’s daughter arranged to work remotely from Athens, helping her practice English and navigate campus life. Reading textbooks on a screen made Wang “dizzy,” so she ordered printed copies and asked her husband to bring them to Greece.

The effort showed. While many students skipped lectures, Wang rarely missed one. She sat in the front row, stayed after class to ask questions even when she could not fully follow the answers, and spent weekends catching up on coursework. Before long, she was using AI to review her exams and identify mistakes.

She even won over classmates by showing them photos of her cats. “No one can resist kittens,” she said. She also discovered that gray hair was no obstacle to using her student ID for a 10% discount at KFC.

Studying the Peloponnesian War changed how Wang thought about conflict. She began to see the same struggle playing out beyond ancient Greece. “One side wants to preserve the existing order, while the other wants to change it,” she said. “That’s how many conflicts in the world work.”

She came to see traditional expectations around family and marriage as part of that same order. She wanted to break away from them, while her husband, who benefited from the arrangement, was more comfortable preserving it.

“My life used to be a multiple-choice question with only one correct answer,” Wang said. “Work, love, marriage. There was always something I was supposed to do at each stage, and I was carried along by society. People were always defining me: whose daughter I was, whose student I was, whose wife I was, whose mother I was.”

“Now my definition comes from myself,” she said. “I no longer care about those labels. I even have a new name: Ella. I’m Ella.”

Wang has thought about becoming a museum guide or writing a memoir after graduation. But she said those plans matter less than what she has already discovered. “The biggest thing I’ve gained over the past two years is realizing that learning itself is the goal, not a means to something else. I just enjoy learning.”

Sometimes, Wang still thinks of her hometown’s long winters in Xinjiang. As the eldest of four daughters, she helped her parents prepare vegetables for the cold months ahead. Surrounded by piles of produce, she longed to play with other children but could not leave.

“My body was confined by labor, but my thoughts were free. They had already traveled thousands of miles around the world,” she said.

Decades later, Wang feels she has finally caught up with those childhood dreams.

“Now I am standing in the open field of life,” Wang said. “I am lonely, but I am free. It is the solitude of freedom.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Ella Wang in Athens. Courtesy of Wang)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018814/China-Developed ALS Therapy Shows Early Trial Promise
World.title: China-Developed ALS Therapy Shows Early Trial Promise
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018814/China-Developed ALS Therapy Shows Early Trial Promise
World.content:
Chinese researchers have reported encouraging early results for a domestically developed experimental therapy targeting a genetic form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS. In a six-patient trial published this month in Nature Medicine, the drug was generally well tolerated and reduced key disease-related biomarkers.

Called RAG-17, the therapy uses small interfering RNA, or siRNA, to suppress SOD1, a gene whose mutations can cause ALS. By reducing production of the harmful protein associated with the mutation, the drug is designed to target a biological driver of the disease.

ALS is a progressive neurodegenerative disease that destroys the nerve cells controlling voluntary movement, gradually impairing a patient’s ability to move, speak, swallow, and breathe. The disease gained wider public attention through campaigns such as the Ice Bucket Challenge, but it remains incurable.

China has an estimated 60,000 to 100,000 people living with ALS, with about 23,000 new cases diagnosed each year. Around 2% of patients carry SOD1 mutations, the only genetic form of ALS with an approved targeted treatment. Tofersen, the first approved therapy targeting SOD1-related ALS, received U.S. approval in April 2023 and was approved in China in September 2024.

RAG-17 was jointly developed by a team led by Wang Yilong at Beijing Tiantan Hospital and researchers led by Li Longcheng at biotech company Ractigen Therapeutics.

In the trial, six patients with SOD1-related ALS received repeated injections of the drug into the fluid surrounding the spinal cord over several months. Researchers reported no serious adverse events. Two participants experienced mild muscle tremors that later resolved.

The treatment produced substantial reductions in two disease-related biomarkers. SOD1 protein levels in cerebrospinal fluid fell by more than half, while plasma levels of neurofilament light chain, a marker of nerve-cell damage, also declined.

The changes indicate that RAG-17 reached its intended target.

In preclinical studies, RAG-17 delayed disease progression, preserved motor function, and extended survival in rodent models of SOD1-related ALS. Tests in macaques also found sustained suppression of the SOD1 gene in the central nervous system.

The Chinese research team said a larger clinical trial of RAG-17 is now underway.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Shijue Focus/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018808/Game Changers: China’s Female Football Commentators Take Their Shot
World.title: Game Changers: China’s Female Football Commentators Take Their Shot
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018808/Game Changers: China’s Female Football Commentators Take Their Shot
World.content:
Editor’s note: Once confined by gender stereotypes to largely decorative, in-studio roles, China’s women are breaking down barriers in the male-dominated world of live football commentary — and at the forefront is Liu Chang. With nearly a decade of experience, the 34-year-old was part of the commentary team formed for the 2026 FIFA World Cup by the lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, or RedNote. Here, Liu talks about her passion for the “beautiful game,” her online critics, and her unforgettable farewell to the former France and Real Madrid star Karim Benzema.

For two days before the 2026 FIFA World Cup final, football fans could finally take a break. I couldn’t.

After England’s semifinal defeat to Argentina on July 16, I had to continue livestreaming, reviewing the match in detail, and chatting with viewers online. That day, I still had a program to record. During a major tournament like the World Cup, commentators work around the clock. We can only really rest after the final game.

In China, most matches this time started in the early hours of the morning. For a 3 a.m. kickoff, we usually arrived at the studio around 11 p.m. or midnight to prepare, and we wouldn’t finish work until after 5 a.m. the next day. Once I got home, I would record a post-match analysis video, edit and publish it, then sleep until the afternoon. After waking up, I would immediately begin preparing for the next match. Sometimes I slept only two or three hours a day.

As I began commentating on bigger matches, I knew my voice was reaching a larger audience. But that also brought more criticism. I often saw comments on social media saying they weren’t used to a female commentator, that the voice was too shrill or overly emotional.

I don’t shy away from this feedback. I want to hear genuine reactions from viewers, even though it might be painful.

As for the harsher comments, you have to look at them case by case. Take the criticism about shrill voices — there are historical reasons behind that perception. Honestly, growing up, I hardly ever heard a woman cover a football match. We were used to female commentary for figure skating, synchronized swimming, or diving — sports associated with graceful and delicate imagery, where a softer voice seemed a natural fit.

But football is intense, full of passion, and constantly changing. The drama of the game is inseparable from emotion. So I completely understand why some viewers initially felt uncomfortable hearing a female voice. That’s why I adjusted my vocal technique, shifting to a deeper, fuller tone by relying less on head resonance and more on chest resonance. When emotions run high, I can use professional methods to control my pitch.

Of all the comments, what I care about most is how people evaluate my accuracy. My colleague Wu Tong (another female commentator who covered the 2026 World Cup) and I genuinely want to provide fans with an accurate and reliable reading of the game.

Some viewers noted that our commentary felt even-keeled and impartial — a compliment that, to me, reveals a double standard. If a female commentator shows visible emotion or a hint of bias, viewers are far quicker to mark it down to a lack of professionalism.

There’s been a noticeable change in public perceptions of female football commentators in recent years, though. Today, Chinese fans have a far richer array of ways to engage with a match. Once, they simply stared at the screen. Now they travel to the games, share updates on social media, and create highlight videos on players and teams. Given how much modern sports coverage has evolved, it was only natural that audiences would begin expecting something different from the commentary box.

That means commentators can no longer present themselves as distant authorities. If you want to connect with viewers, you need to be on their wavelength.

When I watched football as a kid, the commentators seemed unreachable — they represented a kind of solemn authority. But expectations have changed. Today, fans prefer commentary with personality, someone who understands internet culture and knows how to weave memes into a broadcast.

This is where my generation has an advantage. I’m a fan first, so I naturally approach the game from a fan’s perspective. When I’m not commentating, I spend much of my time scrolling through sports forums, hunting for hilarious memes and the wildest hot takes.

Over the line

The 2010 FIFA World Cup in South Africa was the first major tournament I followed from start to finish.

My interest in the Spanish national team began in 2008, when gathering information wasn’t nearly as convenient as it is today. Many overseas Chinese fans would share updates from Spain online, and we would meet to discuss the matches and the players. It was a lively community built around a shared passion.

That tournament became the starting point of my connection with other fans. I had only recently left school, had little money, and couldn’t afford many forms of entertainment. Football became one of the few joys that didn’t cost a thing. The game felt pure: there was no script, only the unpredictability of competition and the possibility of victory or defeat.

We were full of curiosity, and football was a window into a world I longed to understand.

I’ve always loved sports, but after graduating from Beijing’s Communication University of China, I initially worked for nine years at CCTV-7 (a China Central Television channel that, at the time, focused on agriculture and military affairs).

Choosing a career in sports media was not an easy decision. My family did not support it at first. By then, I had been taking on more football-related freelance work, often staying up late, while my regular job also required lots of business trips. It became difficult to balance my health, energy, and workload. I kept asking myself: Could I make a living from football?

I decided to take the leap. In 2017, I joined (Chinese tech giant) Tencent, working in the football media. It was a risk, but working in football brought me real joy. It allowed me to fulfill a long-held dream to attend matches, meet players, and share my insights with fans.

During my years at Tencent, I tried almost every kind of role: interviewing players, interacting with guests before and during matches, and working on the front lines of major tournaments. I found all these experiences fascinating.

But after trying so many roles, I realized that what I loved most was still the game itself. Whenever I watched a match, I felt an overwhelming urge to give it a voice — to capture what was happening on the pitch. And there was only one role that could satisfy that impulse.

Calling the shots

My first commentary assignment came by accident. It happened during an English Premier League match between Chelsea and Everton seven or eight years ago. I was supposed to only host the coverage, but just before kickoff the production team got word that one of the commentators would not arrive in time. It was a late-night broadcast, and the studio had only me and one guest. So I stepped in.

If it happened today, with my understanding of the profession and the entire workflow, I probably wouldn’t have dared go on air at such short notice. But I didn’t think much about it at the time. I was just excited — ridiculously so. I had no real grasp of how to share the microphone or coordinate with a partner. I just said whatever came to mind. Fortunately, my partner was highly experienced. Knowing I had been drafted in at the last minute, he didn’t put any pressure on me. It also helped that I’d followed the Premier League for years and knew both teams well.

After the match, I went home to sleep, feeling pleased. The next day, I watched the recording to see where I could improve, only to discover that all my commentary had been cut. It was probably because the platform didn’t want anyone to notice that its scheduled guest hadn’t shown up. Plus, female football commentators were then still a rarity.

My commentary that first time wasn’t preserved, but I had impressed both the production crew and my co-commentator, and the response in the live chat was encouraging. It showed me that commentary was perhaps something I could pursue.

That experience didn’t immediately make me a commentator, but it gave me confidence that I could handle a full match. When my next opportunity came, I put myself forward.

And so, in 2019, I “transferred” to PP Sports (one of the first Chinese platforms to livestream sporting events). The platform broadcast a wide range of competitions at different levels, which gave me invaluable opportunities to practice. There’s a “10,000-hour rule” behind mastering a craft, and in my industry, people can’t deliver a confident, insightful commentary without having handled hundreds of games. After every assignment, I would listen back, reviewing my performance, identifying mistakes, and thinking about improvements.

For late-night matches, platforms often rely on younger commentators. I did my share of games that attracted little attention, where information on the teams and players was scarce. I had to research everything myself. That, too, was part of the learning curve. I still take on many lower-profile matches now. Yet for commentators, each game deserves the same preparation and professionalism.

From my first assignment to where I am today, it took at least six or seven years.

The final whistle

The commentary box is a place of “magic” for me. I’m naturally a low-energy person, but when that countdown to kickoff begins — “five, four, three, two, one” — it feels as if a switch inside me suddenly flips. It doesn’t matter whether you have prepared for years or just days;, the moment has arrived, and you need to deliver.

The commentary box becomes my creative space, and for the next 90 minutes or so, I’m given the power to tell a story.

It is where storytelling meets the unpredictability of professional football. I look forward to every match because the game has no script. No matter how much analysis and prediction you do, you can never know how the action will unfold.

Of all the matches I’ve covered, one of the most unforgettable was (former France international striker) Karim Benzema’s final match for Real Madrid on June 4, 2023. About an hour or two before kickoff, we received the news that Benzema would be leaving the club (after 14 years). Both my partner and I found it hard to process emotionally. We had watched him develop at Madrid, and an entire generation of fans had grown with him.

As I quickly gathered all the memories I had of Benzema, a line from the song “Da Er Wen” (by Singaporean singer Tanya Chua) came to mind. So, when the match finally ended and the camera lingered on Benzema, I read out the lyrics: “My youth was not without its scars / There was rivalry, there was sacrifice / I learned to be earnest, learned to be loyal, and only those who adapt survive.”

It was a broadcast that could never be replicated. After that, I never had another opportunity to weave song lyrics into my commentary.

At the 2026 World Cup, the match that stayed with me most was defending champion Argentina’s knockout-stage encounter with Cabo Verde.

Before the tournament began, I didn’t know much about Cabo Verde. It was only after they emerged as an exciting newcomer that I started doing my homework. Their three group-stage matches showed a team defined by remarkable discipline and collective spirit. But even then, I never expected them to produce such an extraordinary performance against Argentina in the Round of 32. They denied Lionel Messi a goal, scored, and pushed their opponents to the brink. Even in the final minutes, the Cabo Verde players continued pushing forward, forcing the Argentina goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez into a spectacular save.

Judging by the viewers in our livestream, many Chinese fans likely only logged on to check the score after waking up that morning. But when they saw the match was still going — that it had gone into extra time — they rushed to the livestream, eager to find out how the drama would play out.

It was a match and feeling I will remember for the rest of my life.

That, to me, is the magic of football. It can be incredibly distant — many matches are played thousands of miles away, and most fans may never have the chance to watch them in person. Yet at the same time, it can feel incredibly close. It moves you emotionally, making your heart rise and fall with every moment. And when the people around you support the same team, a sense of intimacy emerges almost instantly. That sense of kinship transcends language and borders, creating a shared emotional bond among people who may otherwise have nothing in common.

My greatest lesson from football has been that nothing is truly decided until that final whistle is blown. Life is the same — until the end, everything is possible.

As told to reporter Li Yiming.

A version of this article originally appeared in Fir Record. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Chen Yue; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image): Liu Chang (center) commentates alongside Chinese referee Ma Ning (right) and commentator Yu Xinmiao (left) during the 2026 FIFA World Cup final, July 2026. From Liu’s Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018813/China’s Bank Wealth Products Face Scrutiny Over Yield Displays
World.title: China’s Bank Wealth Products Face Scrutiny Over Yield Displays
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018813/China’s Bank Wealth Products Face Scrutiny Over Yield Displays
World.content:
One wealth management product advertised annualized returns above 3% but delivered a loss. A “stable, low-volatility” investment began declining the day after purchase. Other wealth management offerings highlighted their strongest short-term yields, making it harder for investors to assess their actual performance.

The cases were among those highlighted in a recent investigation by Chinese state news agency Xinhua, which found that some institutions continue to showcase selective short-term returns despite tighter regulatory scrutiny.

By the end of the first quarter this year, the number of bank wealth management investors in China had reached 148 million, while 48,000 products were available on the market, up 18.23% from a year earlier.

According to Xinhua, while regulators have curbed overt “ranking chasing” — the practice of inflating yields to improve performance rankings — some wealth management institutions continue to rely on selective performance displays.

The probe found that even products from the same bank may use different periods to calculate annualized returns, with some showing one-month figures and others three-month figures, making comparisons difficult for investors.

Lin Xiaoyuan told Xinhua that she bought a three-month holding-period product advertised with an annualized return above 3%. When it matured, the investment had posted a loss.

Another investor, surnamed Chen, said a bank wealth manager promoted a six-month “low-volatility” product as a “stellar performer.” But the investment began losing value on the day his purchase was confirmed and continued declining for the following month.

Xinhua also reviewed product pages on bank apps and found discrepancies between promotional displays and recent performance figures.
