One product page highlighted a “positive annual return since inception” and a cumulative return of 10.18%, while further data showed annualized losses over both the previous three-month and one-month periods.

An insider at a bank wealth management firm told Xinhua, “If everyone else is showing 4% or 5%, how can we sell ours if we show the real number?”

The probe also found that some banks use inconsistent metrics to display yields, with products from the same institution sometimes showing annualized returns calculated over different periods.

“This kind of selective disclosure is a key reason investors are being misled,” said Wang Pengbo, a senior analyst at market consultancy Botong Analysys. He added that banks often highlight their strongest short-term figures on homepages and pop-ups, making it difficult for ordinary investors to assess a product’s actual risk and return without digging through the fine print.

In December 2025, the National Financial Regulatory Administration issued rules aimed at curbing misleading performance disclosures, including selective reporting and inconsistent presentation of returns.

Such practices violate both net-value management requirements under China’s asset management regulations and the principle of fair market pricing, Wang added.

Regulators have also targeted wealth management products that use short-term returns to influence performance rankings and attract investors. Xinhua reported that selective yield presentation remains an issue despite the regulatory focus.

Experts advised investors to look beyond short-term rankings, examine longer-term performance, compare returns with benchmarks, and consider volatility alongside headline yields.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: TotalImage/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018804/China’s Changing Climate May Be Why Your Garlic Is Moldy
World.title: China’s Changing Climate May Be Why Your Garlic Is Moldy
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018804/China’s Changing Climate May Be Why Your Garlic Is Moldy
World.content:
You may have had this experience. It’s dinnertime. You peel a clove of garlic and notice a small greenish-gray patch. Do you cut it away or toss the clove and reach for another? It’s a small annoyance that won’t derail your dinner, but, if social media posts are any indication, it’s an annoyance that is happening across the world, with users saying they are noticing it more and more.

It is also a reminder that food quality is shaped long before an ingredient reaches the cutting board. Garlic’s journey often begins in China, the world’s largest garlic producer and exporter, accounting for more than 70% of global production. When the kind of extreme or unusual weather made more common by climate change affects China’s garlic-growing regions, the consequences can travel well beyond the field, reaching processors, warehouses, supermarkets, and kitchens around the world.

In the garlic-producing provinces of Shandong and Jiangsu in the east, and Henan in central China, garlic is planted in the fall. Farmers will break up the soil to create crop rows, separate and select cloves, then press them, one by one, pointy-side up, into the soil. Then, after the cloves are covered with more dirt, watered, and mulched with plastic, they embark on several months of exposure to changing temperatures and moisture conditions.

The timing for this process needs to be exact. Plant too early, and the young sprouts might overdevelop, draining energy. Too late, and the plant doesn’t develop enough. In both cases, it might not be able to defend itself against diseases and the winter cold.

After planting, garlic must undergo a period of cold to initiate a process called vernalization. Only after prolonged exposure to low temperatures will the plants successfully develop bulbs — the cluster of garlic cloves. Vernalization typically requires a temperature range of 0 to 10 degrees Celsius for at least three weeks. Too much cold will harm the garlic; too little will disrupt the plant’s maturation.

Weather extremes can upset this process. In the fall of 2025, for example, excessive rainfall across northern China delayed garlic planting by about three to six weeks. The winter that followed was mild, and as a result, government data show, the garlic harvested in Shandong continued to grow during a period when no growth should have occurred.

Though this period of extra growth, in some ways, made up for the season’s late planting, this additional early-stage growth may have affected resource allocation within the plant. For example, it can cause the bulbs’ side buds — which later become cloves — to develop their own leaves instead of growing in size.

When the seasons change to spring and the world begins to bloom, a slender flower stalk begins to bolt from the center of the garlic plant. This flower stalk, known as a garlic scape, is a beloved vegetable in Chinese cuisine, often stir-fried with meat, eggs, or tofu. For the farmers, garlic scapes are a lifeline, as they represent the first opportunity to turn a profit in the garlic farming season. Large, high-quality garlic scapes can provide needed revenue to cover the costs of seasonal workers, farm supplies, and farm management for the rest of the season. Harvesting scapes also leaves more resources for the developing bulb.

However, the harvest window for garlic scapes is extremely short, often lasting for only one or two weeks. If the scapes are not harvested in time, they become old and lose much of their market value, and harvesting them relies heavily on human labor. Usually, different regions reach their harvesting season at different dates, allowing workers to move from one area to the next.

In many garlic-growing regions, this year’s spring was warmer than usual. When that happens, harvesting timelines start to overlap, tightening the labor market and placing additional strain on procurement and distribution. At this point, the farmers face the difficult decision of whether to pay more to harvest their garlic scapes or let them continue to grow, potentially affecting the quality of their bulb harvest later in the season. News stories about the pressures Chinese garlic farmers faced earlier this year spawned the social media meme, “Got garlic scapes, any takers?”

In early summer, the aboveground structures of the garlic plant begin to shrivel, while the belowground bulbs enter their prime harvest period. In northern China, farmers will bind harvested garlic into bunches and lay them out to dry in the sun. The dried skin encasing the bulb acts as a jacket, protecting it from damage, moisture fluctuations, and mold during sorting, storage, and shipping.

Global warming has caused China’s rain belt to shift northward, leading to record rainfall in northern China. If the main harvest period is hit by persistent rain, the garlic skin can get damaged, and both soil moisture and air humidity rise. Bulbs may not fully dry, and damaged outer skins can both cause garlic to sprout more leaves and make it more vulnerable to fungal growth. While a moldy bulb at the supermarket can also result from mistakes during storage and transport, a rainy harvest amplifies those risks.

The China Meteorological Administration’s Bluebook on Climate Change in China, published last year, states that, as warming continues, China is experiencing changes in precipitation patterns and extreme weather risks. This doesn’t mean climate change can be cited as the direct cause of every heavy rainfall event or every below-standard bulb of garlic; it means farmers, traders, and meteorological services must plan for more unstable combinations of heat, rain, humidity, drought, and winter warmth.

Given the large areas used to grow garlic, it’s not feasible to use greenhouses to shield it from the elements. The real test of adaptation will come from recognizing risks earlier, forecasting with more accuracy, and responding more quickly. Accurate and precise weather reporting is of the utmost importance. According to the China Meteorological Administration, Shandong’s garlic-growing Jinxiang County has created a specialized garlic meteorological service team to provide weather support throughout the production cycle.

The fate of a single bulb of garlic may seem inconsequential — but in reality, it is a signal of something larger. Climate change doesn’t just affect the far-off polar ice caps, and it isn’t just the stories of climate disasters filling our televisions. It may already be sitting on our dinner tables. These changes will not stop at the garlic bulb, but with each accurate forecast, each planting decision, and each decision to harvest, we are gradually building our ability to respond. Viewed in this way, this single bulb of garlic is a microcosm of the ongoing negotiations between humans and our climate.

Translator: Cynthia Lin.

(Header image: A farmer sorts garlic harvested from a field in Yongji, Shanxi province, May 24, 2026. Liu Baocheng/VCG)

World.title: China’s Summer Hit Recasts the Eight Immortals as Con Artists
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018801/China’s Summer Hit Recasts the Eight Immortals as Con Artists
World.content:
Before they were immortals, they were scammers.

That’s the irreverent premise behind “All Wishes Come True!,” a new Chinese animated comedy that has turned a band of mythological figures from Taoist legend into a summer box-office hit.

Released July 18, the film recasts the Eight Immortals — traditionally symbols of people from all walks of life — as con artists who impersonate gods and deceive worshippers before achieving immortality themselves.

In less than a week, the film has grossed more than 370 million yuan ($51 million), becoming the second highest-grossing domestic animated film of 2026 behind “Boonie Bears: The Hidden Protector.” It also holds an 8.3 rating on Chinese review site Douban, the highest among this summer’s new releases.

The film’s biggest twist unfolds in Penglai, a fairyland where gods and humans coexist under a surprisingly modern bureaucracy governed by an immortals management bureau. Deities are assigned temples, evaluated on performance targets, and ranked on giant leaderboards based on the incense offerings they receive.

Unlike traditional tales of the Eight Immortals’ journey toward enlightenment, the film gives the legendary figures a new beginning: they first appear as schemers targeting the riches of Fu, Lu, and Shou, the three deities of fortune, prosperity, and longevity.

Zhongli Quan, traditionally portrayed as a general who became a Taoist immortal, is reimagined as a con artist who leads the group in impersonating deities. Cao Guojiu, traditionally linked to the Song dynasty (960–1279) imperial court, appears as an official in the immortals management bureau.

After taking over a temple, the group finds itself responsible for granting wishes — and eventually becomes known for catching thieves. Their journey later leads to a clash with the war god Yang Jian.

Director Mu Zhengyang said he designed Penglai as a “first-tier megacity,” where gods and humans operate within a modern social system. “At first, audiences should feel that they’re entering a traditional Eastern fairyland. But once inside, it becomes much more like an amusement park,” he told domestic media.

The film’s character-driven approach also extends to its voice performances. Voice director Chen Hao, who worked on the popular “Ne Zha” films, voices Zhongli Quan, while Tieguai Li’s Chongqing dialect adds regional flavor to the character.

The film’s cultural references have also fueled online discussion. On streaming platform Bilibili, videos decoding more than 100 Easter eggs and hidden details have each attracted nearly one million views.

One widely discussed clue is the Eight Immortals’ temple number — 1350, the same number associated with Sun Wukong, better known as the Monkey King, in the “Book of Life and Death,” a mythical register of the underworld in “Journey to the West,” hinting at his possible appearance later in the story.

The same reinterpretation has also drawn criticism from some viewers, who argue that the film alters the identities and values associated with traditional mythology.

Yang Jian, for example, traditionally portrayed as a righteous war god who protects ordinary people, is reimagined as a figure willing to sacrifice heaven and humanity to save his mother. The film’s other redesigns have also drawn attention, including Cao Guojiu’s portrayal as an overweight, flamboyant official and Lan Caihe’s depiction as a toddler.

The debate also extends to the film’s portrayal of immortality. Through the line, “Only immortals can do good deeds,” it offers a new interpretation that some viewers praised, while others argued it differs from traditional Taoist ideas of attaining eternal life.

The production team, based in southwestern China’s Sichuan province, said the Eight Immortals offer creative space for reinterpretation because many audiences know their famous stories but are less familiar with their broader legends. The filmmakers said they hoped to introduce the figures to a new generation through a fresh retelling.

“We didn’t want to simply bring the Eight Immortals in front of young audiences and tell the same story again,” producer Ying Xujun told domestic media. “We had to create something new for a new generation.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A poster for “All Wishes Come True!” From Douban)

World.title: At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018802/At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.content:
This year’s World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai was larger, more crowded, and more politically prominent than in previous editions.

President Xi Jinping attended the event for the first time, while more than 1,100 companies showcased computing systems, AI agents, robots, and other products aimed at workplaces, factories, and consumers. In-person visits topped 400,000, and tickets were reportedly resold for more than 1,000 yuan.

Xi called for wider access to open-source AI, and China launched a 29-country AI cooperation body, placing issues of governance, access, and international coordination alongside the usual displays of commercial technology.

Beyond the speeches and packed exhibition halls, the most revealing conversations were practical: lowering computing costs, putting AI agents to work, managing new safety risks, and building businesses that can last.

Here are four takeaways from this year’s WAIC.

Computing power gets practical

Computing power was one of the most discussed topics at this year’s WAIC, second only to AI applications by number of related forums. But the focus moved beyond building more data centers or training ever-larger models.

Two questions dominated: what the next generation of computing power might look like, and how to make today’s resources cheaper and more efficient.

At one flagship forum on the future of computing, scientists discussed emerging approaches including quantum computing and space-based computing. Among the speakers was Pan Jianwei, a leading quantum physicist and recent recipient of a top United Nations science award, who outlined recent advances in the field.

Pan also urged caution. Although the field has reached a series of important milestones, he said, building a general-purpose quantum computer capable of quickly solving problems with clear practical value will still require years of sustained research. The academic community, he added, has a responsibility to help the public assess the technology realistically and guard against an industry bubble.

Companies also seemed more focused on improving the efficiency of existing computing resources and reducing the cost of each AI query.

Some were working to improve the performance of models trained mainly on Nvidia chips when deployed on Chinese chips. Others focused on allocating and managing computing resources more efficiently.

Rather than chasing only the most powerful and expensive models, many Chinese AI companies appeared more concerned with making AI cheaper to run.

AI Governance and Safety

AI governance and safety were prominent throughout this year’s WAIC, from high-level forums to the opening ceremony and President Xi Jinping’s speech.

Brian Tse, an AI safety expert and founder and CEO of Concordia AI, said he has seen more discussion in China around cybersecurity and the protection of critical infrastructure, especially the risks posed by frontier AI models.

“The threat landscape is evolving rapidly,” Tse said. “Many experts at the forums expressed concern that threats and potential misuse are developing faster than society’s current defenses.”

The concerns also appeared to be shifting beyond large language models and the harmful content they can generate. More attention was paid this year to the risks posed by autonomous AI agents, which can plan tasks, make decisions, and interact with other tools.

On July 15, just before WAIC, China’s new rules on AI anthropomorphic interaction took effect, targeting services that simulate human personalities and sustained emotional interaction. The rules prohibit providers from offering virtual partners or relatives to minors and bar services from inducing emotional dependence or addiction.

In May, regulators also released guidance on the standardized application and development of AI agents, including plans to explore digital identity management for them.

“China is positioning itself as an architect of multilateral AI governance,” Tse said.

AI lands at work

One phrase heard often at this year’s WAIC was AI’s real-world “landing” — the push to move the technology out of demos and into everyday work. Companies ranging from Tencent and Alibaba to smaller startups showed AI products aimed at offices, factories, and consumer services. AI agents were among the most visible examples.

At booths run by major tech firms, exhibitors demonstrated how agents could be built into corporate workflows, from searching internal documents to generating reports and coordinating routine tasks.

The impact could be broad because many of these companies’ software systems are already embedded in Chinese workplaces. Adding AI agents to existing platforms may prove easier than persuading companies to adopt entirely new tools.

Still, genuinely effective applications appeared limited. Office productivity remained the most obvious use case, while other areas were less developed.

Robotics and embodied AI occupied an entire floor at this year’s WAIC. Visitors could still see robots performing awkward dances or taking six minutes to make a cup of tea. But some companies were beginning to move beyond staged demonstrations, showing robots designed for inspection, manufacturing, logistics, and other industrial uses.

The founder rush

Some of the most revealing conversations at this year’s WAIC took place after the official sessions ended.

Across after-hours gatherings, private meetups, and open-mic sessions, young founders and industry professionals swapped ideas on AI agents, robotics, and productivity tools. Some gatherings ran late into the night, with almost any topic open for discussion.

Many entrepreneurs seemed eager to absorb every new idea, experiment, business opportunity, and professional connection they could find.

But that urgency also carried risks. Some founders said their AI ventures were burning through years of savings. Many still lacked a convincing answer to a basic question: how their projects would generate lasting value and revenue.

That tension ran through WAIC: crowded halls, founders eager to share projects and failures, and a palpable fear of moving too slowly and missing the AI wave. The mood mixed optimism with anxiety, much of it fueled by the speed of the technology and the sheer volume of information surrounding it.

The conversations also suggested a maturing industry. More speakers and founders were asking not only what AI could do, but where it could be useful, how it could be governed, and which businesses could survive once the initial excitement fades.

(Header image: A humanoid robot from a Chinese robotics firm waves Chinese national flags during the 2026 WAIC in Shanghai, July 18, 2026. Ng Han Guan/AP Photo via VCG)

World.title: The Soybean That Built Northeast China
World.content:
In 2020, I traveled to Kaishantun, a town in the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture near the China-North Korea border. It fit every stereotype of the deindustrialized Northeast. Young people had left. The government had built two rows of barracks-style apartment blocks for the elderly residents who remained. Kaishantun railway station had long been abandoned. On the station sign, the space for the next stop was blank. North Korea lay only a few hundred meters away.

On the walk back, I wandered into a derelict movie theater and discovered several reels of old film. Later restored, they revealed something astonishing: clips of a symphony orchestra and a traditional folk orchestra.

What kind of small town could support two orchestras of its own?

As I dug deeper into the history of my home region, Northeast China, I found that part of the answer lay in a crop that today frequently appears in international headlines: soybeans. A century before China became a major importer of American soybeans, it was the world’s leading producer.

In August 1872, three Japanese army officers, disguised as merchants and acting on the orders of General Saigō Takamori, traveled through “Manchuria,” the term they used for Northeast China. Saigō was studying relations between Japan, Korea, and China as he prepared a future campaign against Korea. A year later, the officers submitted their “Report on an Inspection of Manchuria,” one of Japan’s earliest intelligence briefings on China. The report includes a detailed discussion of soybeans:

“From winter through spring, soybeans are continuously transported by inland waterways. Regardless of the cold, day and night, dozens of horse-drawn carts move in a single direction. Large merchants purchase the beans and pile them into circular mountains more than two rooms across and over 6 meters high … The quantity stored is beyond counting.”

In 1885, another Japanese military officer, Kikuchi Setsuzō, passed through Northeast China on his return from the Russian Empire. Along the way, he studied how Qing forces fed their military horses, which he regarded as superior to those of Japan and Russia. Qing troops processed the residue left after soybean oil extraction into pressed soybean cakes for animal feed. Each cake weighed about 12.5 kilograms and could feed three horses for a day. Kikuchi even claimed such soybean resources would be “indispensable” for training military horses.

In the 19th century, Kikuchi was among the few who grasped soybeans’ strategic significance. The crop had reached Europe and North America in the 18th century but remained largely a botanical curiosity. A handful of enthusiasts, such as the Austro-Hungarian agronomist Friedrich Haberlandt, sought to introduce soybeans into Western diets. Yet while they imported the crop, they did not import the culinary traditions that had made it a staple across Asia.

In East Asia, by contrast, people had accumulated more than a thousand years of experience cooking and consuming soybeans. They also recognized the crop’s value as animal feed. After the Meiji Restoration in 1868, Japanese rice farmers gradually abandoned traditional fish-based fertilizers in favor of soybean cake. Between 1882 and 1902, Japan’s soybean imports increased four-hundredfold.

The Russo-Japanese War of 1904–05 finally alerted the world to soybeans’ importance. European military observers noted that both sides relied heavily on the crop. Japanese forces consumed soybeans directly and used them in military logistics. Russian forces fed them to cavalry horses. Soybean oil served as a raw material for soap and as a lubricant for artillery equipment and wagon axles.

The soybean trade expanded rapidly. A 1911 report from the Customs Service in Shanghai observed that “It is only in the last three years that soya beans have become important in intercontinental commerce,” calling their rapid emergence from obscurity “one of the most remarkable commercial events of recent times.” In the same year, the U.S. ambassador in Beijing told the State Department that Northeast China had until recently been largely unknown for its commercial potential, despite supplying soybeans to global markets. He observed that its economic trajectory was now drawing attention in major cities including New York, London, Hamburg, and Seattle, and attributed this shift to soybeans, whose rapidly growing demand he characterized as “phenomenal in trade annals.”

Estimates suggest that Northeast China accounted for between 16% and 42% of global soybean production between 1908 and 1930, shipping soybeans, soybean oil, and soybean cakes to the rest of China, Japan, and Europe. Until the eve of World War II, China produced more than 80% of the world’s soybeans. The crop became widely known as the “Manchurian bean.”

Soybeans were also among the most important exports of a then largely impoverished China. After World War I, their importance grew rapidly, and by the 1920s they had overtaken tea and silk to become China’s leading export, accounting for more than 20% of export earnings.

As trade expanded, so did Japan’s territorial ambitions. In the run-up to Japan's formal annexation of Korea in 1910, Yanbian became a frontier along the China-Korea border where Chinese and Japanese spheres of influence met directly. Japanese strategists viewed the wider Yanbian area as a gateway to the interior of Northeast China and sought to build a railway linking the Korean port of Chongjin with China’s inland Northeast. General Hasegawa Yoshimichi, commander of Japanese forces in Korea, regarded Yanbian as a vital supply corridor for sustaining colonial rule on the peninsula. He advocated occupying the region to secure access to strategic commodities such as soybeans.

Over the following three decades, Japan steadily expanded its influence in Northeast China. In 1931, Japanese forces seized the region and took control of its economic resources. This expansion, justified in the name of protecting economic “lifelines,” would later extend across Asia during the Pacific War to the oil fields of Burma, Sumatra, and Borneo; the rubber plantations of Malaya; and the chromium and iron deposits of the Philippines.

In Yanbian, war and colonial rule only reinforced the region’s economic importance. Beyond soybeans, Japanese authorities coveted the region’s timber. In Kaishantun they established the Eastern Manchuria Rayon Pulp Company, whose output eventually surpassed that of most producers in Japan. After the Chinese Communist Party won the civil war and founded the People’s Republic of China in 1949, the new state’s flagship pulp and paper enterprise was established in the same town.

Factories brought more than jobs. They brought hospitals, movie theaters, and even symphony orchestras.

Yet by then Northeast China was no longer the sole center of the global soybean trade. By the early 20th century, American farmers were already familiar with soybeans, using them to replenish soil and support other crops. After the Russo-Japanese War, however, the crop’s industrial potential attracted growing attention.

One unlikely champion was Henry Ford. He used soybean protein and soybean-oil derivatives in automotive components and in 1941 unveiled a prototype car with body panels made largely from soybean-based plastic. To demonstrate its strength, he famously struck it with an axe.

Ford’s soybean car was hardly a commercial success, but it generated publicity for the crop. When Japan severed America’s access to Asian supply routes during the Pacific War, soybeans were transformed from an industrial curiosity into a strategic resource. Combined harvesters and advances in plant breeding helped American farmers scale up production.

By the 1950s, the center of gravity in soybean production had shifted decisively to the Americas.

One final piece was still missing from the modern soybean map: Brazil. In the early 1970s, a major El Niño event, a climate pattern that warms the Pacific Ocean, devastated the Peruvian anchoveta fishery, a key source of animal feed, driving demand for soybean meal. Prices surged, and in 1973 the Nixon administration imposed restrictions on soybean exports.

History then took an ironic turn. Japan, heavily dependent on imported American soybeans, increased its investment in South American agriculture, while Brazil’s agricultural research agency, Embrapa, developed soybean varieties suited to tropical conditions. The result was a dramatic expansion of Brazilian production.

In 2024, more than 70% of China’s soybean imports came from Brazil. When trade tensions between China and the United States intensified in 2025, Brazil became China’s principal alternative for former U.S. suppliers.

Northeast China remains the country’s most important soybean-growing region, producing the beans that become tofu and soy milk on Chinese tables. But it no longer supplies the world with soybean oil and soybean meal. Once-thriving industrial towns have been swept up in the tide of deindustrialization, leaving behind abandoned railway stations and empty movie theaters.

From an unassuming plant in Northeast China to one of the world’s most traded agricultural commodities, the soybean’s history is ultimately a story of globalization. A soybean harvested in Paraguay may be processed in Argentina, sold to China by a trading house in Geneva, and eventually find its way into milk, cakes, or meat products. It shapes what we eat, how we farm, and how nations interact with one another. It also shapes the fate of countless small towns, including places like Kaishantun.

(Header image: A soybean field in Xingkai Lake Farm, Heilongjiang province, 2023. VCG)

WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is set to deliver his State of the Nation Address (SONA) on Monday, July 27, 4 pm, at the Batasang Pambansa in Quezon City.

The situation is markedly different from last year, when Marcos’ erstwhile ally, Vice President Sara Duterte, avoided an impeachment trial after the Supreme Court ruled that the complaint against her was unconstitutional as it is barred by the one-year rule.

This year, as Marcos delivers his fifth SONA, the impeachment trial against the Vice President is in full swing. Leyte 1st District Representative Martin Romualdez, the President’s cousin, is no longer House speaker following his resignation after he was implicated in flood control corruption. Marcos himself had announced a crackdown on those involved in the scandal in his SONA last year.

How will Marcos set the tone for the last two years of his presidency? What promises will he declare as fulfilled, and what remains to be done? What will be his new marching order a year since he called for a crackdown on flood control corruption?

World.title: [OPINION] In the trial vs Sara Duterte, public tolerance has its limits
World.content:
Rules that constrain politicians seem to no longer matter — if the prize is access to more polarized votes. The Senate needs to disincentivize this behavior.

This Sara Duterte impeachment trial began with senators taking an additional oath. Under the rules they imposed on themselves, they swore to “do impartial justice according to the Constitution.” Their Impeachment Rules also require them to observe “political neutrality.” Impartiality and neutrality.

Perhaps this is why some senators saw fit to repeatedly lecture their colleagues about due process as if they were high school students. Some even implied that non-lawyers would be less capable of ensuring the ongoing impeachment trial adheres to constitutional standards.

Yet, nothing says “impartial justice” quite like a senator-judge who reposts a video attacking a member of the prosecution team in between hearings. And nothing says “neutrality” quite like using a spliced video to make it appear that Akbayan Representative and prosecutor Chel Diokno said things he never did. All this just a few days after another senator complained why the prosecution was always “one-sided.” It seems the very concept of a fair trial has been turned on its head.

Restating a couple of basic principles becomes necessary. First, due process exists to deliver justice, not subvert it. It becomes hollow formality when its fundamental requirement is lacking: a fair and impartial judge. Those objections about dates, hearsay, originals, and photocopies become meaningless if the judge is compromised. One can comply with the Rules of Court down to the very letter, but without a fair judge, the proceeding will still be a sham.

Since impeachments are done before senators and not justices, no one is surprised to see partisanship creep in. Politicians being who they are, no one is also shocked to see alliances reflected in the way some senators ask their questions.

But public tolerance has its limits.

Were a member of the Supreme Court to post a manipulated video about counsel in an active case, a thousand lectures on due process would do little to convince the public that the trial remains fair. Sa boxing, minsan may referee na biased. Pero kapag yung referee nakikisuntok na, ibang usapan na yan. (In boxing, some referees may be biased. But if it’s the referee who starts a brawl, that’s another matter.)

Senator Pia Cayetano was present in the Senate when Congressman Diokno delivered his arguments regarding the prosecution’s requests for subpoena. It was a masterclass in calm but effective exposition that earned praise from several sectors. Unless she was busy, or inattentive, there is no reason to believe she failed to grasp what the rest of the country did. And yet, she posted that video.

Chasing online clout

This is the new era of impeachments that the old rules weren’t designed to anticipate. As pointed out by a colleague, social media has introduced a different set of incentives for senator-judges’ behavior that may not be constrained by previous protocols.

In the case of this incident, the temporary bad press is deemed tolerable so long as the post enhances the senator’s online following with her base. Rules that constrain politicians seem to no longer matter — if the prize is access to more polarized votes.

The Senate needs to act quickly to disincentivize this behavior.

First, the Senate’s role as a stabilizing body in highly partisan incidents gets eroded. Second, if impartiality is seen as performative, it encourages more officials to violate it with impunity. Third, this conduct ultimately weakens public trust, which, in turn, gives senators power, and shelter, against an over-reaching executive branch.

There are many ways to resolve this.

In our courts, if a judge feels he or she can no longer remain impartial then it becomes her duty to recuse herself. If a senator is too dedicated to seeing her cause to fruition, then perhaps the body should engage her directly. There is precedent for this, if not within the Senate’s internal rules but, from the body whose impartiality it is trying to mimic. There have been times when the Supreme Court admonished its own justices for certain actions that were deemed unbecoming. There is no reason why the Senate should shy away from doing so.

As for those who view social media likes as a prize worth ignoring norms of statesmanship and judicial decorum, it’s worth nothing that online infamy comes at a price. At least 82% of Filipinos want the Vice President to face the charges fairly. Swing voters react negatively to blatant partisanship in impeachment matters. History bears the names of former senators who became defined by their impeachment antics for decades.

If that is not enough disincentive, a politician should also consider the short-term. With all the open investigations on corruption, a blatantly biased senator who mocks the nation’s desire for fair play becomes an easy target. There will be little public sympathy for those who did the nation a disservice by denying it a fair arbiter in this process.

The public is not so ignorant as to be unable to discern performative lectures on impartiality — especially when it is followed by partisan conduct that leaves little to doubt. If senators mean what they say about due process, or their claims of selective enforcement by the Executive, then they must first practice the neutrality they claim to revere. – Rappler.com



John Molo teaches Constitutional Law and Appellate Advocacy. He is a founding partner of Mosveldtt Law and has handled several landmark cases before the Supreme Court.

World.title: FACT CHECK: No nationwide class suspension declared for Marcos’ 5th SONA
World.content:
Classes have been suspended only in some areas; the Quezon City and Manila LGUs announced localized class suspensions

Claim: Malacañang has declared class suspensions nationwide on July 27, 2026, for President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr’s State of the Nation Address (SONA).

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The Facebook reel bearing the claim was uploaded on July 23 by the Facebook page “Ph News Today Tv” and has garnered 309,000 views, 2,000 reactions, 50 comments, 247 shares, and 184 saves, as of writing.

Its caption reads, “Walang pasok dahil sa SONA ni BBM sa July 27 Lunes (No classes due to [Bongbong Marcos’] SONA on Monday, July 27).”

In the video, a narrator says, “Nagdeklara na ang Malacañang na walang pasok sa Lunes, July 27, para sa ika-limang SONA o State of the Nation Address ng Pangulo sa buong bansa. Pili lamang ang mga lugar na walang pasok sa buong bansa. Tingnan sa post namin ang memo gayundin ang mga lugar na walang pasok.”

(Malacañang has declared the suspension of classes on Monday, July 27, nationwide for the President’s fifth State of the Nation Address. Only specific areas across the country are covered by the suspension. See our post for the official memorandum and the list of affected areas.)

Several social media users were confused by the conflicting information, asking in the comments section whether classes have been suspended in their specific localities.





The facts: No official statements or declarations have been issued by Malacañang or the Presidential Communications Office ordering nationwide class suspensions in connection with the President’s fifth SONA.

Likewise, the Department of Education has not released any memorandum or directive declaring nationwide class suspensions for the occasion. However, some local government units, including Quezon City and the City of Manila, have announced localized class suspensions under their respective jurisdictions.

Fake content: An analysis of the circulating Facebook reel using Hive Moderation indicates that the video’s audio and speech are 99.9% AI-generated, with no indication that it is a deepfake.

Meanwhile, the shortened URL included in the reel’s caption redirects users to an online shopping site and does not contain the supposed government memorandum or official document referenced by the narrator. (READ: Phishing 101: How to spot and avoid phishing)

SONA 2026: Marcos is scheduled to deliver his fifth SONA at the Batasang Pambansa on Monday, July 27.

This is in accordance with Article VII, Section 23 of the 1987 Constitution, which states that the President shall address Congress at the opening of its regular session.

This year’s SONA comes at a critical time amid the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte and investigations into billion-peso corruption scandals that hounded the Marcos administration.

The speech and the opening of the regular session of Congress are scheduled to begin at 4 pm Manila time. (READ: Marcos’ SONA 2026: How to follow Rappler’s special coverage) – Jennifer Pading/Rappler.com

Jennifer Jezreel Kaye Pading is an economics student at Visayas State University in Baybay City in Leyte. An Aries Rufo Journalism Fellow for 2026, she is also the Executive Editor of Amaranth and community officer of AYEJ-Leyte Panaad Ha Sinirangan.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: [EDITORIAL] Ang patlang sa retoriko at realidad ni Pangulong Marcos
World.content:
Sa pagharap ni Pangulong Ferdinand Marcos Jr. sa Kamara upang i-deliver ang kanyang State of the Nation Address ngayong 2026, walang red carpet o celebrity director. Ayon sa spin ng Malacañang, ito’y magiging “simple but dignified.” Pakikiisa raw ito sa sambayanang naka-survival mode sa harap ng oil price hikes, inflation, at global instability.

Pero hindi lang payak ang entablado — payak din ang rekord. Nasaan ang optimismo tulad ng mga starter years, lalo na’t dalawang taon na lang sa puwesto si Marcos?

Kailan nagiging irrelevant o walang patutunguhan ang State of the Nation Address ng isang presidente? We might argue, sa penultimate year, o ang taon bago ang katapusan, dahil lame duck na ang presidente.

Pero may ibang panlulumo na kaakibat ngayong taon: 41 lamang ang naipasa sa 102 na pet bills ni Ginoong Marcos, kabilang na ang mga tinaguriang centerpiece legislation ng mga nakaraang taon.

Sa nakaraang taon, tila pumara ang legislative engine, na kung saan isa lamang sa 52 priority bills ang naisabatas. Maraming mga sangkap ang slowdown — kasama na ang kawalan ng estabilidad sa Senado.

Hindi na tayo magpapaligoy-ligoy pa — ito ang paglalagom namin sa nakaraaang taon: missed opportunities, institutional paralysis, at systemic erosion ng public trust.

Isang taon ang nakalipas, humarap ang Pangulo sa taumbayan at sinabing, “Mahiya naman kayo.” Siya ang nagsimula ng domino effect na dumagundong sa lahat ng sulok ng bansa dahil naging mitsa ito ng pagkakahalungkat ng engrandeng sabwatan. Sangkot sa corruption conspiracy ang mga kongresista at senador, mga ahensiya ng gobyerno tulad ng public works, at pati state auditors. Ito ang nagbuyangyang sa politicontractors — congressmen na nagmamay-ari o may interes sa contractor companies na yumayaman sa biyaya ng substandard o ghost public works.

Pero isang taon ang nakalipas, tila ampaw ang mga nagawa — maliban sa pagtugis sa nagtatagong Zaldy Co, pag-aalis sa puwesto ni Martin Romualdez bilang House speaker, at pagkakakulong ng isang senador, kahit anong timbang ang gawin, tila kulang. May senador pa ngang damay ang pangalan pero tila nakapaglalabada na ng reputasyon sa impeachment trial.

Lagpas sa mga kasong isinampa, ano ang konkretong hakbang na magbibigay ng senyales na natigil na ang pagtagas ng yaman ng national treasury dahil sa korupsiyon — na tinatantiyang umabot ng P8.8 trillion?

Sa pagsadsad ng trust rating ng Pangulo makikita ang kuwento ng credibility crisis niya. Kitang-kita ang patlang sa retoriko at realidad.

Sa pagdedeliver ng pangalawa sa huling SONA, ang hamon sa administrasyon ay patunayang humihinga pa ito at hindi naka-ICU — at kaya pang tumugon sa business ng governance.

Pinakamalaki diyan ang pagtitiyak na may mapapala ang bayan sa impeachment trial ng kanyang kalaban sa pulitikang si Vice President Sara Duterte. Isang prosesong politikal ang impeachment. Habang ang naratibo ng Malacañang ay “above the fray,” kailangan ding ipamukha ni Marcos ang kanyang liderato, lalo na ang pagpapakita na hindi niya palalampasin ang korupsiyon, hindi sa Bise Presidente, at hindi sa kaibigan at kakampi. At higit sa lahat hindi niya palalampasin ang umano’y korupsiyon ng pinsan — lalo na’t tinagurian na si Romualdez ng Ombudsman na “central figure” sa flood control corruption.

Dapat maintindihan ng Pangulo na neutrality is not a virtue, at maari pang tanawin bilang dereliction of duty.

Alam ni Marcos na hindi naman pet bills ang labanan — ang hanap ng tao’y konting dagdag na panggastos sa bulsa, hustisyang ramdam sa mga korte, at isang lider na maaasahang drayber sa matinding krisis.

Nagsasara na ang bintana ng legacy-building, Ginoong Marcos. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Rappler’s Best] Mahiya naman kayo
World.content:
SONA. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. delivers his 4th State of the Nation Address, at the House of Representatives, on July 28, 2025.

It’s been a year since the President’s remarkable SONA, where he vowed to expose and punish public officials who have enriched themselves through corrupt flood control projects. What do we have today?

Yes, it’s been a year since President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s remarkable State of the Nation Address (SONA), where he vowed to expose and punish public officials who have enriched themselves through corrupt flood control projects.

“Mga kickback, mga initiative, errata, SOP, for the boys. Kaya sa mga nakikipagsabuwatan upang kunin ang pondo ng bayan at nakawin ang kinabukasan ng ating mga mamamayan, mahiya naman kayo sa inyong kapwa Pilipino!” Marcos said in his July 28, 2025 SONA. (Kickbacks, initiatives, errata, SOP, for the boys. To those who connive to take government funds and steal the future of our people, feel some shame towards your fellow Filipinos!)

Well, what do we have today?

We have the alleged main executioner of the anomalous projects, resigned congressman Zaldy Co, sweating in a harsh European summer but nonetheless out of government’s reach, and free.

We have the “central figure” in the corruption scheme, former House speaker Martin Romualdez, a cousin of the President, ready with a battery of lawyers once the Ombudsman makes true his various pronouncements of a plunder charge to be filed against him. The Ombudsman has promised; he has yet to deliver.

We have Senator Chiz Escudero, who was ousted as Senate president last year after his top campaign donor was linked to the scandal, now sitting as the presiding officer of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

We have resigned public works secretary Manuel Bonoan — whose department and deputies connived with contractors not only for fat commissions but for taxpayers’ money to be burned in ghost projects — now a state witness because, among others (hold your breath), he can help pin down Romualdez. It bears recalling that under his watch, the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) awarded P2.5 billion worth of projects to his daughter’s business partner.

We have resigned budget secretary Amenah Pangandaman — under whose term the anomalous 2025 national budget was crafted — now appointed as chair and CEO of the state-owned Al-Amanah Islamic Investment Bank of the Philippines.

We have justice undersecretary Jose “Jojo” Cadiz Jr. — whose young son owns a company with hundred-million-peso flood control road projects with the government — still at his post even after he resigned following Rappler’s exposé in December 2025. President Marcos did not accept the resignation of his longtime aide and kababayan, who was described by Zaldy Co as the President’s “bagman.”

This is not to say that nothing has moved. In this report, James Patrick Cruz shows us where we are as far as exacting accountability is concerned.

Cases have been filed against at least 30 individuals in various courts, two dozen of them from the DPWH. The list includes the recidivists: Senator Jinggoy Estrada and former senator Bong Revilla. Read more.

Who are public officials linked to contractors? Here’s a refresher. Who has turned state witnesses? Read here.

The government has recovered only P611.379 million from individuals linked to the scandal, such as P290 million from former DPWH Undersecretary Roberto Bernardo. Check the list here.

Whose assets have been ordered frozen by the Anti-Money Laundering Council? Read more.

In any case, the President will deliver his second-to-the-last SONA today, Monday, July 27, at 4 pm. Can he follow through on his 2025 promise? Bea Cupin tells more in this story.

What has been the success rate of his legislative agenda in the last four years? Not much, based on this report. In fact, the administration found itself dropping Marcos’ own pet bills.

Watch our live coverage here.

Here are some of Rappler’s bests that you shouldn’t miss:

Jairo Bolledo reminds us that it’s not only Zaldy Co whom the Marcos administration has failed to run after. In cases outside the flood control scandal, big-named suspects have also slipped away.

Dwight de Leon writes about the shrinking influence of the President over the legislature.

Val Villanueva explains “why oil forecasts fail when war, inventories, and China rewrite the math.”

Lance Spencer Yu highlights a central bank official’s criticism of the country’s antiquated bank secrecy law in relation to the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

– Rappler.com

World.title: Why Energy Secretary Garin says Pax Silica is ‘too dangerous’ to plug into grid
World.content:
Energy Secretary Sharon Garin tells Rappler why Pax Silica will likely need its own power system if plugged into the Luzon grid

How much electricity is 3 gigawatts? Enough to give Energy Secretary Sharon Garin pause.

Pax Silica, the planned artificial intelligence, semiconductor, and advanced manufacturing hub in New Clark City, could eventually require 3,000 megawatts.

That’s about 19% of Luzon’s projected 2026 peak demand and nearly equivalent to the entire Visayas grid. It’s also close to the combined capacity of five 620-MW Bataan Nuclear Power Plants, the Philippines’ mothballed nuclear plant that never produced commercial electricity.

Or, as Garin put it: “Malaki siya. Malaki.” (It’s big. Big.)

In an exclusive interview with Rappler, Garin made clear that Pax Silica cannot simply plug its full demand into the Luzon grid without exposing households and businesses to serious risk.

“If you put it on the grid, and then suddenly this 3 gigawatt demand will be lost, the grid will just shut down,” Garin told Rappler.

‘Too dangerous for consumers’

Garin’s concern was that introducing a 3-GW load tied to one industrial area could become a problem of grid stability.

“It’s too dangerous for our usual consumers. So, there are ways to do it. But the primary concern is that we don’t destabilize the grid because that will affect other businesses and households,” she said on Friday, July 24.

To mitigate risks, the energy secretary said that the massive US-led project will likely scale up over the years rather than drawing the full 3 GW at once. In the meantime, the Luzon grid might be able to absorb the project’s early phases. (READ: Pax Silica, El Niño: Environmental issues for SONA 2026)

From 100 or 200 megawatts is still manageable. “But once it scales up, we have to provide them with their own power plant,” Garin said.

The quality of that energy supply matters as much as quantity. A data center will need “cheap power and stable power” with a quality component that demands no red and yellow alerts whatsoever.

Asked whether Pax Silica’s demand could drive up prices in the electricity spot market, Garin said she did not expect it to do so. But she urged caution, pointing to the problems other countries have encountered in their race to build out data centers.

“There are problems in other countries already,” Garin said. “So, for us to avoid that, learning from their mistakes, one is to come up with a system or technology that can cater to their needs,” she added in a mix of English and Filipino.

Her preferred solution is effectively a separate ecosystem with its own power, water, and supporting infrastructure.

“If it’s going to be bigger and bigger, I would rather have it on a stand-alone system where it has its own power plant, whether it’s renewable or gas,” she added.

Can that renewable promise even be met?

The Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) has said Pax Silica would rely on renewable energy, mainly solar. The first concrete piece is a deal with Saudi Arabia’s ACWA Power, which leased a 500-hectare site in New Clark City for a solar photovoltaic and battery storage project with a capacity of up to 500 MW.

But that is only one-sixth of Pax Silica’s projected requirement.

There’s also a proposed 1,200-MW LNG or liquefied natural gas terminal and power plant, for which the US International Development Finance Corporation has reportedly approved funding for a feasibility study.

Together, that would provide 1,700 MW on paper, still leaving a 1,300 MW gap.

And even this is generous; remember, a solar facility rated at 500 MW does not deliver 500 MW around the clock. Would the mega-investors being courted for Pax Silica really leave the fate of their data centers at the mercy of passing clouds?

The LNG proposal brings its own problems. Clark has an airport, not a seaport. LNG arrives by ship. The fuel would first have to enter through a coastal import terminal, then be transported inland, most plausibly through a new pipeline from Subic or another port. None of that infrastructure is operating yet, while the proposed power plant remains at the feasibility-study stage.

Gas also complicates BCDA’s green sales pitch. The proposed LNG plant alone would cover 40% of Pax Silica’s projected requirement. But LNG is not considered green or renewable. Unless significantly more renewable capacity is added, fossil gas could end up doing much of the heavy lifting.

Energy industry sources have been raising the same questions with Rappler. Their point is not that solar has no place in the project, but that nameplate capacity isn’t the same as round-the-clock, high-quality power. Facilities that cannot tolerate interruptions would still need substantial battery storage and likely grid support.

And best pray that Pax Silica doesn’t destablize the Luzon grid.

Still early, still talking

Asked whether Pax Silica had been planned from the beginning with a complete energy strategy, Garin told Rappler that much is still being firmed up.

“We’re still in the early stages. But we need to be more rational about it, in the sense that we need to plan properly,” she said in a mix of English and Filipino. There’s been close consultation too with the Department of Energy, Department of Information and Communications Technology, and Department of Trade and Industry.

Garin said actual locators must first make firm commitments so generation can be planned around real demand. Such commitments can justify building a power plant. This has all to be in sync, Garin added.

Power plants take time. Garin estimated three to five years for conventional facilities and around a decade for nuclear.

“Energy is one big factor,” she said, “and I’d rather do it properly.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Dy: House to focus on affordable rice, stronger UHC, more transparency
World.content:
Speaker Faustino Dy III — Photo from Faustino ‘Bojie’ Dy III/Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — For the second regular session of the 20th Congress, the House of Representatives will focus on measures that will lower rice prices, strengthen the Universal Health Care (UHC) Act, and ensure greater transparency, Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III said on Monday.

During the resumption of the session, Dy said that the House will continue working for bills that would directly respond to the needs of the people, particularly the proposed Rice Industry and Consumer Empowerment (RICE) Act, the UHC amendments, the proposed Citizen Access and Disclosure of Expenditures for National Accountability (CADENA) Act, and the proposed Cybersecurity Act.

“For our Second Regular Session, we will continue working to push for reforms that would directly respond to the daily problems of our people,” Dy said.

Article continues after this 

READ: Sona 2026: Marcos urged to restore trust in flood control probe

“Our priority is the passage of the [RICE] Act so that we can bring down the prices of rice and strengthen support to our farmers; amendments to the [UHC] Act so that health services will be of high quality and accessible; the CADENA Act to ensure that details on fund use will be open and transparent; and the Cybersecurity Act which aims to protect every Filipino from the threats of the Digital Space,” he added.

According to Dy, the House has to prove that the people can lean on them during challenging times — and one way of proving this is by working towards a better future for Filipinos.

“While our country faces different challenges, we need to continue helping the people achieve their goal of a better tomorrow. It is in challenging times like this that our people need their representatives, more than ever, to house and shelter their most important dreams,” Dy said.

“Let us prove to our people that we are a Congress that fulfills our duties. With the session opening, you can hold on to our resolve that we will continue to work hard, listen more intently, and serve with accountability,” he added.

Article continues after this 

But aside from legislature, Dy also said that progress can be attained while preserving Filipino core values, noting that the country must never lose sight it.

“However, more importantly, for our country to really move forward, we must never lose sight of what has always been our greatest strength: our Filipino core values,” Dy said.

Article continues after this 

“This is our strength, our true wealth that we have to take care of and be proud of. The biggest danger is if we allow our trait of taking care of each other to be lost. When we stop caring for our fellow Filipino,” he added.

Dy presided over the resumption of session, which started at 10 a.m. During the session, the House adopted House Resolution (HR) No. 1207, informing the Senate that the House has entered the exercise of its functions, and HR No. 1208 informing President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. that the chamber is ready to hear his fifth State of the Nation Address (Sona).

The House and the Senate will convene for a joint session at 4 p.m. to hear Marcos’ report, which comes a year after his controversial Sona speech in which he called out people who allegedly benefited from flood-control projects.

Earlier, church leaders called on Marcos to deliver truth and accountability in his Sona regarding the flood control corruption scandal.

In a statement, church leaders group ONE VOICE recalled Marcos’ revelation of the scandal during last year’s Sona, when he rebuked those who received “kickbacks” from the corruption.

The church leaders also emphasized that the government must conduct an independent investigation and prosecute every individual involved in the flood control anomalies, including “those who have the power to prevent such corruption.”

According to Palace press officer and Undersecretary Claire Castro, Marcos’ fifth Sona will last one hour and 20 minutes.

READ: Marcos’ 5th Sona to last 1 hour, 20 mins – Palace

Castro did not provide further details about the key topics to be discussed, but Marcos said last week that the public should wait for the next chapter of the government’s fight against corruption. /das

World.title: Dy calls for truth as House pushes anti-disinfo, social media bills
World.content:
House Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III. PHOTO BY NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

MANILA, Philippines — Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III on Monday warned of the growing risks of unregulated social media use amid the proliferation of false information online.

In his opening remarks to lawmakers, Dy called on Filipinos to push back against disinformation, saying its unchecked spread threatens to erode democracy.

“Let us not allow the noise of social media to shape our beliefs,” he said in Filipino. “Let us uphold truth over fake news, understanding over anger, and unity over division.”

Article continues after this 

READ: House approves anti-fake news bill on final reading

Dy also said the lower chamber had passed a bill penalizing those who circulate false information online to curb disinformation.

The House is also pushing for a bill prohibiting those under 13 from accessing digital platforms to bolster such efforts, he added.

“We are requesting that this proposal also be included in the Ledac (Legislative-Executive Development Advisory Council) priority bills so it can be enacted at the soonest possible time,” Dy said. /mcm

World.content:
Vice President Sara Duterte. Photo from Inday Sara Duterte Facebook page.

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte dispelled rumors about her resignation, stating that it is “never going to happen” as it would be a betrayal to those who voted for her.

Duterte said this amid recent speculation that she may resign as she faces an impeachment trial over allegations of confidential fund misuse, unexplained wealth and grave threat.

READ: Defense: ‘We’ve never discussed’ Sara Duterte resignation

Article continues after this 

“Never gonna happen. I will not resign because that would be a betrayal to the 32.2 million of our countrymen who voted for me,” said the vice president in a chance interview, as seen on a pro-Duterte Facebook page, Padayon and Updates.

She even addressed President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. directly, daring him to remove her from her post.

“If BBM (Bongbong Marcos) wants to, he can remove me. He can do everything to remove me,” she said.

To recall, Duterte’s defense team in the impeachment trial likewise disputed the rumors by saying that resignation has never been discussed between them and their client.

The Senate impeachment court recently concluded tackling the House prosecution’s presentation of evidence for Article IV of the articles of impeachment against Duterte. /mr

World.title: Minor behind CDO school shooting threat surrenders to police
World.content:
A minor who threatened to harass local schools in a viral video has surrendered to authorities, claiming the act was “just a joke,” as police intensify security across educational institutions in Cagayan de Oro City. INQUIRER FILES

CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY — A minor who threatened to harass local schools in a viral video has surrendered to authorities, claiming the act was “just a joke,” as police intensify security across educational institutions in the city.

The minor was voluntarily presented to a Cagayan de Oro City Police Office (COCPO) station by his guardians out of concern for his safety. He is currently undergoing investigation and assessment with his legal guardians and a Women and Children Protection Desk (WCPD) investigator, in strict compliance with child protection laws.

READ: Cops cordon CDO public school due to student’s shooting threat

Article continues after this 

COCPO director Col. Dexter Paje issued a stern warning following the incident, emphasizing that the police will pursue legal action against anyone who disrupts public order.

“Let this serve as an unequivocal reminder: statements, posts, or messages that threaten the safety, security, and peace of mind of our schools, students, and communities are never a joke,” Paje said.

“These acts carry serious legal consequences, regardless of claims that they were made for fun or just for laughs,” he added.

In a coordinated response, Paje directed Police Station 7 to lead a thorough investigation in the Bulua area.

The COCPO has also tapped the WCPD, the Department of Education (DepEd) – Division of Cagayan de Oro, and the Philippine National Police Regional Anti-Cybercrime Unit to trace online content and validate the threats.

Article continues after this 

Paje also called on parents to take responsibility for monitoring their children’s digital footprints.

“Guiding our youth means more than providing for their needs — it means staying aware of what they say, post, and do, and teaching them early that every word and action carries accountability and impact on others,” he said.

Article continues after this 

Authorities assured residents that police visibility and intelligence monitoring have been heightened across all schools.

COCPO urged the public to remain calm, report verified threats directly to police hotlines, and refrain from sharing unverified information to prevent unnecessary panic./coa

World.title: Kazakhstan’s 30-Year Education Drive: From Flagship Excellence to Nationwide Reach
World.content:
Less than two years after independence, Kazakhstan made a bet that education could not wait for the economy and institutions to catch up, it would have to lead them. On Nov. 5, 1993, the government established the Bolashak International Scholarship, sending promising young citizens to top universities abroad to become specialists in a fledgling state urgently needed economists, engineers, diplomats, administrators. Knowledge, in effect, became national infrastructure, ranked alongside new laws and new ministries.

More than 13,000 Bolashak graduates have since come home. But the sharpest test of that 30-year strategy did not happen on a foreign campus. It came in December 2023, when the OECD released the results of its 2022 PISA test, a global assessment of 15-year-olds’ skills and Kazakhstani teenagers scored below the OECD average in mathematics, reading and science alike. That gap is not a verdict on three decades of reform. It is the next milestone in the same strategy.

Betting on flagships

By the late 2000s, sending students abroad was no longer enough, Kazakhstan needed institutions at home that could operate under different rules. The Nazarbayev Intellectual Schools opened as laboratories for new curricula and assessment. In 2010, Nazarbayev University opened in Astana as an autonomous research university, and a 2011 law carved out a distinct legal framework giving both institutional autonomy and academic freedom the rest of the system did not have. That same year, Kazakhstan became the first Central Asian country to join the European Higher Education Area, aligning its degrees with the Bologna framework and opening the door to academic mobility with Europe. The strategy worked, narrowly, it let officials pilot new admissions systems, teaching methods and research practices without waiting for the whole country to move together. But it also created Kazakhstan’s central education challenge that Excellence built under exceptional conditions does not spread on its own.

Five ministers, one dilemma

The education ministry’s revolving door shows the reform agenda evolving in real time. Bakhytzhan Zhumagulov, minister from 2010 to 2013, built the new architecture. His successor, Aslan Sarinzhipov, who served until 2016, pushed university autonomy and closer ties between education and industry. Yerlan Sagadiyev, from 2016 to 2019, carried reform into ordinary classrooms, rolling out revised curricula modeled on the Intellectual Schools; by 2018, nearly three-quarters of students were learning under it. The pace showed political resolve, but also its risk that schools absorbed new curricula, assessment methods, digitalization and language policy almost simultaneously, faster than teachers could build the judgment needed to make any of it stick.

Askhat Aimagambetov, minister from 2019 to 2022, pivoted toward the people actually delivering reform. A 2019 law strengthened teachers’ legal protections, and the government launched a four-year plan to double teacher salaries. After a decade spent rewriting what teachers were expected to do, Kazakhstan finally addressed the conditions they did it under.

The scoreboard

PISA 2022 measured how much of that work remains: 50% of Kazakh students reached basic proficiency in mathematics, against a 69% OECD average; 36% in reading, against 74%; 55% in science, against 76%.

The 2022 split of the old Education and Science Ministry into schools and vocational training in one ministry, science and higher education under Sayasat Nurbek in another that closed that first reform era. In three decades, Kazakhstan built an internationally recognized scholarship brand, autonomous flagship institutions and stronger legal protections for teachers faster than it built the everyday classroom capacity to match them.

Kazakhstan is now positioning itself to become a regional higher education hub, an ambition that builds on this same lesson that carrying what already works at Nazarbayev University and the Intellectual Schools into ordinary schools far from the capital. Kazakhstan has spent 30 years proving it can build excellence. The next chapter is carrying that excellence nationwide.

The author is Saqib Raza, a PhD scholar in education and an MSc graduate in Educational Leadership in Higher Education from Nazarbayev University Graduate School of Education, Kazakhstan.

World.title: Why Almaty’s Fountains Are More Than Just Decoration
World.content:
ALMATY – For generations of Almaty residents, fountains have marked the rhythm of summer. They are meeting places, playgrounds, works of art and fragments of history hidden among the city’s trees.

Today, Almaty operates more than 120 fountains and fountain complexes, making it the undisputed fountain capital of Kazakhstan. Sixty-three belong to the municipality, while the remainder are privately owned. Unlike many cities where fountains exist primarily for decoration, in Almaty they were conceived as part of the city’s environmental infrastructure.

Nestled against the northern slopes of the Zailiysky Alatau mountains, the city experiences long, hot and relatively dry summers. The fountains, together with the famous network of mountain-fed irrigation canals known as “aryks,” were designed to cool streets, humidify the air and make public spaces more comfortable long before air conditioning became commonplace.

Before Almaty became a megapolis

For decades, guidebooks confidently stated that the city’s first fountain appeared in 1948, when ornamental fountains were constructed near the Abai Opera and Ballet Theatre. Local historian Alois Nazarov, however, challenged this widely repeated claim.

According to Nazarov, the 1948 date referred only to the first fountains constructed from durable materials – not the first fountains themselves. The earliest documented fountain connected with the region dates back even further.

According to the archival documents, in 1878, physician, botanist and explorer Albert Regel visited the summer residence of Semirechye Military Governor Gerasim Kolpakovsky near the mouth of the Butakovka River. His travel notes describe a landscaped estate complete with a pond and two fountains. Although these stood outside the city of Verny (now Almaty) and cannot truly be considered urban fountains, they remain the earliest recorded examples in the area.

One curious reminder survives in the city’s old street names. Present-day Tulebayev Street was briefly known as Fontannaya (Fountain Street) in the early twentieth century. The name had nothing to do with decorative fountains; instead, it referred to one of the city’s first wooden water pipelines, completed in 1901. Along the pipeline stood public water basins and columns where water gushed with enough force that residents likened them to fountains. True ornamental fountains would arrive only after the city assumed a new role.

Building a socialist capital

Everything changed when the capital of the Kazakh Autonomous Socialist Soviet Republic (ASSR) moved from Kyzylorda to Alma-Ata in 1929. The city suddenly found itself at the center of an ambitious urban transformation.

Government buildings, theaters, schools and apartment blocks rose rapidly across the expanding capital. Architecture embraced the functional aesthetics of Soviet constructivism, but planners also wanted the new socialist city to appear welcoming and modern.

Fountains became one of the easiest ways to soften the austere geometry of new public spaces. A historical newspaper, Socialist Almaty, from the late 1930s reveals a surprisingly vibrant fountain culture.

In the former Dzerzhinsky Children’s Park, visitors were greeted by sculptural storks pouring water from their beaks into ornamental pools. Further inside stood a fountain featuring two young pioneers, while another displayed playful dolphins.

Panfilov Park featured its own artistic compositions. One fountain depicted a mother with two children near what is now the Ascension Cathedral, while another, nicknamed “The Mushroom,” allowed visitors to sit beneath a concrete canopy before suddenly surrounding them with a curtain of water, creating what newspapers described as a refreshing summer pavilion.

Fountains also appeared in front of hospitals, cafés, factories and schools. By the end of the decade, they had become almost mandatory components of new construction.

A city discovers water

Fountains flourished in a city that constantly struggled with water shortages. Before the mid-twentieth century, Alma-Ata relied primarily on mountain streams and irrigation canals for its water supply.

The breakthrough came thanks to renowned Kazakh hydrogeologist Ufa Akhmedsafin, who identified vast underground freshwater reserves beneath the city during the 1940s. For the first time, the city possessed enough water not only for industry and households but also for ambitious landscaping projects. The expansion of the municipal water system allowed fountains to multiply across parks, boulevards and public squares.

The golden age of fountains

The real boom arrived during the 1960s and 1970s. Under Dinmukhamed Kunaev, who personally oversaw much of Alma-Ata’s development, fountains became symbols of the city’s identity. Several of today’s best-known landmarks date from this period.

Architect Mels Safin created the celebrated Zhetysu Fountain at Abai Avenue and Tulebayev Street in 1970. Seven springs cascade through granite basins, symbolizing the historic Seven Rivers region, while traditional Kazakh ornament decorates the central stele.

Safin also designed the beloved Dandelion Fountain, completed in 1978 outside today’s Kazakh National Academy of Arts. Using 168 precisely positioned nozzles, it creates an almost perfect sphere of water that shimmers like the head of a giant dandelion. The fountain has been under renovation since 2023 and reopened recently. The landmark’s appearance has remained the same, but there is now a light display.

Nearby stands another favorite Almaty fountain – Nedelka (Week). Originally envisioned with twelve arches representing the months of the year, the available space accommodated only seven. Rather than abandoning the concept, the designers embraced the new number, transforming the installation into a symbol of the seven days of the week. Its cascading streams evoke a rushing mountain river, especially when illuminated after sunset.

Perhaps the city’s most artistic fountain is the Oriental Calendar, unveiled in 1979 opposite the National Academy of Sciences. Bronze sculptures representing the twelve animals of the Turkic zodiac surround the basin, transforming an ordinary fountain into an open-air sculpture garden. The project later received recognition from the Union of Artists of the USSR as one of the finest examples of decorative park sculpture of its era.

Meanwhile, fountains appeared beside the Hotel Kazakhstan, the Kazakh Circus, the Russian Drama Theatre, and countless neighborhood parks. Historian Nazarov once described them in his notes as “not roaring dragons, but quiet companions,” places where office workers escaped the summer heat and young couples lingered long after sunset.

Forgotten survivors

Not every fountain survived the city’s rapid modernization. Some disappeared beneath new construction. Others simply fell silent as pipes rusted and infrastructure aged. Yet hidden corners of Almaty still preserve rare examples of the earliest generation.

A neglected fountain remains tucked away inside the courtyard of the Kazakh National Academy of Arts, once the site of the Government House. Another stands near the former National Museum of Books on Kunaev Street.

Though long dry, historians consider them among the oldest surviving fountains in the city and argue they deserve restoration as important examples of early Soviet landscape architecture. Today, fountains remain inseparable from Almaty’s identity. Perhaps that explains why Almaty continues adding new ones.

World.title: Kazakh President Bets on Digital Logistics to Turn Geography into Opportunity at Omsk Forum
World.content:
ASTANA — For President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, geography is becoming one of Kazakhstan’s greatest strategic advantages. Speaking at the XXII Kazakhstan-Russia Interregional Cooperation Forum on July 25 in Omsk, he said that the world’s longest continuous land border shared by Kazakhstan and Russia positions the two countries to play a leading role in shaping Eurasia’s transport and logistics architecture.

“Kazakhstan and Russia, sharing the world’s longest continuous land border, are destined to play a leading role in developing the transport and logistics architecture of the Eurasian continent. This is a key factor in our countries’ global competitiveness in today’s highly complex geopolitical environment,” Tokayev said.

That idea framed much of Tokayev’s address at the forum. While transport corridors remained at the center of discussions, he presented logistics as a broader ecosystem that is intertwined with industrial cooperation, digital technologies, air connectivity and cross-border mobility to strengthen regional integration.

For Marat Ramazanov, head of the Department of European and American Studies at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies (KazISS), Tokayev’s emphasis on logistics reflects broader changes, such as bilateral cooperation, rather than simply growing transit volumes.

“The forum’s theme reflects qualitative changes taking place in the global economy. Today, countries’ competitiveness is determined not only by production capacity but also by their ability to integrate effectively into international value chains,” Ramazanov said.

He said this year’s focus on a global logistics ecosystem reflects broader changes in the world economy, where competitiveness increasingly depends on countries’ ability to integrate into international value chains. In that context, Kazakhstan and Russia are moving beyond individual transport projects toward a more integrated model combining transport infrastructure, digital platforms, industrial cooperation, customs procedures and investment mechanisms.

Kazakhstan and Russia’s geographic position gives them objective advantages in this environment. Rather than focusing on individual transport projects, the two countries are increasingly building what Ramazanov describes as a “single logistics ecosystem” that integrates transport infrastructure, digital platforms, industrial cooperation, customs procedures and investment mechanisms.

Building a seamless logistics ecosystem

President Tokayev outlined several priorities that, in his view, could further strengthen Kazakhstan and Russia’s role as Eurasian transit hubs. Among them, he highlighted the continued development of the North-South International Transport Corridor, which links Russia with Central Asia and South Asia through Kazakhstan, as well as the Western Europe-Western China transport corridor. He also called for expanding railway capacity, modernizing border infrastructure and increasing freight volumes across existing routes.
