World.title: Victorian politics is a mess. Who on earth can you vote for in this state?
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaPolitical leadership Opinion Victorian politics is a mess. Who on earth can you vote for in this state? Michael Bachelard Senior writer, The Age July 27, 2026 — 2:12pm

July 27, 2026 — 2:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Whether or not Jacinta Allan emerges victorious from the leadership spasm now racking her party, we Victorians will confront a serious question: who the hell can we vote for in four months’ time? Under Allan’s leadership, Labor has overseen malfeasance of extraordinary proportions – direct links between ministerial offices and the CFMEU, and from there to standover men, bikies, and an estimated $15 billion in excess costs to the taxpayer. Victorian Premier Jacinta Allan’s leadership is under threat. Penny Stephens Thanks primarily to reporting in The Age, everyone can see this steaming pile of scandal looming over Allan, no matter how hard she denies its existence. The proudest boast of the Andrews government – that it built things – is now hopelessly tainted by corruption. Allan wants to “grind it out”, defying calls for a royal commission that she says will not bring about cultural change. Add another trailer-load to the heap, Jacinta. You don’t want a royal commission because either you know what it will dig up and it will implicate your government, or you don’t know, and what’s buried there terrifies you.



Meanwhile, this government has become so paranoid and centrally controlled that ministers are rarely let out to speak, and when they are, it’s with talking points crafted so narrowly by the premier’s private office that they end up saying nothing. If Allan wins this leadership bout, or stares down her opponents, only the most rusted-on true believer could vote Labor in November, and even if she is replaced by her deputy, Ben Carroll, serious questions remain about the party that’s led us since 2014. Leader in waiting? Education Minister Ben Carroll earlier this month. Ruby Alexander Only the immediate announcement of a royal commission with full powers and the opening of public hearings into the Big Build scandal before the election could, possibly, allow us to take another look. Any other inquiry held under this state’s usual modus operandi (“trust us and shut up”) will fall short. Allan’s proposed solution of a crime commission is of this kind. Our current so-called anti-corruption commission, IBAC, shows why.



Eight years ago, in 2018, it launched a probe into a suspicious deal made between the firefighters’ union and Daniel Andrews. Andrews was interviewed, but in private – not for the only time during his premiership. Nothing of his evidence, or that of the man he allegedly did the deal with, union secretary Peter Marshall, has emerged publicly. Operating under weak laws and a statewide culture of secrecy, IBAC took four years to reach its conclusions, and another four years fighting to release them. Eight years after voters could have benefited from a public airing of these allegations, we are still waiting to know what Labor did in our name. Meanwhile we re-elected them, in a landslide, and in ignorance. Operation Richmond centred on dealings between Daniel Andrews’ government and the United Firefighters Union under Peter Marshall. Marija Ercegovac IBAC is a Potemkin village of an anti-corruption commission – it looks like one at a glance but behind the facade there’s nothing. For the $100 billion Big Build, this is not good enough. Only a credible royal commissioner with the power to demand documents, compel witnesses and air it all in public can do the Herculean work of mucking out Labor’s Augean stable.





The last time Victoria rejected Labor, we picked Ted Baillieu as premier. He served for a brief, indolent and scandal-plagued term (anyone remember MP Geoff Shaw?) before being replaced by Denis Napthine. Related Article Exclusive

Building Bad Allan’s wrong: Top crime fighters insist royal commission only solution Their two main achievements in government were to legislate for a hollowed-out anti-corruption commission and allow Labor time to reset and appoint Daniel Andrews as leader. This year there is a third choice – of sorts – One Nation, and 22 per cent of Victorians seem to be making it, according to The Age’s Resolve poll. It’s a party with no state leader, no candidates and who knows what policies except for “I don’t like it.” Jess Wilson and Jacinta Allan are effectively campaigning against an empty chair and ceding more than one-fifth of the primary vote to it. Allan’s approval rating is minus 42, her likeability minus 36.



How have her party’s once-powerful factions tolerated it for so long? This is shaping as a classic pox-on–both-your-houses election. But if the pox kills off all our genuine governing options, then what kind of zombies will be left holding power for the next four years? That is what causes me to wake up in fright. Michael Bachelard is a senior writer. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Which district spends the most on water, which has the most leaks?
World.content:
A new report has revealed New Zealand's worst and best performing regions when it comes to water management.

This includes which councils were losing the most water through leaks - and the much-maligned Wellington Water barely scrapes into the top 10, with others losing far more - keeping in mind the date range excludes the failure of the Moa Point wastewater treatment plant.

Billed as the first national picture of public drinking and waste water network environmental performance, the report from the Water Services Authority - Taumata Arowai warns of "immense" and "severe" pressures across the country.

WSA head of systems, strategy and performance Sara McFall says with councils' new Local Water Done Well organisations starting up and the Commerce Commission set to oversee pricing, New Zealand is now at an "inflection point" for water.

The report also provides data on council performance on key measures of water management, with a series of charts in the second appendix.

RNZ has reproduced charts showing the best- and worst-performing councils or regions in each category, along with explanations of what is being measured.

As well as the various councils and council-controlled organisations, the report also covers three government organisations (Ministry of Education as the manager of schools; Department of Conservation; and Corrections) as well as the Defence Force.

Note: Statistics for Auckland and Watercare are reported separately, and some councils did not submit data that met the WSA's quality thresholds for measuring their performance. All measurements are for the 2024/25 financial year ending 30 June 2025. Note also that this means the Moa Pt failure in February 2026 is not covered.

Total usage per connection

This category measures how much water is provided across each council's networks, per connection - which is often a household, but can also include farms, businesses and the like.

This measure of total usage includes water provided to homes through taps and toilets, combined with any losses through pipe leaks.

"It is effectively the water entering the distribution network after treatment and before end use," a WSA spokesperson said.

Leaks by volume: Current annual real loss

This category is a measure of how much water is lost from the network through things like leakage, pipe bursts, reservoir overflows etc.

"CARL is usually not measured directly. It is typically calculated using information about water supplied to the network, customer consumption, and other information," WSA said.

Residential usage

This category shows how much each connection used on average (excluding losses).

However, the Water Services Authority warns the data in this category are not entirely reliable - particularly considering it suggests every household in Westland uses nearly 4000 litres of water every day.

"Although reporting coverage increased substantially in 2024/25, without commenting on the specifics of this case, there are still concerns about the accuracy of some reported water consumption values - and in some places mixed rural and household use may be a factor," WSA said.

"So, while the figure does indicate approximately 3929 litres per residential connection per day based on the data submitted (in Westland), it should be interpreted with some caution and may reflect local network characteristics or data limitations rather than actual household consumption alone."

Wastewater overflows as a proportion of network size

This category shows how many overflow events are recorded per 100km of wastewater pipe in the network, and is the first time the Water Services Authority has reported on it.

Note that unlike the above categories, this is shown according to the number of overflows, rather than volumes of water.

Councils have been grouped together where they record the same number, so that both Palmerston North and Ōtorohanga count as the 10th-equal highest, and the six councils with three overflows per 100km count as the 10th-equal lowest number of overflows.

This gives totals of 11 and 13 councils respectively.

Drinking water - spending

This category shows how much is being spent on drinking and wastewater systems per person in the 2024/25 financial year.

World.title: National rules out working with Opportunity Party
World.content:
National has ruled out working with the Opportunity Party, with leader Christopher Luxon saying National would not do business with a party that wants to raise taxes.

Opportunity's leader says New Zealanders are tired of that way of thinking, and suspected Luxon would change his tune if National needed Opportunity come November.

Opportunity was on 4.7 percent in the latest RNZ-Reid Research poll, just shy of the 5 percent needed to enter Parliament.

The party has been open to working with both National and Labour, should either need its support to form a government after the election.

Opportunity's flagship policies include establishing a universal basic income of up to $370 a week, and a 1.75 percent annual tax on the value or urban land and 0.5 percent on rural land.

At his weekly post-Cabinet media conference, Luxon was asked whether National could work with Opportunity.

"We wouldn't be in business with people who want to increase taxes," Luxon responded.

He added that it was his "very, very strong position" that National would not work with Opportunity.

"It's a vote for Labour and the Greens because essentially, at the moment, and I look at their policies, you've got a universal basic income that wants to make every New Zealander a beneficiary. You've got a land tax sitting there that actually is going to be massive."

Pressed on whether that meant National would not go into a governing arrangement with Opportunity in any form, Luxon said it would not be a surprise that National did not want to "do business" with Opportunity.

Afterwards, Luxon's office confirmed to RNZ this amounted to a formal rule-out.

Opportunity was on 4.7 percent in July's RNZ-Reid Research poll. Supplied / Facebook/ Opportunity Party

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong said the rule-in, rule-out game was "the old school way" of doing politics, which New Zealanders were tiring of.

"The tribalism is not taking us anywhere, and it's not solving our big issues. So we've really got to start leaving ideology at the door, and looking at the policies and the ideas that are going to take New Zealand forward."

Wong said Opportunity's door would remain open for National, but she encouraged the party to engage with its policies constructively.

"Our tax policy overall actually would be a tax cut for 70 percent of New Zealanders. They would be better off under our full tax policy. 20 percent would be about neutral, and then only 10 percent would be paying slightly more," she said.

"The fact that we are offering a tax cut to hardworking New Zealanders, many people who rent, that is something that the National Party has campaigned on in the past, and I would think would be open to. So I would encourage them to look a bit deeper and come and have a conversation with us about it."

Labour's campaign chair Kieran McAnulty suspected Luxon had ruled Opportunity out by accident.

"I think they themselves are surprised by the decision that the prime minister has announced today," he said.

McAnulty said Labour would announce who it would and would not work with "very shortly".

Labour is yet to make a call on New Zealand First, despite New Zealand First ruling Labour out.

World.title: Sinkhole appears in Auckland street damaged in 2023's floods
World.content:
A large sinkhole has opened up on a street in Auckland's St Mary's Bay.

The area, in a dip in the road on Hackett Street, was badly damaged in the 2023 Auckland anniversary weekend floods and has been covered by a steel plate since then.

Local residents say the hole emerged on Thursday, after which some reported losing water for several hours.

The hole is approximately five metres long, three metres wide and over a metre deep in parts.

Nick Monro

A steady stream of water can be seen running through the hole beneath the street.

St Mary's Bay man Tony Skelton said he was concerned about ageing infrastructure that lay beneath the hole.

"All the infrastructure here is 126 year-old clay pipes," he said.

Tony Skelton. Nick Monro

"If there is further damage, that could undermine our properties and could cause considerable problems."

He was particularly concerned about what would happen after the next downpour.

"The next heavy rain event, we don't know what's going to happen."

Nick Monro

Water contractors were onsite on Monday, investigating what caused the section of road to collapse.

Watercare's chief operations officer said Hackett Street was closed at the site of the hole but residents could still access their properties.

World.title: New Zealander caught as last of three Tonga prison escapees recaptured
World.content:
After nearly a week on the run, a New Zealander who escaped jail in Tonga last week with two others, has been caught, the last of the three to be returned to custody.

Nine days ago, the three males escaped custody at the Central Police Station in Nuku'alofa.

Police say Liuaki Kokohu Vi, a 35-year-old New Zealand citizen of Tongan descent, was detained on Saturday alongside a 41 year-old Tongan man, who is alleged to have been an accomplice who harboured and assisted Vi.

A 16-year-old on remand for theft, Angelico Fa'aoa, was the first recaptured, in Mataika last Tuesday.

The second, Adam Hussein, a 35-year-old Fijian national, was caught last Thursday.

Police had offered TP$5000 (approx. NZ$3400) for information leading to each of the last two arrests.

Tonga's Police Commissioner Geoff Turner warned that anyone assisting escapees could face up to 10 years in jail, while harbouring them carries up to three years.

There is no confirmation as to if the TP$5000 was claimed regarding either Hussein or Vi's recapture.

World.title: Fuel support for families being reconsidered, PM says
World.content:
The government will get advice on Wednesday that will inform whether or not to keep the support for families affected by the fuel crisis.

But Finance Minister Nicola Willis said that does not mean the support will end, and she was keeping an eye on international fuel prices.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and Willis briefed media at their regular post-Cabinet briefing on Monday afternoon.

Watch the briefing:

The news comes after Luxon announced on Sunday that National will extend paid parental leave to 30 weeks if re-elected into government. The party would also make it so parents could take their leave at the same time if they wanted to.

Labour earlier criticised the party over the parental leave policy, pointing to National having blocked an extension to paid parental leave in 2016, and saying cuts to Best Start payments, reduced funding for school lunches, and restarting pay equity negotiations had made things harder for young families. But Luxon said he was focused on the future - not what happened before he was in politics.

Future of fuel crisis support being considered

Since April, 143,000 families have been able to receive support through the in-work tax credit.

The support will cease after twelve months, or until the price of 91 petrol drops below $3 a litre for four consecutive weeks.

Prices dipped below $3 in late June, but on Monday morning fuel monitoring website Gaspy reported petrol prices had returned to an average of $3 exactly.

Finance minister Nicola Willis said she had received three weeks of official data, and would get data for the fourth week on Wednesday.

"We anticipate that will show fuel prices below $3 for the week previous, which will trigger me to take advice to Cabinet on what we do with the scheme going forward," she said.

"However, officials have advised me that, given the significant increase in international fuel prices in the past few weeks, they are anticipating that the fuel price in future weeks will have spiked up above $3 again."

Willis said Cabinet would consider whether it was appropriate to remove the support, given the lower fuel prices could be a "welcome blip" rather than sustained.

Prime minister Christopher Luxon said all parties in the coalition were aware of the "potential yo-yo effect" of the conflict, and he expected they would be pragmatic about what the advice said before making a decision.

Willis and Luxon also announced more than 97,500 families had received FamilyBoost payments.

Of those, Willis said 6566 families were receiving the maximum payment of $120 a week.

The scheme, a flagship campaign policy from National in 2023, refunds up to 40 percent of early childhood education costs.

It was reviewed in 2025 after it was revealed just 249 families had consistently claimed the full amount, well short of the 21,000 initially estimated.

Since July 2025, the proportion of early childhood fees people can claim back increased from 25 percent to 40 percent.

The amount families could earn per year to be eligible was also increased, from $180,000 per year, to $229,000.

World.title: Pacific news in brief for 27 July
World.content:
Solomon Islands

There are fears that a landslide at Gold Ridge Mine in the Solomon Islands may have claimed lives.

Gold Ridge Mining Limited today released a statement confirming that an incident occurred at the mine site in the early hours of this morning, 27 July.

The company said no injuries, fatalities, or equipment damage have been confirmed, and that mining and construction activities continue without disruption.

Earlier, In-depth Solomons reported that up to ten people may have been buried as a result of the ground collapse at the mine.

The Solomon Islands Police Force have been approached for comment.

Kiribati

The Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the Kiribati government have signed an agreement for an US$11 million grant for health.

The ADB said the signing marks a major step toward completion of the new Betio Hospital, and strengthening health services for communities in South Tarawa and the outer islands.

The hospital is set to be completed and operational by the end of the second quarter of 2028.

Fiji

The Fiji High Court has granted a permanent stay on criminal proceedings against British and Fijian national Charlie Charters.

Charters had been charged with two counts of aiding and abetting.

fijivillage.com reports that in his ruling on Friday, (24 July), Justice Pita Bulamainaivalu found the anti-corruption commission had violated Mr Charters' constitutional rights and abused the court process.

Justice Bulamainaivalu gave the commission 30 days to appeal.

Fiji

China says its defence cooperation with Fiji is not aimed at excluding other countries.

FBC reports Chinese Embassy Defence Attaché Zhang Yu saying China is committed to working alongside Fiji's existing security partners.

He said China-Fiji defence and security cooperation is never meant to shut anyone out.

Zhang said China stands ready to work alongside all of Fiji's defence partners in joint efforts in boosting the Fiji military's operational readiness.

He said also includes tackling climate change and maritime security threats, and countering transnational organised crime such as drug trafficking.

More than 40 officers from Fiji's Ministry of Defence and the military reportedly participated in exchange programmes in China over the past year.

Vanuatu/New Zealand

It is Vanuatu Bislama Language Week in Aotearoa New Zealand.

The theme translates to: "Talk about climate change - it is real, and we must look after life".

Around 300,000 people speak more than 100 indigenous languages across more than 80 islands in Vanuatu. This gives Vanuatu one of the highest numbers of languages per capita anywhere in the world.

In the country itself, English and French are official languages, while Bislama is the national language and the most widely spoken.

American Samoa

American Samoa's congresswoman has spoken out against what she calls mischaracterisations of her position on seabed mining.

Aumua Amata Coleman Radewagen's comment comes after the United States government proposed a series of deep-sea mining leases in American Samoan waters.

Aumua reiterated firm opposition to seabed mining in American Samoa, and warned that others in the US political space have tried to mischaracterise her stance.

Aumua said she is confident the people of American Samoa support her call against seabed mining.

Bougainville

A two-week specialist eye outreach programme is underway at Buka General Hospital in Bougainville.

The programme, led by doctors from Papua New Guinea provinces of Western Highlands and East New Britain, offers eye screening, consultations and cataract surgery.

Health extension officer and ophthalmologist Tracey Riaman told NBC Bougainville the outreach is life-changing, giving patients a second chance of sight.

The programme runs until 31 July, with more than 200 patients already registered.

Solomon Islands

Prime Minister Matthew Wale has opted out of a six percent payrise given to all MPs in the country by the parliamentary entitlements commission this month.

This has been widely criticised as it comes only two years after MPs received massive pay rises of between 37 and 39 percent just before the election in 2024.

In comparison, public servants last year only received a pay rise of 3.5 percent.

In a statement from Tokyo where he was on a state visit last week, Wale criticised the commission's decision saying the realities facing Solomon Islands citizens must remain at the forefront of any decision-making process.

Wale said he was committed to undertaking constitutional reform to replace the current parliamentary entitlements framework with a more comprehensive and equitable mechanism.

He said this will involve the establishment of a Higher Salaries Commission, mandated to determine the remuneration of all public sector employees, not just MPs.

Vanuatu

Vanuatu's former speaker of parliament Seoule Simeon is among 13 detainees granted a presidential pardon by President Nikenike Vurobaravu.

VBTC reported Simeon was convicted last year and sentenced to two years in prison for unlawfully taking a state-owned vehicle.

The State Office confirmed other pardoned individuals included people with serious medical conditions and those who were already out on parole.

It said the latter group were pardonned to clear their records and improve their prospects of securing employment.

New Caledonia

The French government is launching phase two of its US$2.3 billion (CFP240 billion) investment programme in New Caledonia.

It said it has approved 50 projects worth a total of US$100 million.

The funding will support transport infrastructure, water and sanitation networks, disaster resilience, tourism and new economic activity.

Paris said grant recipients must start work as soon as possible, and no later than the end of 2026.

World.title: Thames Four Square owner forced migrant workers to pay $120,000 to secure jobs
World.content:
A Thames Four Square and its owner has been ordered to pay $44,000 in penalties after making two migrant workers pay $120,000 to secure their jobs.

The Employment Relations Authority (ERA) ordered the company, A Dharni Enterprises Ltd, trading as Four Square Martina, to pay a penalty of $32,000.

The company's director, Jaswinder Singh, has been ordered to pay a penalty of $12,000. The workers will each receive $1000 of the penalty paid by the company.

The ERA found Singh had used the workers' money to pay their wages.

But the arrangement didn't last long.

The two workers only worked for the Four Square briefly because Singh felt they had misrepresented their ability to speak English.

Singh repaid the workers their money when the Labour Inspectorate became involved, earlier on.

Northern Labour Inspectorate investigations manager Katriona Ikenasio said the workers paid to get their jobs after being promised the possibility of a better life in New Zealand.

World.title: Timeline: the deadly Mount Maunganui landslide, the inquiry and the long road to reopening
World.content:
Tauranga is on alert after three more slips at the site of a deadly landslide that claimed six lives in January.

The latest slips occurred at the weekend, taking place over a 48-hour period.

Experts were assessing the site on Monday after Tauranga City Council warned of a "major regression" at the site of January's deadly slips.

Here's a timeline of Mount Maunganui's deadly landslide:

Three further slips at Mauao, Mount Maunganui during weekend Morning Report Download MP3 6m

January 2026

Six people died after a landslide at Beachside Holiday Park in Mount Maunganui, Tauranga, on Thursday, 22 January.

As heavy rain brought widespread flooding to the North Island - and some regions saw their wettest days on record - the landslide in Mount Maunganui hit campervans, tents, vehicles and an ablution block near the Mount Hot Pools at 9:30am.

Half a dozen people were quickly confirmed to be unaccounted for. Rescue efforts commenced, with emergency services painstakingly searching through the slip layer by layer.

Two days later, those efforts at Mauao transitioned into a recovery operation, and the victims' identities were confirmed by police.

They were Lisa Anne Maclennan, 50, from Morrinsville; Måns Loke Bernhardsson, 20, from Sweden; Jacqualine Suzanne Wheeler, 71, from Rotorua; Susan Doreen Knowles, 71, from Ngongotaha; Sharon Maccanico, 15, from Auckland; and Max Furse-Kee, 15, from Auckland.

The six victims of the Mt Maunganui landslide - Måns Loke Bernhardsson, 20, Lisa Maclennan, 50, Susan Knowles, 71, Sharon Maccanico, 15, Max Furse-Kee, 15, and Jacqualine Wheeler, 71. Supplied

As the community reeled from the news, the Tauranga community held a vigil on the Sunday after the deadly slip to remember those who lost their lives.

Another two people were killed when a landslide struck a property on Welcome Bay Road in Pāpāmoa.

On 27 January, police identified those victims as 10-year-old Austen Keith Richardson and his grandmother, 71-year-old Yao Fang.

February 2026

A few weeks after the deadly landslide, the government confirmed it was launching an inquiry into the events leading up to the disaster.

Geotechnical engineers continued to carry out assessments in the area, with the council confirming that a number of closures would remain in place.

At the time, they told media that the Pilot Bay boat ramp would be closed for the foreseeable future, and a red building placard was issued for Mount Maunganui Surf Club.

An automated alarm system was installed at the site of the campground, which would sound if there were further slips, and shipping containers were put in place to prevent any potential movement of debris.

Near the end of the month Tauranga mayor Mahé Drysdale said he remained confident Mauao would reopen despite the extensive damage to the landmark.

Tributes to victims of the landslide earlier in the year. RNZ/Nick Monro

March 2026

On 17 March, Emergency Management and Recovery Associate Minister Chris Penk confirmed the inquiry was moving forward, with Cabinet agreeing on the Terms of Reference and membership for a government inquiry.

"The Inquiry will establish how the fatal landslides occurred, report on whether relevant agencies took appropriate steps to manage any apparent risk in the period immediately prior to the two fatal landslides - including steps to warn and evacuate people likely to be affected by the landslides - and identify any lessons that can be applied to reduce the risk of similar tragedies in future," he said in a statement at the time.

"Those responsible for the Inquiry will be required to communicate with the families of the victims about its progress. It is my expectation that this engagement will be conducted with respect and sensitivity, and that the work will proceed as efficiently as possible," he said.

The inquiry would begin considering evidence and information on 30 March, and be required to deliver a final report with recommendations by 3 December, 2026.

Mauao remained closed.

Closures remained in place for extended periods following the January landslide. RNZ/Angie Skerrett

April 2026

In mid-April, Mount Maunganui Ratepayers, Residents and Retailers Association president Michael O'Neill accused the city council of excluding residents from plans to fix and reopen Mauao.

He said officials had "shut the doors to us as locals" and protests were possible unless things improved.

The local business association also said council engagement had been limited, with little collaboration and information, despite offers to help.

On 20 April, Tauranga City Council and the Mauao Trust released a statement confirming their continued commitment to restoring public access to Mauao.

Reopening Mauao would be staged and evidence-based, they announced, guided by geotechnical advice and joint decision-making through the partnership between Mauao Trust and Tauranga City Council.

They noted that the maunga remained a high hazard environment, with 42 identified landslides, including 12 classified as severe. Ongoing instability and the potential for further slips meant access still could not be restored.

On 30 April, almost 100 days since the landslide that killed six people, the council hosted a community meeting to update locals on progress with efforts to reopen Mauao.

Accommodation manager Gail Fagan welcomed the council's engagement with the public, telling RNZ that businesses were hurting.

"A lot of businesses are down 50 percent or even more because people aren't coming to the Mount... so the last few months have been extremely frustrating for most of us," she said at the time.

Local businesses have struggled in the wake of the disaster. Jason Dorday

May 2026

At that community meeting, Tauranga's mayor confirmed restoration works at Mauao would begin early in May.

Halfway through the month, additional monitoring of the main landslide area was set up.

The council also debated building a $215,000 temporary bund to replace the shipping containers used as a landslide barrier.

June 2026

In June, Tauranga City Council extended the deadline for its external review into the landslide by a month.

A statement said: "While the Terms of Reference originally anticipated the report would be completed by 30 June, that timeframe has been extended until the end of July by [retired High Court Judge Hon Paul Davison] to allow sufficient time for all relevant information to be sourced and carefully considered."

Mayor Mahé Drysdale said he supported the delay.

"We know people want answers, and we remain committed to being open and transparent as this external review process continues," the mayor said in the statement.

Tauranga Mayor Mahé Drysdale Hayden Woodward

July 2026

Near the end of July, disaster struck again at the site of the landslide that claimed six lives.

Three new slips occurred, forcing officials to close a road at the base of the mountain.

The council released a statement on 26 July: "We have seen a major regression at the site of the original landslide. The regression extends approximately 20 metres with a run out of approximately 100 metres. While it has not extended as far as the original run out, the material is saturated, mobile and fluid."

"We are currently unable to confirm if the closure of Adams Avenue will be lifted on Monday, 27 July 2026. Geotechnical assessments are ongoing and a further update will be provided when more information is available.

World.title: Sydney shark attack hero wins world paddleboarding championship
World.content:
A volunteer lifeguard who helped save a woman attacked by a shark on a Sydney beach has won the world paddleboarding championship amid hurricane conditions.

Charlie Verco competed in the 27th Moloka'i 2 O'ahu Paddleboard World Championships in Hawaii on Sunday.

Almost 100 participants from around the world paddleboarded a 52-kilometre stretch of open ocean from Moloka'i to O'ahu in the central Pacific.

It included crossing the Kaiwi Channel, known as the "Channel of Bones", which is home to sharks, jellyfish and other marine life.

The organisers described it as being "widely regarded as the sport's ultimate open-ocean endurance challenge", testing paddlers' skills, endurance and ocean knowledge.

The 24-year-old from Sydney won the event for the fourth time, finishing in 4 hours, 18 minutes and 3 seconds, breaking the world record.

The elite paddleboarder walked out of the water on foot smiling after finishing the race. (Supplied: Moloka'i 2 O'ahu Paddleboard World Championships)

"I'm so stoked, it's so incredible. I've never felt so good in body and mind after the race and it's extra special that I was able to set a record at the same time," he said in a post-race interview.

"I've put years and years of work into it, training two to three time a day, six days a week."

Verco, who regularly trains in the northern beaches and Sydney's east, was training when he helped save shark attack survivor Leah Stewart at Coogee Beach in June.

"It has definitely helped remind me that the ocean is something you have to respect," he said.

Shark attack victim update The 34-year-old's brother said she was awake, speaking with loved ones and her medical team and "remembers the whole event in detail".

" I'm hoping Leah is doing alright and I feel incredibly grateful that I get to have an experience like this in the ocean. "

Hurricane conditions

Verco had to navigate through "really big swells" and "strong winds" caused by category one Hurricane Fausto, which was heading towards the Hawaiian Islands.

Throughout the week, organisers had been monitoring the hurricane forecasts from the Central Pacific Hurricane Center in coordination with the United States Coast Guard and local emergency management partners.

"I think with the cyclone we were a little worried about impacting, but it managed to stay far enough away that there was just good wind behind us," Verco said.

Supporting him along the way in the escort boat was his brother and his father, Jamie Verco, who said the beginning of the race was "quiet".

Mr Verco was supported by his father and brother in the escort boat. (Supplied: Moloka'i 2 O'ahu Paddleboard World Championships)

"The swell wasn't lining up with the wind at all and you have to be very patient not to burn a lot of energy trying to chase the swell that would take you in the wrong direction," he said.

"Through the middle of the channel he started to speed up and by the end he was really flying.

" About an hour and a half out he said he'd have a crack at the record and his brother just said, 'Yeah, go for it'. "

The paddleboarder's mother and sister were watching from home.

Jamie Verco said he was "so proud" of his son.

"He's worked so hard and he's a humble kid who's put in the hard yards and does all the work and he's got the rewards today," he said.

"He's been quietly pleased with himself, I think."

Race organisers said more than 35 Australians competed in the prone paddleboard competition with Verco, with 38-year-old Stewart Mclachlan coming in second and 28-year-old Stone Harrison in third.

Verco said this year's focus was to not "get ahead of himself".

"My goal was just to have fun with it. It was the same attitude I had throughout all my training, is not to be so stressed out."

World.title: Quick hits: Wiggles star's daughter shines, netball 'cleaner' goes viral
World.content:
Two Aussie besties share a podium, a hometown hero fights his way to the final, and a very famous face wiggles his way into the stands.

Here are the quick hits from day three of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Cleaning up never looked so good

Every major sporting event has its surprise star.

Sometimes it's an underdog athlete. Sometimes it's a mascot. And sometimes it's a cleaner with a mop and a sense of rhythm.

A short clip from the Commonwealth Games netball venue has captured exactly why sport is about more than the result.

Loading Instagram content

A cleaner who danced as he mopped the court has become an unexpected crowd-pleaser on social media.

The routine, which was done to I Want To Break Free by Queen, had it all: the splits, the worm and twerking. If there were judges, he would have scored 10 out of 10.

Was the "cleaner" just a dancer with a mop employed to entertain the crowd?

That's for you to judge. Either way, he brought a lot of joy to people in the stadium.

2. Brilliant besties prove the power of friendship is real

With a medal each to their names, attention turned to Aussies Gemma Sellick and Victoria Belando Nicholson as they stepped up to be interviewed after the women's 100m backstroke S9 event.

But the pair had eyes only for each other, their friendship taking centre stage as they gushed about sharing a podium.

"This is my best friend," Sellick said, grinning ear to ear, a question from the media suddenly feeling rather inconsequential.

"This was not even a thought I had; I was not expecting this at all," Belando Nicholson told the ABC.

"To do it with my best friend is actually insane."

As they headed to pick up their medals, the pair were already planning a "debrief later tonight" to celebrate their silver and bronze medals.

3. Silver is sweet for Canada's Dolci after epic gymnastics comeback

The Arena in Glasgow was the venue for one of the maddest competitions at the Games so far: the men's all-around final at the artistic gymnastics.

At the end of the day, Flower of Scotland was on full blast (followed by the latest rendition of The Proclaimers' 500 Miles) as Reuben Ward became the first Scots gymnast to win the competition in Commonwealth Games history.

Jesse Moore also flew the flag, so to speak, as he became the latest Australian gymnastic medal-winner at these Games with a bronze, coming after he had to withdraw halfway through the Games four years ago with a shoulder injury.

But with respect, both these performances were left in the dramatic shadows by the competition of Canada's Felix Dolci.

Felix Dolci was down in 17th place in the men's all-around gymnastics final after falling off the pommel horse twice, before the Canadian made a miraculous recovery. (Getty I,mages: Francois Nel)

The men's all-around features all six disciplines: vault, rings, pommel horse, parallel bars, horizontal bars and floor exercise. Gymnasts are split into groups doing the six in different orders, maximising the drama.

Dolci was in a decent spot when he went on the pommel horse, but everything went pear-shaped as he fell off, twice. He ended up 17th out of 18 competitors after two rounds.

Game over, right? Wrong. A score of 14.200 on the vault, followed by 13.950 on the parallel bars, left him in with a vague hope.

And then he delivered on the horizontal bars, absolutely nailing his landing and scoring a whopping 14.500 to finish with the silver medal. Amazing stuff.

4. Hometown hero Goodburn not done yet

The men's 50m breaststroke is a fairly stacked event, with English legend Adam Ramsay-Peaty, Australia's Sam Williamson and South African speedster Michael Houlie all in the field.

But if you look beyond the very top times, you find Scottish swimmer Archie Goodburn.

The Edinburgh-born Goodburn was the British champion in 50 breaststroke in 2023, and had a chance of going to the Paris Olympics. But then he was diagnosed with three inoperable brain cancers in early 2024.

He was in the eighth and final heat on day three, up against Williamson.

Archie Goodburn of Scotland during the men's 50m breaststroke semifinals in Glasgow yesterday. (Getty: Rob Casey)

The 50m breaststroke is not quite the same "splash-and-dash" as the 50 freestyle, but it's not slow.

Williamson surged through to win in 26.75, with South Africa's Chris Smith second, and Goodburn made the home fans happy coming through for third.

He backed it up in the semifinal to squeeze into the final tomorrow morning (AEST) in lane one.

Regardless of his eventual placing, you could argue that no-one is flying the Saltire higher at these Games than Goodburn.

5. The Red Wiggle watches daughter star in wheelchair basketball

The Red Wiggle was wearing green and gold in support of daughter Georgia Munro-Cook. (ABC)

The Australian women's wheelchair basketball team notched its first win of the Games on day three, downing South Africa 20-5.

Georgia Munro-Cook was the star for the green and gold, finishing with 10 points in a dominant performance.

Watching on in Glasgow was her father, Murray, who, despite not sporting his famous red skivvy, will be a familiar face to many Australians.

The Red Wiggle was as proud as punch after his daughter's performance.

"She's worked so hard, the whole team has worked so hard, to see them get a win like that is just really exciting," he told ABC Sport.

Munro-Cook was over the Moon to have her mum and dad in the crowd, and said it was an interesting role reversal for the family.

"I think it's so funny, I used to go around watching him on stage, and now he's here watching me," she said.

World.title: Mayo wins All-Ireland title, ending 75-year 'curse'
World.content:
In one of the greatest upsets in Gaelic football history, Mayo has beaten Kerry in the All-Ireland football final in Dublin to break a 75-year title drought and end what some people call "the Mayo curse".

Whether the curse was hokum, a story or a real psychological issue that had simply bedevilled generations of Mayo footballers, the victory by 1-20 (23 points) to 1-17 (20 points) at Croke Park immediately drew a line under three quarters of a century of heartbreak and became one of the biggest headlines in Gaelic games history.

And one of the stars of the unlikely victory is a footballer who many think could be a generational talent although he has only just finished school, and is headed to the AFL.

The story goes that after beating Meath at Croke Park in the 1951 All-Ireland final, a jubilant Mayo team travelled home to the western province of Connacht on the back of a truck, celebrating the whole way.

While passing through the village of Foxford though, the players passed by a funeral that was taking place.

The local priest apparently took a dim view of the players continuing to celebrate while the funeral was taking place, placing a "curse" on the county, that it would not win the title again until all the team that played that day had died.

Mayo's 70-year wait goes on amid All-Ireland 'curse' Sporting curse or psychological barrier? Whatever it is, Mayo's All-Ireland Gaelic football title drought reaches 70 years after another final of blown chances against Tyrone at Croke Park.

After 1951, it took the Mayo senior team 38 years to return to the All-Ireland final. In total, before this year, it had played in 11 All-Ireland finals since 1951 and lost them all.

In 2016, Mayo conceded two own goals against Dublin, forcing a draw and a replay, which it lost.

The last of these finals, in 2021, came a few weeks before the final playing member of the original team, Paddy Prendergast, died aged 95.

The team did not make it back to Croke Park for the All-Ireland final until Sunday's decider against defending champions Kerry, who were trying to extend their record by winning a 40th All-Ireland crown.

So this year was the first opportunity to win the biggest game of the season since the elements of the "curse" had been met.

Things did not start well, with Kerry superstar forward David Clifford burying a shot in the net in the 15th minute.

But Mayo fought back to be a point down at half-time, 1-8 (11) to 0-10 (10).

Manager Andy Moran had backed young talent, with 18-year-old Kobe McDonald and 19-year-old Darragh Beirne key to the team's success.

McDonald, who was selected by St Kilda late last year as a Category B rookie and is expected to head Down Under shortly to join the team, would score three points in the final

Beirne's brilliant finish scored Mayo's only goal that sparked the county's run to victory.

Rollercoaster ride to All-Ireland title for Mayo

It had not been an auspicious start to the football season for Mayo, as it was beaten by 10 points by Roscommon in the Connacht provincial championship. The team in red and green was all but written off for the All-Ireland.

Andy Moran (right) got stuck into the media for laughing at long-suffering fans' celebrations. (Getty Images: Sportsfile/Ramsey Cardy)

It entered the All-Ireland Championship series still looking shaky, beating Monaghan by a point before a single-point loss to Tyrone left it on its final chance.

Mayo bounced back with a win over Meath to reach the quarter-finals, then downed Cork at Croke Park to make the last four.

The semi-final turned out to be a one-sided affair against Louth, with Mayo winning by 17 points. But the run was expected to end against Kerry. The questions started after the semi, with Moran asked if fans would lose the run of themselves celebrating given the county's horror record in finals.

Moran hit back hard.

"You laugh at that, lads. I don't laugh at that," Moran said at the press conference.

"I find it very, actually, dismissive, if I'm being honest. I think it's a bullshit question. I think it's a disrespectful question.

"Our county has been starved the last four or five years. If they [fans] go a bit nuts, let them."

He then set his sights on the football reporters present.

"You're going to go to a game tomorrow. Every single one of ye, you're going to write that Kerry or Dublin will go to win the All-Ireland final, right? Right?

"Does anyone here think we're going to win the All-Ireland final? No. Thank you."

Kobe McDonald has just finished school, but the Mayo young gun now has an All-Ireland medal and is set to come to the AFL. (Getty Images: Sportsfile/David Fitzgerald)

When the final siren went on Sunday, it set off emotional scenes at Croke Park among the 80,000-plus crowd.

The Saw Doctors' hit The Green and Red of Mayo, written by a group of Galway musicians about what Mayo means to the people, blasted out of the speakers at the stadium as joy mixed with disbelief for the fans.

After the game, McDonald, like his teammates, was elated and he was trying to focus on the now, rather than what's next.

"Look, to be honest I'm not thinking about Australia right now. I'm just going to soak in every minute of this. To give the people of Mayo something to celebrate, it's special," he told Irish broadcaster RTE.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I know every team probably says it but we're like a family. When we're in training three days a week it's like 40 brothers.

"We know every single person in there has each other's back and whatever is being said outside the group doesn't affect us."

Gaelic games, football and hurling, are amateur sports, and there has been plenty of debate over the years about the loss of talent to the AFL.

The rest of Mayo, and quite possibly the rest of Irish Gaelic games, hopes that McDonald stays with Mayo and doesn't take his skills to Australia.

But whatever happens from here, McDonald and the rest of the team have written their names in Irish sporting history and moved their county forever beyond the ghosts of losses past.

A huge crowd of Mayo supporters travelled to Dublin and were overjoyed after their team's shock win. (Getty Images: Sportsfile/David Fitzgerald)

World.title: Scottish-blooded Anderson thrilled to win gold in Glasgow instead of Victoria
World.content:
There are a lot of Australians bemoaning the 2026 Commonwealth Games being held in Glasgow instead of regional Victoria, but don't make the mistake of thinking Iona Anderson is one of them.

Anderson emerged as Australia's biggest backstroke star of these Games when undisputed queen Kaylee McKeown withdrew due to glandular fever.

In the 200m, she finished sixth, over two seconds slower than the time she swam at the Australian trials in June.

But in the 100m, she touched first and it could not have been a better place for her first individual gold medal at a senior meet, storming past Canadian veteran and nine-time Commonwealth medallist Kylie Masse.

360 moment for Vicky Belando Nicholson Victoria Belando Nicholson was a baby when she was pulled lifeless from the water after falling from a refugee boat. Now she's a swimming bronze medallist for Australia.

Anderson got it done in the home of her forebears, if not herself, welcoming the controversial late change to the Scottish capital.

"Personally, for me, I think Glasgow's better than Victoria. Sorry," she laughed.

"I love the Scottish. I've got quite a few friends here and obviously my family. So it was great to come back here and do it."

Basically her entire family is from Scotland, Grangemouth on her mum's side and Dumfries and Galloway on her dad's.

Anderson was even named after the small island of Iona off the west coast of the country.

As she took her victory lap, the 20-year-old found her grandma Pam, who had been riding every drop of water displaced by Anderson's furious charge home.

"She was pretty emotional, there wasn't many words," she said.

"She's just really happy and stoked for me. She's always messaging me and always giving me good luck wishes, so that was really special to see her after the race."

The victory was comfortably the tightest of the night by any of the Australian swimmers as the Dolphins took home five more golds and 14 medals in total.

Cam McEvoy completed the full set of 50m freestyle titles by adding Commonwealth gold to Olympic and world titles, baton bearer Tim Hodge enjoyed another moment in the sun with gold in the 100m backstroke S9, Kai Taylor swam a glorious final leg to win the men's 4x200m relay, and Lani Pallister romped home in the women's 1,500m final for her second gold of the Games with the 200m and 800m to come.

Her victory gap of almost 18 seconds was 299 times bigger than Anderson's 0.06 margin over Masse.

A teenage Iona Anderson finished fifth as Kaylee McKeown completed the third leg of her double-double in Paris. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

"I kept my blinders on so I'm really happy I got my hand on the wall," Anderson said.

"I could see some splashes, but to be honest, I closed my eyes at the end and hoped for the best."

The difficulty for Anderson is the spectre of McKeown.

The 25-year-old's double-double – winning the 100m and 200m backstroke at successive Olympics – has raised the bar for how greatness is defined in that discipline for the entire swimming world.

Perhaps that is why Anderson's distant finish in the longer race did not stay with her too long.

"I know I'm capable of more in the 200m but I've got to take away the positive that that's my third best swim ever," she said.

"I really just picked myself up and moved on."

World.title: AFL confirms State of Origin future with Victoria left out of 2027 game
World.content:
The AFL has confirmed the future of State of Origin, with Western Australia to host South Australia in 2027.

South Australia will then host Victoria in 2028 at Adelaide Oval, before Victoria and Western Australia meet again in Perth in 2029.

The State of Origin concept returned to the AFL in 2026, with Victoria beating Western Australia at a sold out Perth Stadium.

South Australia and Western Australia last played each other in 1998 at Football Park, with South Australia winning by 36 points in front of 18,000 fans.

AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon said the success of Origin's return earlier this year showed the event could go on to get bigger and better.

Trent Rivers of Western Australia kicks the ball during this year's AFL Origin match at Perth Stadium. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

"No one really knew what the game was going to be like, and what we saw was actually footy at its finest, the ball moved around … it was a quick game, lots of scoring, so I think what we'll see is there'll be a different build-up for the players," he said.

"State football is one of the great traditions of our game, and we are pleased to see it continue in 2027 and beyond after the huge success of its return earlier this year which saw more than 58,000 people fill [Perth] Stadium in Perth.

Andrew Dillon says the success of February's WA-Victoria clash shows the concept has a future. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)



"Origin inspires passion, state pride and draws upon decades of rivalries that are central to the history of our game and our greatest players." "Origin inspires passion, state pride and draws upon decades of rivalries that are central to the history of our game and our greatest players."

"Locking in the structure for the next three years provides fans, clubs, players and stakeholders certainty on Origin, allowing them to embrace the state rivalry and celebrate our great game."

WA ready to resume SA rivalry

WA Origin chair of selectors and former player Glen Jakovich said the state had a similarly strong rivalry with South Australia as there was with Victoria.

"Same reason, they think they're better than us," Jakovich said.

"The South Australians, they don't leave the welcome mat out for you, so I've got to return the favour.

"I've got up to six or seven months to start planning the demise of South Australia."

West Coast Eagles great Glen Jakovich is parochial when it comes to State of Origin football. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Jakovich said this year's clash with Victoria had showed just how much it meant to the players to represent their states.

"Led by Patrick Cripps … at his age, two Brownlow Medals, achieved a lot in football, and he put it right up there as one of the pinnacles of his career," he said.

"He led the state with such great honour, so I look forward to that happening again. It's a great privilege."

Political football

WA Premier Roger Cook has challenged his South Australian counterpart Peter Malinauskas to a bet on the outcome of next year's game.

"I reckon the loser needs to provide a carton of quality beer from their state to the other, so I'm very much looking forward to getting a carton … from Mali any day after the match," he said.

Roger Cook wants to put a friendly wager on the outcome of the game. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

No other states have been marked to play in the Origin series, with the Allies concept — Tasmania, New South Wales, Queensland, ACT, and Northern Territory merged together — last used in 1998.

New South Wales joined with ACT and Queensland joined with the Northern Territory in 1993, with Tasmania fielding a standalone team.

World.title: 'Don't know how I do it': Pogačar claims fifth Tour de France title
World.content:
Tadej Pogačar confirmed his status as one of cycling's all-time greats after winning a record-equalling fifth Tour de France title in emphatic style.

Daring mountain attacks from deep, multiple stage wins and an ice-cool temperament all helped the 27-year-old Slovenian seal his victory overnight. He joined Belgian Eddy Merckx, Spaniard Miguel Indurain and Frenchmen Jacques Anquetil and Bernard Hinault as the only riders to win five Tours.

"I'm speechless. It's an incredible day, there was an incredible atmosphere," Pogačar said.

"I've ridden seven Tours already, and I've always finished on the podium. You might think this is a fairytale, it's incredible for me too."

After competing strongly in the 21st and exciting final stage in Paris, Pogačar finished 6 minutes, 26 seconds ahead of Belgian rider Remco Evenepoel in the overall standings.

Two-time Tour champion Jonas Vingegaard was Pogačar's main rival heading into the race, but the Dane crashed out on the 15th stage.

"Shame that Jonas and others crashed out of this Tour," Pogačar said.

"I hope we can all fight again next year."

Pogačar's UAE Team Emirates XRG teammate Isaac Del Toro, a 22-year-old Mexican making his Tour debut, was third at 9:42 back from Pogačar, who smiled and held up his hand to signify his wins. His teammates then joined him as they stood proudly on the Champs-Élysées.

"I don't know how I do it," Pogačar said. "I now have to find a new goal to chase. Which goal? Let's just not jump ahead of ourselves, and enjoy this moment."

Pogačar won the Giro d'Italia in 2024 but has not won the Spanish Vuelta, which starts on August 22.

"Will I be at La Vuelta in a few weeks?" he said. "Let's see."

Pogačar won five stages at this year's race to take his impressive tally to 26 overall.

He tried to win overnight too, but victory ultimately went to Dutchman Mathieu van der Poel, who just held off the chasing pack on the home straight for his second stage win at this year's race and fourth overall.

The 88.7km stage looped around Paris and was mostly processional, although less so than in previous years, which were usually entirely flat stages for sprinters and not for the rest of the peloton.

The stage was shortened from 133km, and its starting point in Thoiry, west of the capital, was changed to Paris to reduce pressure on emergency services combating wildfires in the south-west. Some security forces initially mobilised for Paris were redeployed to help response efforts.

For the second straight year the stage featured the hugely popular uphill climb through the Montmartre district, a sharp 1km dash which riders tackled three times before finishing on the Champs-Élysées.

It proved even too much for Pogačar, who could not match Van der Poel's raw power in the closing stages.

Shortly before 6pm local time, Pogačarshook hands at the start line with Evenepoel and Ecuadorian veteran Richard Carapaz, wearing the polka-dot jersey for the best climber.

"I battled hard to win this jersey, it was a great fight," the 33-year-old Carapaz said. "It's the best feeling to win it."

Van der Poel and Dane Mads Pedersen, the green jersey winner as best sprinter, were among the expected contenders for the stage win.

Crowds roared as the riders began the first climb up Rue Lepic in Montmartre, with the famed Sacré-Coeur basilica looming over them.

Pogačar moved ahead after the second ascension of Montmartre, with Van der Poel, Evenepoel and Pedersen alongside him.

Van der Poel attacked on the third and final climb with Pogačar responding well, and the one-day classics rivals surged ahead.

But they were caught with 700 meters left and, after Pogačar faded, the 31-year-old Van der Poel still had work to do.

He got his bike just over the line ahead of Belgian Jasper Philipsen, his Alpecin-Premier Tech teammate, and Pedersen. Pogačar eased up and finished 30th.

"I thought the sprinters would catch us up, so I launched [my attack] from very far away," Van der Poel said. "I gave everything I had left in my legs, and it was just enough."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.
